10182e77cf4259d9: PETALING JAYA: Education minister Fadhlina Sidek has questioned why politicians continued to be personally involved in distributing school aid under a Johor scheme even after the state assembly was dissolved for fresh elections.

Fadhlina said the Bantuan Kasih Johor had reportedly created difficulties for older people who had to stand in long queues and wait for hours to receive assistance. Their problems should not be overlooked, she said, as government aid should ease the public's burden, not create further hardship, Bernama reported.

In a series of social media posts, Fadhlina responded to remarks by Johor menteri besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi at the state assembly yesterday comparing the education ministry’s Early Schooling Assistance programme and Johor's in-person cash aid distribution method.
She said the two schemes had different purposes and rationales, and Onn Hafiz should not cite the ministry scheme to justify Johor's means of distribution, which reportedly inconvenienced the public.
She said the ministry scheme follows the school calendar and allows parents and teachers to meet face to face, rather than having them meet the prime minister, ministers or other politicians.
“We want parents to leave school with more than just RM200 in their hands. We want them to have a better understanding of their children's development,” she said.

Fadhlina also called for serious attention to be paid to the 2025 findings of the Programme for International Student Assessment which showed that just 34% of Malaysian pupils discussed school-related problems with their parents or guardians at least once a week, compared with 46% in 2022. “This decline needs to be taken seriously,” she said.

Fadhlina said the country now faces various education challenges, including student discipline and mental health issues, which cannot be left to teachers alone and require active parental involvement.
0cb532a174dbb2a5: NOTTINGHAM: Chelsea suffered an embarrassing 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest on Friday as Morgan Gibbs-White's double piled pressure on beleaguered Blues boss Xabi Alonso.
Alonso's side crashed to a fourth defeat in their last five Premier League matches after another laboured performance at the City Ground.
Igor Jesus's early opener set the tone for Chelsea's dispiriting evening by the banks of the River Trent.
Gibbs-White's second half penalty increased Forest's lead and Emmanuel Emegha's quick reply proved a false dawn for Chelsea.
Gibbs-White struck again and Emegha's second goal came too late for ashen-faced Alonso as the reality of Chelsea's plight sank in.
After last weekend's dismal 4-1 home loss to Leeds, Chelsea's tame surrender was the last thing Alonso needed as he struggles in his first season in charge.
Chelsea are languishing in eighth place after a sixth defeat in their 12 league games under Alonso, a position that is likely to get even worse after the rest of the weekend's fixtures.
Chelsea's third successive defeat will inevitably trigger speculation that Alonso is in danger of being sacked after a miserable start to his first spell as a Premier League manager.

The absence of injured Brazilian striker Joao Pedro has stalled Chelsea's previously powerful attack, while their error-prone defence has already shipped 23 league goals after allowing lowly Forest to run riot.
Failure to beat bottom of the table Crystal Palace on Wednesday would turn the heat up even further on the former Real Madrid and Bayer Leverkusen boss.
Admitting his team needed "strong characters and big personalities", Alonso handed starts to vastly experienced duo Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck.
But Chelsea's grizzled veterans could do nothing to stop Forest taking the lead in eye-catching style in the fifth minute.
Daniel Munoz's cross arrowed towards Jesus 12 yards from goal and the Brazilian unleashed a blistering volley that flashed into the top corner as Chelsea keeper Emiliano Martinez grasped at thin air.
Chelsea struggled to respond to that blow and even when they had a rare sight of goal, Morgan Rogers blazed wildly over.
Despite having Levi Colwill available, Alonso opted to start Ecuador midfielder Moises Caicedo at centre-back in a move that backfired badly.

Intriguingly, Wesley Fofana featured for Chelsea after apologising for a controversial YouTube interview in which the defender joked about his penalty miss in a League Cup shoot-out defeat against Liverpool this season.
The Chelsea fans packed into one end of the City Ground weren't as forgiving as Alonso, subjecting Fofana to jeers whenever he touched the ball.
The Blues were desperately short of intensity and rhythm, mustering just three touches in the Forest area in the first half, so Alonso sent on Emegha for Welbeck at the interval.
But the striker's introduction ignored the holes in Chelsea's porous defence and their situation grew more desperate in the 51st minute.
Fofana's approval rating with Chelsea supporters plunged even lower as he carelessly bundled over former Blues striker Liam Delap to concede a penalty that Gibbs-White dispatched with ease.
Fofana was hauled off to save him from any further opprobrium.
Emegha reduced the deficit three minutes later, firing into the bottom corner after Pedro Neto's effort deflected to him 10 yards from goal.
Alonso's men tried to rally, appealing in vain for a penalty after Jair Cunha's arm made contact with the ball.
But Forest delivered the knockout blow in the 72nd minute.
Xaver Schlager floated a pin-point pass behind the flat-footed Chelsea defence and Gibbs-White made a perfectly-timed run to clip a composed shot past Martinez from close-range.
Emegha's 89th minute strike gave the scoreline a more flattering look than Chelsea deserved for a moribund performance.
cb2aff909e3919b2: PARIS: Paris FC missed the opportunity to join capital rivals Paris Saint-Germain at the top of Ligue 1 as they lost 1-0 at Brest on Friday, with Luck Zogbe's solitary goal instead firing the Brittany side into the Champions League places.

Liam Rosenior's Paris FC, backed by the billionaire Arnault family, have big ambitions and knew a fourth consecutive Ligue 1 win would allow them to go level with neighbours PSG at the top of the standings.

But their winning streak came to an end as Egil Selvik performed heroics in the Brest goal, allowing the home side — who had to deal with the tragic death of coach Eric Roy during the close season — to claim a fourth victory on the bounce and rise to the giddy heights of third.
"Four clean sheets in a row and we defend like hell, so it's a great feeling," goalkeeper Selvik told broadcaster Ligue 1+.
"We can be proud but we still have to continue the work. It's a long season but we are happy."

Paris FC therefore remain three points behind Luis Enrique's PSG, who can extend their advantage at the top with a win at home to Lorient on Saturday. Brest climb above Lille, Lyon and Marseille and are two points behind Paris FC.

Brest went ahead midway through the first half when a Ludovic Ajorque effort came back off the post and the ball rebounded out to Zogbe, the young Ivorian full-back converting for his first senior goal.
Selvik then saved superbly to keep out a header from Ligue 1's leading scorer Lassine Sinayoko, the first of eight remarkable saves made on the night by the Norwegian international goalkeeper.
He denied Sinayoko again at the start of the second half, with Rudy Matondo hitting the follow-up off the crossbar.
Selvik, signed in the close season from English second-tier outfit Watford, intervened time and again to frustrate the visitors, keeping a fourth straight clean sheet.

The last time Brest won four successive Ligue 1 matches was three years ago under Roy, during the 2023/24 season, when they finished third to qualify for the Champions League for the first time in their history.

fb80548ea30ef61f: NOTTINGHAM: Chelsea suffered an embarrassing 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest on Friday as Morgan Gibbs-White's double piled pressure on beleaguered Blues boss Xabi Alonso.
Alonso's side slumped to a fourth defeat in their last five Premier League matches after another laboured performance at the City Ground.
Igor Jesus's early opener set the tone for Chelsea's dispiriting evening by the banks of the River Trent.
Gibbs-White's second-half penalty increased Forest's lead, while Emmanuel Emegha's quick reply proved a false dawn for Chelsea.
Gibbs-White struck again and Emegha's second goal came too late for ashen-faced Alonso as the reality of Chelsea's plight sank in.
After last weekend's dismal 4-1 home loss to Leeds, Chelsea's tame surrender was the last thing Alonso needed as he struggles in his first season in charge.
Chelsea are languishing in eighth place after a sixth defeat in their 12 league games under Alonso, a position that is likely to worsen after the rest of the weekend's fixtures.
Chelsea's third successive defeat will inevitably trigger speculation that Alonso is in danger of being sacked after a miserable start to his first spell as a Premier League manager.

The absence of injured Brazilian striker Joao Pedro has stalled Chelsea's previously potent attack, while their error-prone defence has already conceded 23 league goals after allowing lowly Forest to run riot.
Failure to beat bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace on Wednesday would turn the heat up further on the former Real Madrid and Bayer Leverkusen boss.
Admitting his team needed "strong characters and big personalities", Alonso handed starts to vastly experienced duo Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck.
But Chelsea's grizzled veterans could do nothing to stop Forest taking the lead in eye-catching style in the fifth minute.
FOFANA JEERS

Daniel Munoz's cross arrowed towards Jesus 12 yards from goal and the Brazilian unleashed a blistering volley that flashed into the top corner as Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez grasped at thin air.
Chelsea struggled to respond to that blow and, even when they had a rare sight of goal, Morgan Rogers blazed wildly over.
Despite having Levi Colwill available, Alonso opted to start Ecuador midfielder Moises Caicedo at centre-back in a move that backfired badly.

Intriguingly, Wesley Fofana featured for Chelsea after apologising for a controversial YouTube interview in which the defender joked about his penalty miss in a League Cup shoot-out defeat against Liverpool this season.
The Chelsea fans packed into one end of the City Ground were not as forgiving as Alonso, subjecting Fofana to jeers whenever he touched the ball.
The Blues were desperately short of intensity and rhythm, managing just three touches in the Forest area in the first half, so Alonso sent on Emegha for Welbeck at the interval.
But the striker's introduction did nothing to address the holes in Chelsea's porous defence, and their situation grew more desperate in the 51st minute.
Fofana's standing with Chelsea supporters plunged even lower as he carelessly bundled over former Blues striker Liam Delap to concede a penalty that Gibbs-White dispatched with ease.
Fofana was hauled off to spare him further criticism.
Emegha reduced the deficit three minutes later, firing into the bottom corner after Pedro Neto's effort deflected to him 10 yards from goal.
Alonso's men tried to rally, appealing in vain for a penalty after Jair Cunha's arm made contact with the ball.
But Forest delivered the knockout blow in the 72nd minute.
Xaver Schlager floated a pinpoint pass behind the flat-footed Chelsea defence and Gibbs-White made a perfectly timed run to clip a composed shot past Martinez from close range.
Emegha's 89th-minute strike gave the scoreline a more flattering look than Chelsea deserved for a moribund performance.

3de113bb2194bf4d: NEW YORK: Wall Street's main indexes ended higher on Friday and posted weekly gains as investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday and flocked to hard-hit AI-linked shares.
US stocks have swung sharply this week, with Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO and Anthropic's brief fall below its initial public offering price adding to volatility across the AI trade.
Investors have alternated between bargain-hunting after a steep selloff and fretting over soaring AI costs, heavy borrowing and doubts about companies' returns on investment.
"The market is so oversold that a bounce was inevitable," said Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group.

Chipmakers that investors battered this month recovered ground, with Micron and Marvell gaining 7.6% and 7.3% respectively. The broader chip gauge also climbed 4.7%. Nvidia, after remaining weak for most of the session, ended 0.8% higher.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to 50,774.94, the S&P 500 gained 114.71 points, or 1.60%, to 7,297.49 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 543.70 points, or 2.31%, to 24,129.50.
AI beneficiaries, including data-storage firm Sandisk, surged almost 16%, while optical-products maker Lumentum and server maker Dell also gained sharply.
AI hyperscalers — tech companies that run large data centers — also rose, with Amazon.com, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Oracle posting gains. Tesla surged 5%.

"There is a bounce in technology which started Monday, continued Wednesday with an intraday reversal and now continues today," said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.
For the week, the S&P 500 gained 5.6%, the Nasdaq rose 6.68%, and the Dow climbed 5.46%. The S&P 500 weekly gain was the index's biggest since April 2025.
The S&P 500 bank index rose 1.6%, fueled by JPMorgan Chase's almost 2% gain.

The market's gains have done little to erase November's losses. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq are on track for their worst November since 2008, pressured by concerns over tougher AI regulation following the Democrats' US midterm election victory and expectations that monetary policy will remain restrictive.

Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December after data this week showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated further in October.
Gold and silver miners rallied as precious-metal prices recovered from a bruising few sessions. Newmont gained 5.4%, while the Global X Silver Miners also advanced.
Vertex Pharmaceuticals slid 5.2% after the US Food and Drug Administration extended its review of the company's kidney-disease drug by up to three months.
US equity markets were open for a half-day session on Friday, following Thursday's Thanksgiving holiday.
Volume on US exchanges was 10.97 billion shares.
Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.25-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 55 new highs and 73 new lows on the NYSE.
On the Nasdaq, 3,677 stocks rose and 1,135 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.24-to-1 ratio.
The S&P 500 posted 12 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 96 new lows.

ef1cb3f577436b94: BENGALURU: OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices, after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple's employment practices were designed to "trap" employees and prevent them from working on competitors' technology.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf," the company said in its Friday court filing.

OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by re-hiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI's roadmap for future hardware products.
"Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place," OpenAI said.
Apple and OpenAI did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology.

Earlier this year, Apple sued OpenAI and former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner's foray into consumer hardware. Tan, a 24-year Apple employee who was a vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch, was part of the group that launched io Products before it was acquired by OpenAI in 2025.

OpenAI and the employees have denied those allegations, and said that Apple's lawsuit depended on its unauthorized monitoring of Liu's personal messagesafter he stopped working for Apple. Attorneys for Tan and Liu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In Friday's filing, OpenAI criticized Apple for encouraging employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for new jobs.

OpenAI said that Apple continues to access former employees' personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to "monitor and ensnare departing employees" when they leave for competitors.
OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

b9dea758e0f37914: BOLOGNA: Italy will have to win a deciding doubles rubber for the second time this week to keep their hopes of a fourth successive Davis Cup title alive after the Czech Republic's Jiri Lehecka beat Flavio Cobolli to level the semi-final at 1-1 on Friday.
Lorenzo Musetti had put Italy ahead with an assured 6-3 6-4 defeat of Jakub Mensik in the opening singles but Cobolli came up short despite loud home support in Bologna.
The world number seven lost 6-2 1-6 6-3 to Lehecka, who produced a rock-solid deciding set to keep his side alive.
Lehecka used his powerful forehand and serving to great effect in the opening set to dominate, but Cobolli flipped the match on its head as he found his range in set two.
It looked as though the Italian had the momentum heading into the decider, but Lehecka had other ideas and seized control with some thunderous baseline hitting.
Cobolli did have a chance to break back when trailing 4-2 but missed an attempted backhand pass and Lehecka calmly claimed his second victory of the week.
Italy captain Filippo Volandri opted to send out Musetti alongside Andrea Vavassori to face the Czech pairing of Lehecka and Tomas Machac in the deciding doubles rubber.
Doubles specialist Vavassori partnered Matteo Berrettini to the decisive doubles win against South Korea on Wednesday.
The Czechs are bidding to reach the final for the first time since 2013 when they won the title for the second year in a row.
Musetti, who returned to Davis Cup action for the first time since 2024 this week, looked in great shape against Mensik with a single break of serve in each set enough for his win.
The second semi-final takes place on Saturday when Spain face Britain.

b92af50bb8bbb74f: DOHA: Kimi Antonelli was fastest under the floodlights in both Qatar Grand Prix practice sessions on Friday in a dominant Mercedes one-two with George Russell.

The 20-year-old newly-crowned Formula One world champion lapped the Lusail circuit with a best time of one minute 23.217 seconds in the first session on the medium tyre, with Russell 0.507 slower on softs, and then delivered a best effort of 1:23.077 in a twice red-flagged FP2.
Russell, then on mediums, closed the gap to 0.127 in the later practice that ended with the top 10 places filled by five teams in two-by-two formation.

The McLarens of 2025 world champion Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were third and fourth, with Norris 0.445 off Antonelli's time, Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar fifth and sixth and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton seventh and eighth.
Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10, with the session ending with a virtual safety car after Hamilton stopped on track with a loss of power.
"It was a productive day," said Antonelli, who predicted a tight battle with Russell and the others always a threat by the time it comes to qualifying.

Norris was not so sure about that: "I don't think we're too bad relative to most but to Mercedes, they're a little bit further off so they just seem in a different category compared to us today," he said.
"Quicker in every single corner by a mile, so I would say the battle's for P3 ... I would say we're around six, seven tenths off the Mercedes a lap. So it's not even worth thinking about them."
Verstappen said it had been a difficult day with the car's balance "too disconnected" to go fast.
Both titles have already been won by Mercedes, with Antonelli the youngest ever champion.
Hadjar was third fastest in the opening practice for the penultimate round of the campaign with Norris fourth, one hundredth of a second quicker than Piastri in fifth.
"The Mercedes are hugely fast, Antonelli looks to be in a class of his own," Alpine's managing director Steve Nielsen told Sky Sports television.

Verstappen, winner of three of four Qatar Grands Prix to date, was sixth fastest in FP1 and 0.916 slower than Antonelli. Leclerc and Hamilton were seventh and eighth, with Lindblad ninth and Alpine's Pierre Gasly 10th.
"Did other people have degradation? Because mine is massive," asked Hamilton over the team radio. "Yes, we confirm much higher than expected on all compounds," came the reply.
Pirelli have prepared for that tyre wear, with teams limited to 27 laps per set and the race sure to be at least a two-stopper.

Hadjar had an anxious moment when he was cleared to leave the pits with a mechanic still busy with the rear left tyre. The mechanic jumped away and was unhurt, although there was contact with the wheel according to the incident report.

Stewards fined Red Bull 30,000 euros (US$33,000) with 20,000 suspended. Red Bull explained that a new team member had placed a blower to cool the car's left rear brakes, which was not a normal procedure. The car then started to leave with part of the blower still in place.
Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Williams' Carlos Sainz almost collided in the second session while Hamilton and Verstappen also had a close call.
The second session was extended by 13 minutes after Leclerc, who missed 20 minutes of track action as Ferrari changed the car's floor, spun and shed debris on track and Gasly got stuck in the gravel.
e23c60dddfceb63c: ISLAMABAD: The Mecca defence alliance nations of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey on Friday denounced continued attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels in the region and vowed to strengthen ties.

"The three sides reiterated their strong condemnation of the persistent and heinous attacks by the Houthi militia, targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," Pakistan's foreign minister Ishaq Dar said at the conclusion of the meeting.
He added the three nations "reaffirmed their collective resolve to continue and intensify efforts to support the Kingdom in safeguarding its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity".

"The parties reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in defence industries, joint technological development, training, and capacity building," Dar added.

a3c2df64e8bf674e: Human rights groups reiterated that to get true justice in Myanmar, the junta rule must end
Originally published on Global Voices
Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh. Photo by CAPTAIN RAJU. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on November 19 that Myanmar’s military forces committed genocide against the Rohingya people during a brutal 2017 crackdown in the western Rakhine state.

Voting 9–6, the ICJ verdict found the military’s “clearance operations,” which led to the mass murder of at least 10,000 people and the forced expulsion of more than 700,000 Rohingya to the neighboring country of Bangladesh, constituted genocidal acts.

Myanmar has more than one hundred ethnic groups but refuses to recognize the Rohingya, who are considered illegal immigrants even though they were born in Myanmar, and many have been there for generations. The Rohingya have been viciously persecuted for decades and targeted by hate speech and violent acts not just by state forces but also by hardline Buddhist nationalists.
It was The Gambia, with the support of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, that initiated the ICJ complaint in November 2019.

This is the first time the ICJ has found a state liable for committing genocide. The Myanmar military government, which grabbed power in a February 2021 coup, described the decision as unfair and a “great disappointment” while pointing out that the verdict was not unanimous.
The National Unity Government of Myanmar, which represents the pro-democracy forces, said in a statement that the pursuit of justice cannot be realized without ending the junta rule.

“The ICJ judgment is an important step in the pursuit of justice, but it cannot be the end. Lasting peace requires accountability, protection for all communities and the dismantling of the structures that enable persecution and impunity.”

The ICJ ruling was eagerly awaited, especially by Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. In one interview, 58-year-old Monajat Alam from one of the refugee camps shared, “The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied. Today, the truth has been recognized.”
Here’s the reaction in a Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh to the International Court of Justice ruling that Myanmar committed the crime of genocide https://t.co/OUxhAg5qBn
— Elaine Pearson (@PearsonElaine) November 19, 2026
Shwe Maung, a former Member of Parliament in Myanmar, emphasized that unity and national reconciliation cannot be achieved without recognizing the need to attain justice for the Rohingya.

As a former Member of Myanmar’s Parliament representing Buthidaung Township, I have long maintained that justice for the Rohingya and justice for the wider population of Myanmar are not competing causes.
They are inseparable.
Myanmar cannot build genuine federal democracy, national reconciliation, or lasting peace while denying grave crimes committed against one of its communities.
The Karen National Union, which represents the Karen ethnic community, reiterated the call to hold the Myanmar military accountable.

“The same Myanmar military that committed genocide against the Rohingya continues to commit atrocities against civilian communities across Burma. We must keep working together to bring justice to all the people of Burma who have suffered these crimes.”

The UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, Kelley E. Currie, hailed the ICJ ruling. “Today the world court has called the crimes by their true name: genocide. That name matters. It is a recognition of what was done, and it puts us on the path to justice.”

The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar highlighted the call to sustain the verdict with decisive action. “Justice has been decided, but not yet delivered,” said Yanghee Lee, a founding member of the council.
Rohingya refugees, Burmese people react to ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling

Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh express “immense happiness and emotion” after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the minority group. https://t.co/rEQowEqYDZ
— AFP News Agency (@AFP) November 23, 2026
Human rights activist Razia Sultana, who testified about the horrific violence endured by Rohingya women, asserted the urgency of ending the atrocities committed by the junta.
For the women who shared their testimonies with me, justice cannot remain only a judgment written on paper.
It must mean safety, recognition, accountability and the opportunity to rebuild their lives.
I think again of the women I met in the refugee camps, of what they described and the courage it took to speak.
Their voices travelled from the camps to the United Nations Security Council and became part of the wider international struggle for justice.
Thinzar Shunlei Yi shared the impact of the ruling on pro-democracy activists like her.
This verdict brings a sense of healing for me, too. It feels as though one of the chronic diseases Myanmar suffer has finally been named.
Having faced oppression myself as a woman and a political dissident, I know the scale of their suffering is incomparable—yet so many of us desperately needed to see that justice is possible.
Journalist Nyein Chan Aye is concerned over the recent rise of social media posts inciting hate against the Rohingya.

Rohingya civilians are not the enemies of Rakhine Buddhists, nor are Rakhine civilians the enemies of the Rohingya. Neither community is the enemy of Myanmar’s people. Their grievances and rights cannot be settled by another campaign of suspicion and hatred.

Around 14 countries have already acknowledged the ICJ ruling. Sanctions have been imposed as well by the United Kingdom government on senior military officers of Myanmar. Meanwhile, China raised the issue of “jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation” and warned that the ruling could undermine the settlement of disputes.

The junta remains in power, but pro-democracy forces are relentless in the struggle to restore civilian rule. Millions of stateless Rohingya are scattered in various camps, but the landmark ICJ ruling is a step forward in the pursuit of justice and the advancement of the demand to allow the persecuted minority to return to their home.
Written by Mong Palatino

c212765bc089123b: FIFTEEN months after spotting a job ad seeking a new leader for a political party, Qiulae Wong will help decide New Zealand's next government after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's right-wing coalition lost its majority.
The 38-year-old former KPMG consultant took over a party polling at about one per cent in August last year.

Since then, the Opportunity Party has secured seven seats and 6.1 per cent of the vote in this month's election, placing it in prime position to play kingmaker as Luxon rushes to piece together a workable coalition.
Wong preaches "pragmatic politics" as a counter to growing polarisation, saying she wants to "bring the heat down a little bit and actually just focus on moving the country forward."
Establishment parties worldwide have been losing support in recent elections, replaced by a surge in populist movements touting more radical policies on the left or right.
But Wong, who is of Chinese and European descent and was born in Fiji, said following the election she believed the result showed voters were tiring of that kind of politics.
"I think we are seeing a push globally for more pragmatic politics," she told journalists.
"We've seen that populism doesn't deliver results," she said.
"It is paper thin; it doesn't have substance around taking countries forward.
"So it's really encouraging to have had that support."
Wong worked in sustainable fashion before entering politics.
A mother of two, her social media emphasises her ordinariness – moving effortlessly from pints in the sun and ice creams with the kids to political rallies and media events.
All that has prompted comparisons to former prime minister Jacinda Ardern, whose star power made her a global progressive icon.

"I think the way in which both of those two relatively young women are attempting a different style of politics is something that marks Wong apart," Massey University politics professor Richard Shaw told AFP.
He said Opportunity's rise had been 'remarkable', given its differences to other New Zealand political parties and due to the relative inexperience of Wong.

"At a time when the politics of this country are becoming more fraught and more feral and more shouty, and there is horrendous online trolling of women in public life, you've got this woman who's coming in saying 'I'm leading a party and we're going to do it this way'.
"I think that appeals to people."
Luxon had previously ruled out working with Opportunity.
He now faces an embarrassing volte-face, admitting Friday he will need the centrist outsiders' support if he wants to stay in office.
All eyes are now on Wong as the country faces weeks of political wrangling.
She has said she will work with Luxon – but insisted that her party's 'bottom lines' are non-negotiable.

Those lines – on climate change action, regulations on political lobbying, healthcare reform, phasing out bottom trawling, and cost of living – could be a hard sell in talks with Luxon's right-wing partners, the populist NZ First and libertarian ACT.

On the campaign trail, she also ruled out working with a government in which NZ First leader Winston Peters was foreign minister, after he told a Chinese-born lawmaker to 'go back to your own country.'
And on Friday she refused to rule out taking the country back for a second election if talks don't work out.
"All we can do is be as constructive and proactive as possible to make this happen. But it's not just us around the table," she said.

Local farming is heavily reliant on imported fertiliser and sensitive to feed price fluctuations, while extreme weather, such as floods and a forecasted Super El Niño next year, is also a concern.
They have already been cited as factors behind Malaysia's padi output falling 4.5 per cent below the national five-year average this year.
In the next 10 years, the National Agrofood Policy 2021-2030 and phased import-reduction road maps intend to reduce the import bill by 13 per cent, or RM93.7 billion, annually.

To meet this goal, Agriculture and Food Security Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu announced an ambitious plan to increase padi yields in Muda Agricultural Development Authority (Mada) areas to 10 tonnes per hectare by 2030.
This target is attainable through modern technology, improved fertilisation and better farming practices.
Mada covers 100,685ha across the rice bowls of Kedah and Perlis, the nation's largest granary area accounting for 40 per cent of its rice production.
In comparison, Thailand averages 2.85 to three tonnes per hectare nationally across 10 to 11 million ha.

Malaysia's rice authorities are rolling out drones, technical and vocational education and training and better fertilisation practices while continuing to provide RM2.6 billion in subsidies for local production to boost productivity.
Each extra tonne per hectare adds RM500 for farmers. Of course, there are obstacles: Mada averages only five to 5.22 tonnes per hectare, a two per cent yield increase in the latest season.

To double the average by 2030, Mada needs rapid, widespread adoption rather than isolated gains, swifter modernisation and better preparation against the elements. And to somehow make farming "cool" for the next generation.

34b2539e46c709a1: JERUSALEM: Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to form the next Israeli government, on Friday accused the party of caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections.
Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party has in recent days agreed coalition deals with two allied parties, but the route to a parliamentary majority is still far from certain.

After the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc, Yashar has also held talks with Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party over the possibility of forming a national unity government involving both parties.
But no breakthroughs on that front have ostensibly been reached.
"Likud, for its part, was unwilling to compromise and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table," Eisenkot said in a statement on Friday.
"Their conduct points to an effort to run down the clock until the mandate expires, split the Change bloc and drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government," he added.
Eisenkot has until Dec 6 – a deadline which can be extended by 14 days – to form a government to replace Netanyahu.
His wide-ranging camp has faced divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties or the Arab-majority lists or whether to form a unity government with Likud.
"We are approaching a moment of decision," Eisenkot said on Friday.

"The question is whether Likud will engage in serious negotiations and commit to a partnership that requires compromise or keep up appearances and continue to stall," he added, but maintained he was still open to talks if Likud was "genuinely prepared to change course".
Likud, in turn, accused Eisenkot of working to form a "dangerous left-wing government" but nonetheless said it would still be open to a unity government.
Eisenkot's Yashar party has so far agreed to coalition deals with the left-leaning Democrats party and the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party.
Together, they have a combined total of 36 lawmakers – far short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority.

On Friday, Israeli media reported that Mansour Abbas, the leader of the Arab-Israeli Raam party, was expected the following day to recognise Hamas as a "terror group" – a move that could pave the way for his party to join a possible Eisenkot-led coalition.
But some of Eisenkot's allies have voiced opposition to relying on the support of the Arab-majority lists, which won unprecedented gains in the election.
6662b1027d8bd17c: SOCIAL media algorithms are a powerful feature of online life, serving up content to users based on their browsing habits or personal data.
Users in Australia will be able to opt out of them in a year's time, under new legislation approved in parliament that also imposes fines on tech giants if they fail to remove content deemed harmful.
Open TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, YouTube or other platforms, and you'll see a scrolling feed or recommendations bar showing content targeted to your interests.
These posts are selected for users based on programming rules called algorithms that predict what you will engage with — whether it's something you like, or that riles you.

Broadly speaking, the recommendations are based on what the machine knows about you: what you've interacted with or posted about online, or information such as your age, job, location and marital status.
Social media giants usually keep the coding behind these algorithms — the so-called "secret sauce" that drives traffic to their platforms — closely guarded.
It's a familiar pattern for many — open your phone on a break and before you know it, an hour has passed and you're still scrolling.
That's by design, researchers and activists say.

"These platforms have engineered addictive features that keep children and adults online longer than they intend, often at the expense of sleep, well-being and real-world connection," said Mark Williams, honorary professor of cognitive neuroscience at Macquarie University.
In a landmark trial in Los Angeles this year, tech giants were accused of creating "addiction machines".
Experts point to strategies companies use to encourage scrolling, like never-ending feeds, intermittent rewards and time-sensitive notifications.
"This unpredictability triggers the dopamine system, creating a compulsive cycle of seeking and anticipation," University of Leicester lecturer Quynh Hoang wrote.
Such dependence is similar to substance addiction, research published in online medical journal Cureus last year found.
By pushing people to content they respond to emotionally, many say social media can drive us into "rabbit holes" that are difficult to escape.

The recommendations "are designed to hold our attention, and too often that means privileging provocative and extreme content because outrage drives engagement and engagement drives profit", said Steven Roberts at Monash University.
Algorithms have been accused of pushing teenage boys towards the "manosphere" — communities and influencers that promote misogyny and violence against women.

Research from Melbourne-based men's health charity Movember found that social media guided young men to that content whether they wanted it or not, a path leading from innocuous posts about working out and sports to violent, extreme content.
"We can already see the consequences in Australian schools," where "misogyny is rife", Roberts said.

"Our national survey of more than 2,600 teachers found that... 70 per cent had frequently or occasionally seen the impact of manosphere social media influencers present on student attitudes and behaviour."
Under Australia's new rules, social media giants must allow users to "opt out" of the algorithm.
They also hold the firms responsible for protecting under-18s from pornography, online bullying and content that glorifies crime or encourages eating disorders.
The "my feed, my way" initiative aims to bring social media back to basics — a feed focused on updates from friends, family and pages you follow.
"The government has handed Australians a switch. Whether anyone flips it is another matter," said Lisa Harrison, a lecturer in communication and media at Flinders University.
In a survey last year of over 6,000 people in six countries, only one in five said they would switch off personalised recommendations if they could, she noted.
"The algorithm is good at its job, and the minority who do opt out will find a feed of friends and creators feels quieter than the one they left."
* The writers are from AFP

cae5fe596cf1ba5a: Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028.

That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker, which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers.

The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market.

Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns.

The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC, memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing.

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones.

Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported, memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026.

For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases.
"The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang.

"Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets."
Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years.
Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing.

A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery.

"The unusually low 2027 base creates the potential for a robust rebound in 2028 once the memory bottleneck begins to ease. But this should not be interpreted as a return to the old market trajectory," Wang said.
"Some low-end demand has been permanently lost, and the 2028 market will still be about 14 percent below 2025 shipments."
Potential availability of 6G-capable smartphones toward the end of the decade could give the market a boost, but Counterpoint does not expect it to regain its 2025 shipment levels by 2030. ®

7115a912a88f6f99: WHAT will tomorrow's Europe look like? The answer may hinge on a looming year of back-to-back elections, with France at centre stage, that could change the face of the European Union and potentially jam its decision-making.

Between now and the end of next year, four of the EU's five largest countries will choose new leaders in contests marked by the rise of eurosceptic forces — groups wary of Brussels' influence which seek to grant more power to individual member states.
It will be an unprecedented series of political tests for the bloc.
The most consequential vote takes place in April and May in France, where far-right leader Marine Le Pen is running in the lead.
Depending on the outcome in France and elsewhere, "what we risk is paralysis" in European decision-making, summed up one Brussels diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive matter.
The high-stakes electoral cycle kicks off tomorrow in Spain. Shaped by heated debates over immigration and housing, that vote could end the era of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
After more than eight years in power, Sanchez is one of the last remaining socialist leaders in the 27-nation bloc, often at odds with his counterparts, including on migration and defence.
Most polls show him losing to conservative rival Alberto Nunez Feijoo.
The vote could also see the far right enter government for the first time since Francisco Franco's dictatorship ended in 1975, with the Vox party seeking to play kingmaker.

Looking into next year, close attention will focus on Italy, where hard-right leader Giorgia Meloni faces a challenge on her right flank from former general Roberto Vannacci, an anti-migration hawk opposed to military aid for Ukraine.

And Brussels will be scrutinising parliamentary elections in Poland, set for a new showdown between the camp of pro-European Prime Minister Donald Tusk and that of nationalist President Karol Nawrocki.
Next year will also bring elections in a host of smaller EU nations, such as Estonia — an ardent backer of Ukraine which accuses Russia of targeting it with a campaign of sabotage.
Polls are likewise scheduled in Greece, Finland and Slovakia, where Prime Minister Robert Fico maintains friendly ties with the Kremlin.
But no race is causing more concern in Brussels than the French presidential race.
Frontrunner Le Pen is pushing a vision for Europe in stark contrast to the one championed by President Emmanuel Macron over the past decade.
The National Rally (RN) leader has made clear she would shelve plans for further EU enlargement and pull the plug on funding for Ukraine.
Le Pen recently travelled to Brussels to make her case, vowing to pare back the European Commission to a "secretariat" serving member states and slash France's contribution to the EU budget.
Celia Belin, of the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Le Pen's "radical" policies on Europe "would be putting France on a collision path with EU institutions".
The bloc's top officials have yet to establish meaningful contacts with Le Pen, making it all the more difficult to predict the knock-on effects her election could have in Brussels.
It is an open question how discussions among the bloc's 27 leaders might unfold during late-night European summits, if a victorious Le Pen decided to play hardball.
With German Chancellor Friedrich Merz already weakened in Berlin, would her election cause the EU's decision-making machinery to grind to a halt?
Could commission chief Ursula von der Leyen suffer the consequences? Some in Brussels are already gaming out worst-case scenarios.
Others prefer to downplay Le Pen's statements, arguing that if she comes to power, she will have little choice but to work within the EU framework — as did Italy's Meloni.
"Not everything has to be the end of the world," countered one diplomat. "If there is a vacuum, other countries will fill the gap."
Others caution against reading too much into polling, arguing eurosceptic forces may fail to convert momentum into votes.
But officials and diplomats AFP spoke to broadly agreed on one thing: the EU needs to bolster its ability to weather electoral shocks in the months ahead.
That effort starts now with hard-fought negotiations to agree the bloc's next seven-year budget, and to secure funding for Ukraine through next year.
* The writer is from AFP

e6e21c878f7e77a8: PETALING JAYA: The Kota Kinabalu High Court has given the Sabah Attorney-General’s Chambers three days to clarify the state government’s position on a suit challenging the federal laws governing Sabah’s continental shelf and territorial waters.
Justice Alexander Siew said the state AGC had had three years to determine its position since Sabah Action Body Advocating Rights (Sabar) filed the suit against the federal government in 2023.
Sabah AG Brenndon Keith Soh had applied for the state government to be included as an intervener respondent, saying its position was “more aligned with Sabar’s position”, the Daily Express reported.
However, Siew said the position was vague; the state government must specify whether it agreed with all or only some of the five declarations sought by Sabar.
“More aligned? What does that mean? Halfway aligned? Seventy per cent aligned? Fifty-one per cent aligned? This is a court of law. We have to be very precise," said the judge.

Soh said the Sabah government supported the outcome sought by Sabar but might take a different approach in interpreting the relevant constitutional provisions and statutes. He added that he would file another affidavit to clarify the state government’s position.

Among the court orders sought, Sabar seeks to obtain declarations that the Continental Shelf Act 1966 and Petroleum Mining Act 1966 are unconstitutional and inapplicable in Sabah, and that the state’s Mining Ordinance 1960 remains valid.

It also seeks recognition of Sabah’s continental shelf rights and its territorial waters extending 12 nautical miles, instead of the three nautical miles stipulated under the Territorial Sea Act 2012.

Sabar filed its originating summons in September 2023, naming the federal government as the sole defendant. In August, the Federal Court dismissed Sabar’s bid to intervene in a separate suit by the Sarawak government against the federal government involving natural resources and continental shelf rights.
4058bf3361557885: GENEVA: The UN's refugee agency said on Friday it was seeking a much-reduced US$7.1 billion to protect stateless people and respond to emergencies in 2027.

UNHCR chief Barham Salih warned last month that his agency was being "asked to do the impossible", overstretched by a huge funding shortfall and near-record-high population displacements around the world.
UNHCR's 2026 appeal targeted US$8.5 billion – of which only US$2.9 billion has been raised to date.
"The appeal comes amid immense humanitarian needs and an exceptionally difficult funding environment. As a result, UNHCR's 2027 budget prioritises the most urgent needs," the agency said.
If fully funded, UNHCR would use the money next year to provide protection services for 13.6 million refugees and asylum seekers and 6.7 million internally displaced people (IDPs).
"We also aim to provide financial assistance to 3.9 million refugees and two million IDPs, and shelter and housing assistance for 1.8 million refugees and 850,000 IDPs," the agency said.
Some 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced from their homes at the end of 2025, according to UNHCR – down slightly from 2024's record 123.2 million.
Of those 117.8 million, 35.6 million were refugees under UNHCR's mandate, with two-thirds coming from Afghanistan, Sudan, Syria, Ukraine and Venezuela.
Despite those elevated numbers, the agency has had to slash its workforce due to budget cuts.
The US – traditionally the world's top donor – has cut foreign aid under President Donald Trump, while other major donors have also tightened their belts.
Since 2024, nearly 8,000 employees have left UNHCR, with its workforce falling from nearly 20,000 to just under 12,000.
In 2025 UNHCR sought US$10.6 billion and ended up with US$3.8 billion to spend; in 2024 it sought US$10.8 billion and got US$5.3 billion.

UNHCR spokesman Matthew Saltmarsh told reporters that the agency's strategy remained "protecting people forced to flee, reacting very quickly to emergencies when they arise, but also, crucially, to help refugees to move beyond aid."
The appeal was launched ahead of UNHCR's annual pledging conference in Geneva on Tuesday.

b1d4b3b2dfda0a5a: KUALA LUMPUR: Seorang lagi pegawai Tentera Udara Diraja Malaysia (TUDM) dan empat orang awam ditahan semalam bagi membantu siasatan berhubung kegiatan sindiket penyeludupan dadah rentas sempadan menggunakan aset ketenteraan.
Pengarah Jabatan Siasatan Jenayah Narkotik (JSJN) Bukit Aman, Hussein Omar Khan, berkata penahanan terbaharu itu menjadikan jumlah keseluruhan individu yang ditahan setakat ini seramai 18 orang.
Beliau berkata, tangkapan itu hasil risikan berterusan dan soal siasat terhadap 13 suspek yang ditahan sebelum ini dalam usaha mengenal pasti dalang utama di sebalik kegiatan sindiket berkenaan.

“Pegawai TUDM berusia 29 tahun yang bertugas di TUDM Tawau, Sabah itu ditahan di pekarangan pejabat Cawangan Penyiasatan Jenayah Zon Tengah, Pangkalan Udara Subang, Selangor kira-kira 6.40 petang semalam,” katanya dalam kenyataan.

Susulan penahanan itu, Hussein berkata JSJN Bukit Aman melancarkan beberapa serbuan di sekitar Lembah Klang kira-kira 10.20 malam, sebelum menahan tiga lelaki tempatan berusia antara 26 hingga 28 tahun dan seorang lelaki warga China berusia 30 tahun.

Beliau berkata semakan mendapati ketiga-tiga suspek lelaki tempatan itu masing-masing mempunyai antara satu hingga dua rekod jenayah lampau, dengan seorang daripadanya pernah ditahan mengikut peruntukan Langkah-Langkah Pencegahan Khas (LLPK).

“Daripada semua 18 suspek yang ditahan yang terdiri daripada lapan pegawai dan anggota TUDM serta 10 orang awam, lapan individu telah dituduh di mahkamah di Kuala Lumpur dan Selangor hari ini mengikut Seksyen 39B Akta Dadah Berbahaya 1952.
“Lima suspek masih dalam tahanan reman, manakala siasatan dan risikan lanjut diteruskan bagi mengenal pasti dalang utama serta individu lain yang terlibat dalam rangkaian sindiket itu,” katanya.

Sebelum ini, kegiatan sindiket penyeludupan dadah rentas sempadan itu terbongkar selepas 96.64kg dadah disyaki metamfetamina bernilai RM4.83 juta serta 6.98kg bahan kimia ditemukan ketika hendak dimuatkan ke dalam sebuah pesawat TUDM di Pangkalan Udara Subang.
Susulan penemuan itu, beberapa siri serbuan dilakukan di Lembah Klang, Labuan dan sebuah pangkalan udara di Tawau, Sabah, yang membawa kepada penahanan beberapa suspek.

d1172e44d2bf9820: Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse.

Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF].
The report, from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million.
The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues.
"The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said.
It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software.

The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems.

Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts. It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor. The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt, an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system.

It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless.
The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay, now rebranded as Civica Income Management.
Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill.
For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools, but that was excluded from the reimplementation.
Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example.

A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026.
Council taxpayers can be assured the new system has gone live without major problems, but that is hardly cause for celebration. ®

3e3c3c872311b597: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 27 — News of Jensen Huang’s shocking return to Nvidia had barely landed when President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated image of the Nvidia cofounder holding up a red bra, surrounded by security personnel whisking him offstage, blood streaked across his face.

The image was based on a real photo taken in 2024 when Trump survived an assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, and implied that Huang, too, had survived a bid to take him out.
For many women, though, the image spoke insultingly to longstanding frustrations about sexism, double standards and a lack of accountability for men in power — across politics and business.
Meanwhile, many “tech bros” rushed to Huang’s defence over the past couple of weeks. Billionaire Elon Musk was among many people who signed a petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement.
Venture capitalist Jason Calacanis described Huang as a “hero” and downplayed the scandal that led to Huang’s resignation as less important than the United States winning the AI race against China.
“They’re standing up for the idea that certain men can do whatever they want,” Cleo Capital Managing Director Sarah Kunst told AFP.
Part of the problem might be “hero worship,” she said.
It also reflects the tech industry’s mythology around “founder mode” — the belief that companies thrive when founders stay hands-on rather than cede control to executives.

Huang resigned on November 12 from Nvidia, the company he cofounded and has led for more than three decades, amid allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman that US officials suspect was working for Chinese intelligence, triggering national security concerns.
Another of Huang’s alleged lovers was a subordinate at Nvidia.
“This is a great example of why integrity matters,” Kunst said. “As soon as I heard about the honeypot element, it was clear to me that there were lapses in judgment that were really big.”
On November 17, board Chairman Harvey Jones said the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Then President Donald Trump intervened.
“I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC, referring to Huang’s reinstatement.
Trump himself was found liable in 2023 for sexual assault and defamation and ordered to pay millions as punishment.
Dreaded “glass cliff”

For an industry with very few women as executives, Huang’s departure became a brief opportunity for the company’s chief financial officer to step into one of the most prominent roles in tech. Nvidia’s advanced chips are used to train and run the AI models reshaping modern life.
The board appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO on November 12 while they searched for a permanent chief.

It’s unclear if Kress wanted the job permanently, but women are often thrown into leadership positions during times of crisis and frequently blamed for any subsequent failure or replaced after things improve.
Nvidia declined to comment.

Australian National University Professor Michelle Ryan coined a term over two decades ago that describes this situation: the “glass cliff” — women or other under-represented people being appointed to senior roles during a crisis, when risk of failure is high.
Ryan is also the director of the university’s Global Institute for Women’s Leadership.
A “glass cliff” situation can also come with intense scrutiny, Ryan told AFP last week, before Huang’s reinstatement.
“When you’re dealing with a crisis, there’s a whole lot of things that you have to be dealing with. It’s not just sort of everyday business and just get on with being a CEO,” Ryan said.
Kress tried to reassure analysts and investors that it was “business as usual” during Nvidia’s quarterly earning call on November 17, when the company reported blockbuster results.
“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing, our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this,” Kress said on the call.

The results turned out to be a brief salve for Nvidia’s share price, which dropped nearly three percent the following day after already losing more than a quarter of its market value since the initial revelations concerning Huang in late October.

“I can say with a high degree of certainty that what the interim CEO will face, and is facing, is a question of legitimacy,” Berkeley Professor Laura Kray told AFP last week. Her research includes the intersection of gender and business management.
Ultimately, a multifaceted pressure campaign from employees, billionaires and President Trump ended Kress’s tenure as CEO prematurely. — AFP
7ae4942683eb6c46: MANILA, Nov 27 — Noel Celis’s pulse still races whenever a motorcyclist pulls up alongside him at a red light, a legacy of countless nights photographing Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody drug war.

“They call it riding in tandem,” the freelance photographer told AFP of the two-man teams that once roamed the capital, Manila, dealing out death, conceding it remained “scary” after years of death threats tied to his work.
Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30 for the “crime against humanity of murder”, over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.
For photographers like Celis, it is as if that period happened yesterday.
The 43-year-old, who worked for AFP at the time, photographed about 200 drug war killings.
One picture showed a young woman cradling the bloody body of her boyfriend shortly after he was gunned down at a busy intersection.

To the mainly Catholic nation, it bore a disturbing resemblance to Michelangelo’s “La Pieta”, a sculpture of the Virgin Mary cradling Christ after his crucifixion. It swiftly became the defining image of the crackdown.
Those working the drug war beat took to calling themselves “nightcrawlers”, after a Hollywood film about Los Angeles camera crews chasing late-night mayhem.
Mental map of death
At first, the journalists said, the police had no qualms about tipping them off about the killings.
But they clammed up as the public outcry grew, and the photographers resorted to chasing after mortuary vans summoned by police to collect the dead.

It all came flooding back for Dondi Tawatao, 46, when he returned with AFP to a garbage-strewn street where, on a rainy night 10 years ago, he took pictures of two bodies beneath the exposed roots of a banyan tree.
Near them were two handguns he believed were planted there.
“It was very dark, very sinister. It’s supposed to be the tree of life, but on that night, it became the tree of death,” he told AFP.
After shooting the drug war for four years, the killings became “normalised” to the point where he stopped visiting crime scenes unless they involved at least three corpses.
The long nights rearranged how he saw Manila, he said.
“You sort of have a mental map of where the killings took place. Like randomly, you would be walking, then you realise, ‘this was where so-and-so was killed’.”
He later left the profession, “primarily to take a rest mentally”.
‘We went to apologise’
Freelancer Kimberly dela Cruz, 36, found her first victim on Manila’s rail tracks, and another atop a major bridge.
“It was a full moon, and I thought, ‘What a beautiful evening it would have been — except somebody died’,” she told AFP of the first.
The head of the man at the second scene was wrapped in packaging tape. He lay next to a cardboard poster that read: “I’m a drug pusher, don’t emulate me.”
Some of her colleagues would require professional counselling. One suffered from recurring nightmares about the drug war dead coming back to life.
Celis’s memories centre on the heart-wrenching keening of victims’ wives and mothers, and the sharp, metallic smell of blood.
Residents of the mainly slum-area killing grounds could fear journalists as much as they did police, dela Cruz said.
“I was an outsider. They thought I was an (intelligence operative), police, or somebody that would bring evil,” she said.
Celis said photographers wrestled with feelings of guilt over not being able to help, and accusations of “profiting from the suffering of other people”.
When he and a colleague attended the wake of the “La Pieta” victim, they half-dreaded a lynching by angry relatives.
“We went there to apologise for not being able to help,” he said, telling the victim’s girlfriend the pictures could be evidence were charges ever brought.
‘I was shocked’
“A picture is powerful,” Celis said, “especially at this time, when standing history on its head is in vogue”.
Alluding to Holocaust deniers, Tawatao said the photos provided “incontrovertible proof that it happened”.
None of the photographers interviewed by AFP believed the drug war solved the country’s narcotics problem.
They remain convinced the police murdered thousands to enforce Duterte’s will.
But for all, Duterte’s arrest and handover to the ICC last year seemed an impossibility — until it happened.
“I was shocked, because I didn’t think it was possible. We’ve only seen the powers that be get away with it,” Tawatao said.

b1e8ed0d87ebd51a: MUNICH, Nov 27 — Bayern Munich head to Hamburg on Saturday in the middle of a crisis which threatens not only to derail the club’s sporting ambitions, but their identity itself.
Bayern, who are in the midst of an injury crisis which has decimated their forward line including Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, sit two points behind Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga table.
But Bayern’s treatment of midfielder Jamal Musiala by their hierarchy has led to a growing rift between the club and the playing group.

Shortly after Bayern lost 2-1 to Lille on Wednesday, ending their run as the final unbeaten team in Europe’s top-five leagues this season, vice-captain Joshua Kimmich suggested the club had fallen out of step with their values.
“It’s completely unacceptable and is not Bayern-like,” Kimmich said on Wednesday, adding that Musiala’s treatment was inconsistent with the club’s “sense of togetherness”.
‘Mia san mia’
This week, Bayern’s hierarchy suggested Musiala take a pay cut as the 23-year-old battles his way back from a neurological condition which causes absence seizures.

While the condemnation from media, player unions and former players was swift, Kimmich — who was wearing the captain’s armband with Manuel Neuer out injured — was the first member of Bayern’s current squad to speak out.

Despite their status as one of football’s perennial heavyweights, Bayern have always sought to emphasise their Bavarian roots and member-ownership in contrast to the American and Gulf-owned behemoths that loom over the European landscape.
But their cold-hearted treatment of Musiala, a fan-favourite and popular inside the dressing room, threatens their carefully crafted identity.
The club’s vaunted “Mia san mia” motto, which appears on every modern Bayern kit, translates to “we are who we are”.
Midfielder Aleksandar Pavlovic, a product of Bayern’s youth system, in 2025 said: “For me, ‘Mia san mia’ means being a family, standing together in good times and bad.
“That’s what we live by here from a young age, that we always stick together.”
Musiala’s return
Just two months after signing a contract extension in February 2025, Musiala began treatment for symptoms of the neurological condition.
After missing two months with an unrelated muscle injury, Musiala was warmly welcomed back by Bayern’s 75,000-strong Allianz Arena on Friday.
Minutes after full-time, club powerbroker Karl-Heinz Rummenigge suggested Musiala’s condition meant he might be unable to deliver on his lucrative deal and should take a pay cut.
“If he doesn’t return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation... because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable,” he said.
The firestorm began to spread immediately, with Bayern’s untimely announcement of a record turnover of close to one billion euros (RM4.5 billion) at their AGM a day later fanning the flames.
On Saturday, international player union FIFPRO said that Bayern “should know better”, identifying a void between the German giants’ values and their behaviour.
Former Bayern and Germany goalkeeper Oliver Kahn, who previously served as Bayern’s CEO, issued a harsh critique.
“To put the player under pressure now and appeal to his decency through the public sphere, urging him to forgo part of his salary, is simply absurd,” Kahn said.
But Kimmich’s words have had the biggest impact as they provide a rare insight into the dressing room.
“It is understandable that the club might be concerned because of the illness. What I don’t understand is the way this is being communicated publicly,” Kimmich said.
“It must not happen that a player is made to bear the brunt of it.” — AFP

ab9a7b7cc5d1247c: The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures.

Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed.

The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared.

In its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027.

"Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) says.

"Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI."

But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests.

This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance.

The government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning.

Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources.

If this has a ring of familiarity, it is because President Trump earlier this year introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which hyperscalers and AI companies agreed to protect US consumers from any bill shocks due to the energy and infrastructure requirements of their datacenter projects. It seems that where the US leads, the UK still often follows.
The Covenant sets out efficiency targets and reporting expectations, but does not explain how compliance will be enforced or specify penalties for failing to meet its tests.
Protect the Wild notes that it "barely acknowledges wildlife, habitats or biodiversity. In fact, it doesn't mention any of those things at all."
The Covenant does, however, call on operators to "protect nature," without spelling out specific safeguards for wildlife, habitats, or biodiversity.

While the government encourages all server farms to meet the tests, only those it considers "strategic" are required to do so, as we noted above. And even that is only in order to qualify for extra government support, not in order to gain approval for a project.

Further, the campaign group contends that having environmental concerns addressed on a project-by-project basis at the planning level is a major barrier to tackling greenhouse gas emissions at a national level.

It cites the draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres, under which operational emissions from nationally significant projects in England, including those from on-site power generation, would be managed against national climate commitments at an economy-wide level rather than assessing each application's contribution to those targets.

Protect the Wild also argues that project-level assessments do not adequately capture nationwide habitat loss, even though the planning process requires consideration of cumulative environmental effects.

Datacenters have become a growing public concern in the UK, although opposition has not reached the level it has in the US, where anti-datacenter sentiment played a major part in political campaigns for the recent midterm elections.

But there were protests around the country at the start of November, such as in London and at Great Torrington, a town in Devon where a proposed 1.5 GW data campus and battery energy storage facility would cover 850 acres of nearby farmland.
Celebrity TV cook Delia Smith recently joined protests over a proposed datacenter on the edge of Norwich in Norfolk over concerns it may threaten a nearby nature reserve.

Protesters are unlikely to find much sympathy in Westminster. The government has already pinned its hopes for growing the economy on AI, as detailed in its AI Opportunities Action Plan last year, and it sees building more datacenters as key to achieving this.

The Guardian reports that Natural England, the government's own advisory body for the natural environment, is being threatened with abolition weeks after raising objections to a large AI campus near Bristol because of the threat it poses to protected wildlife and habitats.

A separate report found that the government met with 137 different businesses to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026, but did not meet a single community group or environmental organization during the same period. ®
