9eb6249e049dc617: BRUSSELS, Nov 27 — Belgian authorities have ordered Google to suspend construction of a data centre in the south of the country because of a lack of proper planning permission, a regional official said Friday.
“We have identified a major offence: the illegal construction of a building covering three hectares,” or 7.4 acres, Nicolas Yernaux, spokesman for the Wallonia regional authorities, told AFP.
The “stop-work” order at the former mining site covering some 50 hectares in total comes after NGO Greenpeace accused Google of carrying on construction despite lacking the correct permits.
The regional authority said that inspectors visited the site on Thursday to inform Google representatives to halt construction.
The mammoth project has been locked in legal litigation for months after Google applied to amend the terms of its planning permission.
The application sought to allow a cooling system for the facilities using water drawn from the nearby River Sambre, whereas the initial project had envisaged air cooling, Belgian media reported.
The move stirred local opposition as severe droughts since spring exacerbated fears about tapping the river — and regional officials refused the application over the summer.
Google has challenged that decision in court and a hearing is scheduled for January.
But a report this week by Greenpeace Belgium said that drone footage showed work was still progressing in the meantime.
“The tech giant is currently continuing its work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this data centre was revoked,” the environmental group said.
“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region. Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”
Google did not immediately respond to a request from AFP to comment.
The legal row over the Belgian data centre is the latest confronting Google in Europe as tech giants push to build data centres to support the Artificial Intelligence boom.
In October Finnish authorities ordered work on two Google data centre sites in the country to be halted until mandatory environmental impact assessments could be completed. — AFP

668efd6679523792: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 — The World Bank’s downward revision of its 2026 global growth forecast does not signal an impending recession, according to World Bank economist Deisigan Shammugam.
He said the global economy was still expanding, but more slowly and with higher inflation.
About two-thirds of economies now face weaker growth prospects than the World Bank projected in January, largely due to the economic fallout from the Middle East crisis, he said.
“The revised outlook should not be interpreted as a recession warning.

“And just to be clear, it is not a recession call. The world keeps growing, but more slowly and with higher inflation,” Deisigan said yesterday at the National Economic Outlook Conference organised by the Malaysian Institute of Economic Research (MIER) here.
Why the slowdown in 2026?
Deisigan said one of the biggest shocks was the Middle East crisis, which was working its way through the economy via several channels.
“We’ve had many energy crises in the past and the four channels are very familiar: energy prices, inflation, interest rates and tighter financial conditions.
“We are pretty well aware of these channels, but what is really different this time is the shipping and the supply chain,” he said.
He said the World Bank report pointed to broader disruptions to global supply chains and higher input costs.
“It shows in retail fuel prices like diesel.
“Since March, wholesale prices of diesel and jet fuel have climbed considerably more than crude oil, while refining spreads are hovering well beyond their historical norms.
“So it is no surprise that AirAsia is finding it difficult this time around,” he said.

Deisigan cautioned policymakers against relying on Brent crude prices alone to estimate retail pump prices, as shipping disruptions, supply constraints and sharply higher insurance costs for tanker fleets were also pushing up costs.

“So if you proxy Brent to retail using just the APM formula like how we do in Malaysia, you are going to miss the market price, the true market price of the retail price,” he said, referring to the Automatic Pricing Mechanism.

He added that global oil supply is projected to fall by around 5 per cent this year due to production cuts linked to the Strait of Hormuz crisis, with gains elsewhere offsetting only a small share of the Middle East losses.
“Consumption is also expected to fall 2.5 per cent, the third-largest decline in energy consumption on record,” Deisigan said.
He said global growth was expected to pick up to 2.8 per cent in both 2027 and 2028 as energy supplies recover, monetary easing resumes and trade strengthens.

Among emerging market and developing economies, growth is projected to slow from 4.4 per cent to 3.6 per cent, while China’s growth is expected to ease to 4.2 per cent amid weakness in its property sector, labour market and consumer confidence.

However, the World Bank expects that if the recent increase in crude shipments from the Gulf proves durable, global oil production will recover towards 2025 levels in 2027, consumption will rebound slightly, and the market will return to surplus by the second quarter of next year.
Turning to financial markets, Deisigan said emerging economies could face greater uncertainty as fiscal vulnerabilities and high debt levels in major economies push up global borrowing costs.
He said rising fiscal risks could increase the term premium demanded by investors, potentially raising borrowing costs across markets.
Deisigan also warned that increasingly concerned investors could move their money out of emerging markets into safer assets, particularly from economies seen as having weak governance.
He said this made structural reforms and stronger governance important for emerging economies seeking to maintain investor confidence.
“The solution, sorry to say, boring old answer from an economist: structural policies are the answer,” he said.

5e96240516134d99: PETALING JAYA, Nov 27 — Grab Malaysia is moving away from a one-size-fits-all commission model, saying e-hailing drivers should be paid for the time and distance they spend travelling to pick up passengers, not just for the trips they complete.

Grab Malaysia executive director Rashid Shukor said the revised Grab Service Fee (GSF) structure takes pickup time and distance into account when calculating the fee charged to drivers, with the aim of improving their earnings without raising passenger fares.
“We want to make sure we fairly compensate the driver to the best of our ability,” he said at a briefing today.
Under the previous arrangement, Grab charged a fixed 30 per cent commission regardless of how far drivers had to travel to collect passengers.
Rashid said this had long been a concern among drivers, who argued that they spent time and fuel reaching passengers but still received the same pay.

Using the example of a RM10 fare, he explained that under the revised model, the passenger’s fare would stay the same, but Grab’s service fee would vary depending on how far the driver had to travel to the pickup point.
A driver already near the passenger would pay a higher service fee, while one coming from farther away would pay less, keeping a larger share of the fare.

“In an extreme case where a driver had to travel from considerably further away to fulfil a booking, the service fee could turn negative, meaning the driver would receive more than the passenger’s fare for that trip,” Rashid said.
He added that the change was meant to cover the part of a journey that drivers previously felt went unpaid.

“The driver could be here, the fare that’s calculated, whether it’s RM15, RM10, whatever, that you pay only calculates from your pickup point to your drop-off point. It doesn’t account for this,” he said, referring to the distance travelled before reaching the passenger.
He said the revised structure could also improve driver productivity by encouraging them to accept bookings they might previously have turned down because of the extra pickup distance.
On the results of the proof of concept (POC), Rashid said drivers who opted into the revised structure earned more than 5 per cent more than those who did not take part.
He said the POC was approved by the Transport Ministry in August 2024 and had been running for about two years.
Beyond the commission percentage
Rashid said driver earnings should not be judged solely by the percentage platforms deduct, as actual income also depends on the number of trips completed, incentives, bonuses and working hours.
He said Grab focuses on the stability of drivers’ weekly earnings rather than on whether the commission on any single trip is higher or lower.
“Ultimately, whether it’s higher or lower, what we really anchor on is the stability of the driver’s earnings,” he said.
He added that keeping earnings stable required the platform to keep investing in drivers, generating passenger demand and improving the efficiency of its services.

These investments include driver incentives and bonuses during festive periods, weekends and other peak periods, as well as regulatory costs such as permits, reimbursements for Public Service Vehicle (PSV) licences, vehicle inspections and medical examinations.
Grab also provides upskilling programmes, discounts on fuel, lubricants and vehicle maintenance, personal accident insurance and compensation for certain incidents involving passengers.
Rashid said the platform had also invested in marketing, promotions, maintaining its technology and developing new features that benefit both drivers and passengers.
“Grab has also been working to improve driver flexibility while ensuring passengers could continue relying on its services.
“One feature gives drivers a window of time to decide whether to accept a booking, while another allows post-trip adjustments when journeys take longer than initially estimated.

“For example, a journey initially expected to take 30 minutes could stretch to 45 minutes because of heavy traffic or rain, with the adjustment allowing drivers to receive additional compensation for the longer trip,” he said.

He said Grab was also expanding its services to create more earning opportunities, including rides to public transport stations, group rides, Grab Assist for persons with disabilities and women-only rides.

a555d35dd70cdc08: Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles.

Gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion. For 2026, it estimates spending growth of 20.7 percent in North America and 13.7 percent in China.

"The world seems to be racing towards this AI goal of where the large language model provider is going to be, and the race seems to be between North American-based providers and some Asia Pacific providers," John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, told The Register.

He said Europe had traditionally trailed in IT uptake. "We saw that happen when global sourcing, cloud, and software as a service all came along. It's down to the pushback against the idea of creative destruction," where new technologies replace old ones.
Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent.
Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment.

"For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he said. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use."

The gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced new rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much.
"Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign.

"They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their company in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us.

Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach.
"The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," said Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®

ede849de9c06ce80: BANGKOK, Nov 27 — As pollution mounts in its rivers, food and water, Thailand is pressing neighbouring Myanmar to tackle unregulated mining, while urging China to exert its influence in the war-ravaged nation.
Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended earlier this month after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times government limits.

Bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group on the issue — also attended by the Chinese ambassador — where it said tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were causing the pollution downstream.
The two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers.
But there was no public agreement to Thailand’s request for a six-month suspension of operations, and how one could be implemented remains unclear, with Myanmar’s military not in full control.
Bangkok is also looking to China, the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, to pressure private Chinese operators, as a months-long concern becomes increasingly urgent.
Authorities warned residents this week against eating certain shellfish and other river species after tests in northern and northeastern Thailand found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead.
Saengwaree Suvirakan, a farmer from Tha Ton in Chiang Mai province who joined a protest in Bangkok this week, said fish stocks were declining in any case.
“Now with the mines the fish are all gone,” she said.
‘Not from nature’
At the joint talks, Thai ministers said high arsenic levels in the Kok and Sai rivers could only have come from rare-earth and gold mines on the Myanmar side.
“Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar’s) Shan state, no-one disagrees,” Science Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said.
But how to tackle it remains an issue.
Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), welcomed the agreement on joint sampling sites.
“This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity,” he told AFP.
But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be “really difficult”, he added.
Multiple ethnic armed groups have been operating there for decades, while a 2021 military coup sparked an ongoing civil war.
Thai officials pinpointed two gold mines just over the border from Mae Sai as the main source of high arsenic levels in the Sai River.
Different groups control different parts of the wider area, among them Myanmar military and the United Wa State Army, an ethnic armed group with close ties to China.
Mining suspension
Many mining operations in Myanmar are run by Chinese companies, and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul raised pollution with President Xi Jinping this month.
“China acknowledged that they are aware of mining by private Chinese companies in Shan state,” Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said.
“China made clear that they do not support activities that are improper, illegal or cause harm.”
Thailand sought China’s backing for its six-month mining suspension, officials said.
But China’s foreign ministry declined to comment, with a spokeswoman saying only that Beijing “pays close attention” to the pollution issue and would provide technical support.
The SEI’s Thanapon said Thailand could help “slow down mining activity” by pressuring the supply chain on its side of the border.

Thailand is planning to ban exports to Myanmar of two chemicals used in rare-earth mining, and restrict imports from the country of six minerals including gold and rare earths, to limit unauthorised mines’ access to buyers.
For farmer Saengwaree, there is no time to waste.
Even traditional customs were being hit by the pollution, she said, noting this week’s Loy Krathong festival, where residents and tourists send out small floats into waterways.
“Usually it is very busy,” she said, “but right now there is nobody in Tha Ton, there are no tourists.” — AFP

b856a387a314d8a4: PARIS, Nov 27 — Marc Marquez will bring the curtain down on his MotoGP career after this weekend’s season-ending Grand Prix in Valencia, following a historic season in which he won his record-equalling eighth world title.
Spaniard Marquez claimed his eighth title in the premier class of motorcycling last weekend at the Portuguese Grand Prix, his second in as many years for Italian team Ducati.

“It is official. @marcmarquez93 has decided to retire from @motogp, and the 2026 Valencia Grand Prix will be his final race as a professional rider and with the #DucatiLenovoTeam,” said Ducati on social media on Friday.

Marquez, who was second fastest behind Marco Bezzecchi in Friday’s free practice session, then relayed his own message, via a video recorded on the paddock at the Ricardo Tormo circuit, with a series of placards held up to the camera.
“Thank you to everyone who’s been part of this journey, I hope you’ve enjoyed it as much as I have,” said Marquez, who is set to speak to reporters at 12.15pm local time (1115 GMT).
“This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history.”
Marquez’s latest success pulled him level with Italian great Giacomo Agostini who won his titles between 1966 and 1975.
He also overtakes his great rival Valentino Rossi, who won seven MotoGP titles, although the swashbuckling Italian has 89 individual race wins in the top category to Marquez’s 80.
The latest triumph is even more remarkable given the 33-year-old’s injury and crash-blighted campaign in which he had to wait until the eighth race in Hungary on June 7 before claiming his first win.

Marquez suffered a flat tyre in the season-opener in Thailand in March, fell at the Spanish GP in Jerez and again at the French GP where he picked up a foot fracture which ruled him out of the following race, the Catalan GP.

Making his comeback at the Italian GP in Mugello he trailed Bezzecchi by a massive 102 points in early June, just weeks after undergoing foot surgery on top of a previous operation on his injured shoulder.
But once he got rolling he roared into a regular winning run with seven Grand Prix and 10 sprint race victories in all this season.
Marquez became the youngest ever MotoGP champion, at 20 years and 266 days old, in his debut season in 2013 and then went on to win the title in five of the next six seasons.
He looked set to dominate the sport for years to come but a horror crash at the start of the 2020 season left him with a broken arm which would hamper his return to the top for several years.

Marquez didn’t win another race until the Aragon GP in 2024, when his impressive third place in the riders’ championship was rewarded with promotion from satellite team Gresini to Ducati’s factory outfit.
From there Marquez went from strength to strength, winning two consecutive world titles and assuring his place in motorcycling’s history books. — AFP

0ae2924ce73a0941: The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN.
RETN says that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components.

As Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN says optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months.

This is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders. The issue now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies.
In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN says developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening.

The sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN says. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the issue.
However, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time.

Network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report says. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now.

The aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly.

RETN also says AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available.
Remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this issue earlier this year.

For sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site.

Some developers are prepared to swallow the cost: RETN says a major cloud provider is exploring converting an abandoned factory in Central Europe into a large-scale server farm, despite little existing fiber in the area.
However, RETN's warning is that connectivity must be planned alongside power and construction, not left until the datacenter is nearly ready to open. ®
929f0212acf91e79: NOVEMBER 27 – Imagine sitting at a coffee shop when the phones around you begin sounding an unfamiliar emergency alert. Nobody downloaded an application, subscribed to a service or provided their phone number.
In the few seconds it takes to read that message, an enormous amount of work will have happened out of sight.

Much of the conversation surrounding Malaysia’s Early Warning System (EWS), known as MySiren, has centred on policy and public safety. Far less attention has been given to the technological undertaking behind delivering a single warning to potentially millions of devices, in the right places, at the right time.
The concept sounds simple. Making it work reliably across an entire country is anything but.
Not just another text message
At the heart of MySiren is a technology known as the Cell Broadcast System (CBS).
Think of conventional SMS as a postal service. Each message is addressed to an individual recipient and goes through a delivery process that may experience delays when networks are congested.
Cell broadcast, by contrast, works like a public loudspeaker. A warning is broadcast through selected mobile network cells to compatible phones within their coverage areas.
Whether there are 100 or 100,000 devices within the targeted area, the system does not need to send a separate message to each recipient.
It requires neither mobile data nor Wi-Fi, although devices must still be connected to a participating 4G or 5G mobile network.
Unlike many digital services we use today, MySiren does not identify individual recipients, nor can authorities determine whether a particular person has received or read an alert.
The invisible machinery behind a single alert
Consider a district facing an imminent risk of flooding.

Once the threat has been identified and assessed, designated and trained personnel within authorised disaster management agencies prepare, approve and issue a warning through the secured MySiren platform.
The affected geographical area must then be translated into the relevant mobile network cells.

Here lies an interesting technical challenge. Flood zones follow rivers and terrain, while mobile network coverage is shaped by telecommunications infrastructure. The two do not always align, meaning people just outside an affected area may also receive an alert.
Once issued, the warning passes through participating telecommunications networks before compatible phones display it through their built-in emergency alert functions.
Coordination is the real infrastructure
Malaysia’s telecommunications landscape comprises different network operators, equipment and technical configurations, alongside millions of devices running different operating systems.

Getting these technologies to work together goes beyond ensuring that mobile networks can broadcast a warning. Devices must also support Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) and Malaysia-specific software configurations.
Even two people sitting at the same coffee shop may receive an alert at slightly different times, depending on their network connections and how their devices process the warning.
Beyond engineering lies the challenge of coordinating regulators, disaster management authorities, technical agencies, telecommunications providers and device manufacturers.

The system must also contend with circumstances that could compromise it, such as floods disrupting electricity supplies or damaging telecommunications infrastructure. Unlike network congestion, a complete loss of mobile connectivity can prevent alerts from being received.

This puts the nationwide public alert test scheduled for November 29 into perspective. MySiren is expected to be operational by the end of 2026, subject to the necessary testing and readiness assessments.
Testing is not simply about whether a phone rings, but whether the different components can work together reliably.
Public readiness matters too. Keeping devices updated and relevant emergency alert settings enabled is important, while existing warning channels such as SMS, television and radio remain essential.
The social media paradox
In today’s environment, communicating an initiative of this scale may not be the hardest part, given the reach of social media.
Ironically, it is also because of social media that the challenge becomes greater.

Screenshots can circulate without context, while messages impersonating MySiren may spread through SMS, messaging applications and social media. Genuine MySiren alerts, however, appear through a phone’s built-in emergency alert function.
A fabricated warning could cause unnecessary panic, while a genuine one dismissed as another viral message could have serious consequences.
Engineers can build a system capable of broadcasting warnings to millions of devices. What they cannot engineer as easily is the public trust needed to make people act on them.

Ultimately, the success of MySiren should not be measured by how loudly our phones ring during a nationwide test, but by how reliably warnings reach those in danger and whether people know how to respond.

For the public, it may be nothing more than a notification on a screen. Behind that apparent simplicity is an entire ecosystem of technology, infrastructure and people working together to make those few critical seconds count.*This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
a769a8eb87909b5c: LONDON, Nov 27 — Manchester United are error-prone, leaky at the back and desperately short of confidence as they face the growing nightmare of a Premier League relegation battle.
Talk of the Red Devils going down still appears fanciful but analysts Opta say they have a 27 percent chance of dropping into the Championship as they prepare to host impressive Brentford.
At the top end of the table, Manchester City’s match at Arsenal appears to be a must-win for Enzo Maresca’s team, who have fallen off the pace after a barren spell.
AFP Sport looks at three talking points ahead of the weekend action:
United’s error count
Midfielder Kobbie Mainoo warned “no one’s coming to save us” after Manchester United’s 4-0 hammering by Liverpool last week left them in the relegation zone.
More mistakes, notably from goalkeeper Senne Lammens — together with some controversial refereeing decisions — cost them a morale-boosting Champions League win at Sporting Lisbon in midweek.

Following their 2-2 draw, United had conceded the most goals (36), the most penalties (five), and had received the most red cards (five) of any Premier League team this season across all competitions.
New manager Mauricio Pochettino will now be in no doubt as to the scale of the job at Old Trafford as United chase just their second league win of the season against Brentford.
“I think we need to encourage and we need to really believe in our play,” Pochettino told TNT Sports after Wednesday’s match in Portugal. “We need to believe more and more and more.”
But until he finds a way to cut out individual errors, opponents will always fancy their chances against the struggling giants.
Blunt Arsenal
Champions Arsenal, despite their impressive results, are showing a worrying inability to kill off opponents.
In their past nine matches in all competitions, the Gunners have won just one game by more than a single goal.
They had 30 shots in their midweek 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund but just four of those were on target.
Kai Havertz has a paltry three Premier League goals this season while fellow forward Viktor Gyokeres has yet to get off the mark in the top flight.
“The feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put (in) that kind of performance, the amount of chances, the situation,” Arteta said after the Dortmund draw.
“There is an element of luck, there is an element of us finishing the actions better.”
City, already six points behind Arsenal, travel to the Emirates low on confidence after taking a single point from their past four league matches.
Chelsea’s wobbly defence
Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea started the season as the swashbuckling entertainers of the Premier League but defensive problems are threatening to derail them.

Only the bottom two teams, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, and promoted sides Ipswich and Coventry have poorer defensive records than the Blues, who have conceded 20 goals in their 11 league games.
Chelsea have lost three of their past four matches and are already five points behind fourth-placed Liverpool in the race for Champions League qualification.

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher was critical of Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill after last week’s 4-1 mauling by Leeds, questioning whether they have the physical presence and leadership required to form a successful partnership.
He believes the club must strengthen their defence in the January transfer window if they are to remain in the mix for Champions League qualification.
“Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” he said on Sky Sports.

e1f026f633510ed3: LABUAN, Nov 27 — The Labuan branch of the Royal Malaysian Customs Department (JKDM) has recorded a total of 167 smuggling-related cases involving seizures, with an estimated value including duties and taxes of RM18.83 million, from Jan 1 to Nov 15 this year.

Labuan Customs director Saidin Jalaludin said the department conducted 12 enforcement operations during the period, including five special operations targeting vehicles, cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, drugs and other commodities.

He said the overall seizures comprised 66 vehicles, 116,396 sticks of kretek cigarettes, six electronic cigarette devices, 1,454 kilogrammes (kg) of tobacco and 187,518.92 litres of alcoholic beverages.

The department also confiscated 7.74 grammes of cannabis, 15 kg of ketum and 15 millilitres of methylenedioxy methamphetamine (MDMA), with all drug-related cases detected through the scanning of courier consignments at Labuan Airport.

Saidin said the five special operations accounted for nearly RM4.96 million in seizures, inclusive of duties and taxes, with vehicles suspected of violating tax exemption conditions applicable to the duty-free island accounting for the bulk of the amount.
“Three vehicle-focused operations, namely Op Radu, Op Radu Bersepadu and Op 90 Plus, resulted in the confiscation of 25 vehicles worth RM4.85 million, including duties and taxes.

“The modus operandi involved vehicles taken out of duty-free Labuan under the 90-day tax exemption facility but which remained outside the island beyond the permitted period, as well as vehicles smuggled out without the department’s approval,” he said at a press conference at the Kiansam Encorcement Division Complex here today.

Saidin said investigations revealed some vehicles had remained outside Labuan for more than two years, far exceeding the permitted 90-day period, with several traced to locations as far away as Kuching, Sarawak.
The department also uncovered cases involving vehicles bearing falsified registration numbers in an apparent attempt to mislead enforcement officers and evade detection.

He said Op Radu, conducted throughout Sabah in February, resulted in the seizure of nine vehicles valued at RM895,000, while Op Radu Bersepadu, carried out in Sabah and Sarawak in June, saw 12 vehicles confiscated, amounting to RM2.67 million.
“Another four vehicles worth RM1.28 million were seized during Op 90 Plus, conducted in selected areas of Sarawak this month,” he said.
Meanwhile, Op Gembleng, jointly conducted with the Labuan Health Department’s Pharmacy Division in April, recorded 26 cases following 40 inspections at courier company premises.

The operation resulted in the confiscation of cosmetic and pharmaceutical products worth RM2,387, suspected of contravening provisions under the Customs Act 1967, Poisons Act 1952 and Sale of Drugs Act 1952.
Saidin said the products were purchased through e-commerce platforms or other online channels and brought into Labuan without the necessary regulatory approvals.

In October, Op Samudera conducted by the department’s Marine Unit in waters surrounding Labuan and along Sabah’s west coast uncovered three cases involving 28,000 sticks of cigarettes and 1,480.08 litres of alcoholic beverages, valued at RM109,811.63, inclusive of duties and taxes.

He said the cases involved suspected offences under Section 135(1)(d) of the Customs Act 1967 for knowingly possessing or keeping uncustomed or prohibited goods, while the maritime cases also involved Section 135(1)(e) of the same Act for knowingly transporting or removing such goods.
Saidin urged the public to cooperate with the department in combating smuggling activities and refraining from involvement in such offences.
“Smuggling not only deprives the country of revenue but also poses a threat to national security and the well-being of the people,” he added.

Members of the public with information on smuggling activities are encouraged to contact the Customs toll-free hotline at 1-800-88-8855 or the nearest Customs office, with the department assuring that the identities of informants would be kept confidential. — Bernama

63167c3504ee3f27: Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson. There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi. He sustained a horrific injury as a teenager, which left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, he uses his own experience to guide his practice as a trauma therapist.

He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand. Unlike standard prosthetics, this one connects directly to nerves in Avi’s arm. He literally has wires coming out of his arm to plug it in with.
Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently, for things like drinking from a cup (which is not easy) and writing (also not easy).
What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself.

He has learned how to use something like seven different prosthetics in the 17 years since his accident. By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job. He had surgery to implant electrodes in his arm and will eventually need another to remove them. And he won’t even get to keep the latest prosthetic long term.

“While it’s unfortunate at times, and irritating at times, I do not regret what has come from [the accident], or the fact that it happened,” he told me. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

The research team at the University of Utah that is running the trial hopes it will answer longstanding questions about the technology. How does it fare in a real-world setting, outside of the lab? What do people end up using it for? Where can improvements be made?

There may be some surprises along the way. Avi has found that his prosthetic wrist can feel sore and stiff when it’s been overused, just like his flesh-and-blood wrist. Weirdly, that feeling can be relieved by stretching it out. What’s going on here? No one really knows.

Scientists don’t know whether Avi’s brain will change as a result of using the bionic hand, either. Before the trial started, they performed brain scans to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs—how might a bionic limb affect their brains?

Avi will have the device until late January 2027 at the least, and potentially for another year. After that? Again, no one knows. It will depend on how the research is progressing, how Avi feels, and how much funding the team can secure. As a result, it’s not clear how long the device might even be expected to last in a person’s body.
I’ll be following this study, though, and will keep you posted.

fd03cdaa4510b90c: Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier.
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) says that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs).
These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a "Hybrid Navy" comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges.

The UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620, built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding company in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company.
We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry.

The contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII says it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting.

HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations.
The new vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open.

By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class, but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems.
The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP, an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance.
The new REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD.
"This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP.

Like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy.

In trials announced in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®

98371666cc7e959f: ISTANBUL: Turkey needs to overhaul its financial regulators after an investment fund scandal that has sent a chill through the country's capital markets, five bankers and a former senior official said.

The crisis centres on groups of funds that poured money into thinly traded stocks, swelling the value of their assets to more than US$20 billion and generating extraordinary returns before they became unable to meet withdrawal demands and were liquidated.

Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) approved 33 initial public offerings in the first nine months of 2026, almost double the 18 approved in the whole of the previous year.

Restoring trust needs to start with the right appointments, Ramazan Basak, a former deputy chairman of Turkey's Financial Crimes Investigation Board, told Reuters.
"These institutions should be led by people who know the sector well, have a reputation for integrity and have no political ties," he said in an interview.
Those detained in recent weeks include several senior former officials from the SPK and Turkey's Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK).
Prosecutors are also set to investigate Sahap Kavcioglu, a former central bank governor who announced his resignation as head of the BDDK this month and has denied wrongdoing.
One senior banker said the problems stemmed from appointments at bodies including the BDDK and the SPK, although he added that the institutions themselves were sound.
The BDDK declined to comment. The SPK and the Finance Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The BDDK had played a major role in putting the banking sector on a sound footing after a 2001 crisis, but had later taken a more passive stance, a second senior banker said.

One problem faced by regulatory authorities over recent years was an exodus of staff to the private sector because of worsening relative pay and conditions, a person in the banking sector said. That led to a shortage of expertise, an executive at a portfolio management company said.

On Thursday, Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said at a press conference that the SPK's powers to intervene against problematic funds were being strengthened and that Turkey was working to meet MSCI Emerging Markets Index requirements by the end of the year.
Early on Friday, Turkey's official gazette showed that Yusuf Kenan Bagir, a former general director and economist at the central bank, had been appointed as the new head of the BDDK.
Ripple effect

Some observers have said the crisis was allowed to brew despite public warnings of market manipulation. But once it broke, swift action by authorities contained any systemic risk, against a backdrop of economic challenges including higher energy prices due to the Iran war, analysts said. Last week, Turkey's foreign reserves dropped to their lowest level since 2024 on a net basis.

"In the past at times of stress in the Turkish economy, Turkish households would start exchanging their savings into hard currency, maybe buy more gold as an insurance," said Magdalena Polan, head of emerging markets macroeconomic research at PGIM.
"Outside of a small wobble in some flows in the FX market from the households, we actually did not see that at all."
While consumer confidence dipped to 84.8 in October from 91.9 in September, it has edged back up to 86.8 this month, data from Turkey's state statistics agency shows.

But the crisis has jolted capital markets. Istanbul's main stock exchange index has fallen more than 18% since September 16, the day before the SPK ordered the liquidation of 131 funds. That exceeds a 1.5% dip in European stocks and the AI-driven 15% drop in MSCI's global emerging market index.

Nearly 130 people had been formally arrested as of last week, said Justice Minister Akin Gurlek, adding that the structure behind the scheme was "not limited to simple stock market manipulation or stock market fraud, but is a comprehensive criminal organisation".

President Tayyip Erdogan said last week there would be "not the slightest compromise" on holding those responsible to account and the government had prioritised paying back small investors. Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on Thursday that 199 billion lira (US$3.93 billion) had been paid back, and that authorities would take steps to protect investors.
'Made to beg for our own money'
Savers among the nearly half a million who invested in the funds are angry over what they see as corruption.

At a protest outside the SPK headquarters in Ankara last week attended by several hundred people, some savers demanded full repayment, with several describing how they unsuccessfully sought to sell their investments as the funds imploded.
"We have been made to beg for our own money," said Murat Galip Alparslan, a roofer, adding that he had lost 26 years of his own savings as well as money saved by his mother.
"My family's future has been stolen," he said.
It is unclear what the total loss to investors will be, with claims leading to a wave of legal action.

Criminal complaints are being filed over trades in stocks that took place up to two years ago and should have been referred to prosecutors much sooner, said Basak, who expects "hundreds of trades" to come under scrutiny in court.

a03f78dab76c974e: ‘All we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.’
Originally published on Global Voices
Jhiko Manyika performing at Zanzibar Reggae Festival. Image by Zanzibar Reggae Festival, used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
When courts stop protecting people, people stop talking. They stay quiet because speaking up could cost them their lives or their families. So who speaks for the voiceless?

In Tanzania, one answer comes with a guitar. Reggae artist Jhikoman, born Jhikolabwino Siza Manyika, has released a song called “Justice,” written for everyone who lost a loved one, and the right to mourn them out loud, after the October 2025 general elections that declared Samia Suluhu Hassan president.
His favorite lyric sums up the song:
“We don’t need no war, all we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.”
Listen to Justice below:
Tanzania’s image shattered

For nearly six decades, Tanzania cultivated an image of calm, consensus, and order. The scale of the 2025 election violence shocked many people because it broke that image. The BBC reported that security forces and unrest killed more than 500 people. International observers criticized the vote for its lack of transparency, and the African Union and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) said the election fell short of democratic standards.
Jhikoman, who watched these events unfold, says the losses moved him to write. He told Global Voices:

“I was deeply moved by reports and accounts of people losing their lives, families losing their loved ones, and citizens being silenced by the authorities when they simply wanted to speak out, seek answers, and mourn those they had lost. That pain became my motivation to write ‘Justice.’”
This song is more than a song; it is a cry for humanity, a call for accountability, and a reminder that the pain of those who have lost loved ones should never be silenced.
A reggae musician from Bagamoyo

Every stage name has a story, and Jhikoman’s is no different: JHIKO (from his first name, Jhikolabwino) plus MAN (from his surname, Manyika). Jhikoman has performed since 1994, blending acoustic reggae with African music and singing in English, Swahili, and his mother tongue, Kinyasa.

His musical life started at home. His older brother played guitar, and young Jhikoman watched, listened and dreamed. In secondary school, he fell for reggae, drawn by its messages of peace, love, unity, equality, and justice. He idolized Bob Marley and Alpha Blondy, and he covered their songs. Then his brother gave him the advice that changed everything: If you want to be a musician, write your own songs.
Jhikolabwino Siza Manyika performing at the Zanzibar International Film Festival. Photo by Micky Grapher, used with permission.

He took the advice to heart. In 1994, he stepped into a recording studio for the first time. In 2000, he released the album “Afro-Caribbean Beat,” and its title track became a local hit. The opportunities followed quickly. In 2001, he performed at the Zanzibar International Film Festival. In 2003, he wrote a song for Participatory Ecological Land Use Management (PELUM) Tanzania, an organization that supports small-scale farmers, and the commission took him to South Africa to perform at the World Forum for Sustainable Development. Since then, his music has carried him across East and Southern Africa and to stages in Europe.
Today he lives in Bagamoyo, where he volunteers as a music instructor at the Bagamoyo Institute of Arts and Culture and mentors young artists. He says:
“For me, music is more than entertainment. It is a powerful tool for communication, education, unity, and social change.”
The violence reaches home
The violence after the 2025 general election touched Jhikoman’s own circle. He says police shot and killed the wife of a close friend while she drove home, in front of her two children. He noted:

“No innocent person should lose their life simply because of violence surrounding an election. The victims and their families deserve justice, dignity, and the freedom to mourn without fear or intimidation.”

According to Jhikoman, the people who spoke out and wanted democratic reform often got silenced. They called for changes to election laws and procedures that would guarantee free, fair, transparent, and credible elections. They also demanded equal opportunities for all political parties, independent electoral oversight, and the freedom to choose their leaders without intimidation.
Why it’s so hard to get justice

Article 18 of Tanzania’s 1977 Constitution guarantees freedom of expression. Jhikoman says that some victims and their families have tried to enforce that right in court. However, getting justice has proved “extremely difficult.”

He points to several cases. After the alleged abduction of opposition activist Mpaluka Nyagali, known as Mdude, in May 2025, his wife filed a habeas corpus petition at the High Court in Mbeya. The court dismissed it on July 9, 2025, and his whereabouts remained unknown. A lawyer for former ambassador Humphrey Polepole filed a similar application after he disappeared in October 2025, and the court dismissed that as well.

Two advocates, Tito Magoti and Bob Wangwe, filed a case at the East African Court of Justice challenging the conduct of the election, and it remains pending. Authorities also arrested Tundu Lissu, chairman of the opposition party CHADEMA, and charged him with treason after he demanded electoral reforms. On November 6, 2026, the High Court acquitted him of treason, convicted him of incitement, and sentenced him to four years in prison. He remains imprisoned.
Jhikoman says:

“The law guarantees freedom of expression, but people who criticize the government face arrest, intimidation, and, in some cases, alleged abduction. The central problem is not simply the absence of laws; it is the difficulty of holding those responsible for violations accountable.”
A song that carries a message abroad

Listeners have responded well to Jhikoman’s message. He says that many Tanzanians feel the song finally carries their message to the international community. They believe the judiciary and parliament have lost their independence, which leaves them with little confidence that local institutions will deliver justice. Many now place their hope in international attention, because Tanzania has signed numerous international human rights agreements.
Some listeners also worry about his safety. They urge him to take care, since abductions and enforced disappearances remain serious concerns in parts of East Africa.

“I take those warnings seriously,” he says. “But I also believe that music can be a powerful tool for speaking out, raising awareness, and standing up for peace, justice, and the dignity of human life. … True peace means treating one another equally, standing up against injustice, respecting human rights, and giving everyone the freedom to express themselves without fear.”

Jhikoman’s story shows how justice shapes daily life long before anyone reaches a courtroom. When people trust that the justice system will treat them fairly and quickly, they speak out, report wrongdoings, and rebuild after loss. When they lose that trust, silence spreads. One reggae song cannot repair broken institutions, but it can name the problem, keep the memory of the dead in public view, and ask listeners to hold their leaders accountable.

542a6ebbdc134cae: The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.
"We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio shows depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.
The PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away.
"We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore."
Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air.
Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down.
One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea.
And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs.
When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded.
Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs.
"Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register.

"After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol."
As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka.
"Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote.
By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again.
"We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote.
The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen.

"It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs.

1343a3d87eb0ded5: AWS now offers two new types of cloudy computers: emulated Androids and simulated iPhones.

The cloudy colossus announced both virtual offerings on Wednesday. They’re part of its Device Farm service, which previously saw AWS offer developers the chance to test their software on actual iOS and Android devices that reside in the Amazonian cloud. AWS will now also host virtual devices running Android and iOS.
AWS touts the virtual mobile devices as superior to physical devices.

“With virtual devices, you can shift testing left to stages that need high speed and volume, such as pull requests, code merges, and smoke tests, and keep real devices for later stages that need high fidelity, such as regression and release testing,” the cloudy business unit argues in its launch announcement.

AWS also says developers can get to work faster on a virtual iPhone or Pixel. “Virtual devices running the latest device and OS typically start in seconds, and others start in around a minute,” the outfit argues.
That may sound appetizing, but Amazon’s menu of virtual devices is short and bland.

When The Register logged on as an AWS user, the only emulated Android phone listed was a Google Pixel 10, running Android 15, 16, or 17. An emulated Pixel tablet running Android 17 is also on the menu.
At the time of writing, we could find only a virtual iPhone 16, running iOS 18.6, 23.61, and 27.0.
Analyst firm Counterpoint’s list of the world’s top 10 best-selling smartphones in Q2 of 2026 does not include a single Pixel device. The iPhone 16 occupies 10th place.
iPhone 17 models occupy the first, second, third, and seventh place on the list.

AWS might excite more developers if it adds emulators for the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy A07 4G, A17 5G, A17 4G, and Galaxy S26, as they occupy the fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth and ninth places on Counterpoint’s list.
Amazon’s choice of a Pixel tablet is also an oddity given analyst firm IDC doesn’t list Google among its top five tablet vendors.

Amazon does offer physical Galaxy A17 devices and three versions of the iPhone 17. But Device Farm doesn’t offer any foldable devices, meaning developers struggling to wrap their heads around the iPhone Duo will need either ask Apple for a loaner or shell out $2,000 to acquire one.
At least developers don’t have to change behavior to access the few virtual devices AWS offers, as existing Device Farm APIs and test frameworks will work on real or notional machines. ®

1ad09001caf799be: From William Ng

Malaysia’s ambition to move up the economic value chain is shared by every serious business owner in the country. We all want higher wages, greater automation and a workforce driven by skills rather than sheer numbers.

Yet, in our haste to reduce reliance on foreign workers, we risk confusing the symptom with the cure. Blocking or limiting the entry of foreign workers in unskilled and semi-skilled jobs across manufacturing, plantations, construction and food and beverage (F&B) does not automatically create higher-paying jobs for Malaysians. Instead, it disrupts the very businesses that keep our economy running and create higher-skilled roles for locals.
The myth of job substitution
The prevailing policy assumption is straightforward: restrict foreign workers, and local workers will step in to fill the gap. This is a myth born out of desperation.

Malaysia’s overall unemployment rate is at a historic low of 2.9%, effectively signalling full employment. Meanwhile, the economy produces hundreds of thousands of graduates annually, while youth unemployment hovers at around 10%. This gap is not caused by foreign workers taking jobs from Malaysians, but by a structural mismatch between job aspirations and skills. In short, our problem is underemployment, and foreign workers have little to do with it.

Critics often argue that Malaysians would readily take up 3D (dirty, dangerous and difficult) jobs if employers simply paid more, pointing to the hundreds of thousands of Malaysians working at F&B outlets, construction sites and factories across the causeway. But that comparison ignores basic arithmetic. An SME in Johor Bahru earns revenue in ringgit based on what local consumers can afford. It cannot charge in Singapore dollars to pay Singapore-level wages without triggering severe domestic inflation.

Even when vacancies are advertised on MYFutureJobs, young Malaysians with diplomas and degrees are not rushing to harvest oil palm bunches at remote estates, pour concrete under the sun, wash dishes in kitchens or operate repetitive manual assembly lines. Research by Khazanah Research Institute has shown that local and foreign workers occupy different segments of the labour market. They complement rather than replace each other.

When a restaurant is restricted from hiring foreign workers, it does not necessarily raise wages and recruit local graduates. Instead, it may reduce operating hours, delay expansion and eliminate supervisory, accounting and managerial positions that Malaysians actually want. Forcing SME manufacturers and F&B operators out of business because of labour shortages does not create automated alternatives. It reduces supply, weakens competitiveness and drives up costs for Malaysians.
The real cost of flawed policy design
Existing labour policies suffer from three structural flaws that penalise compliant businesses without resolving their dependence on foreign workers.

First, there is the assumption that taxing businesses more heavily for employing foreign workers will accelerate automation. The fact is, not every job can be automated. A high-tech semiconductor production line may be highly automated from the outset, but robots cannot climb hills to harvest durians, nor can a machine easily replace a barber.
During the pandemic, labour shortages cost the palm oil sector an estimated RM1 billion annually in unharvested crops. We are already seeing signs of repeating this self-inflicted damage.

Second, there is the misconception that requiring employers to advertise vacancies on MYFutureJobs will encourage locals to take up these jobs. In reality, very few of the positions intended for foreign workers attract applications from Malaysians. The requirement instead forces businesses to wait at least two weeks rather than fill vacancies immediately. The resulting revenue losses can be substantial and illustrate how poorly conceived policies can be when built on flawed assumptions.

Third, excessive restrictions on foreign worker recruitment are fuelling the shadow economy. When legal recruitment channels are frozen, approvals are delayed or worker-to-employee ratios become unrealistic, businesses do not simply shut down overnight. Instead, demand spills into the shadow economy, depriving the government of levy revenue and leaving workers without legal protection.
Why we cannot blindly copy other markets
Policymakers often point to Singapore, South Korea and Western economies as examples of how strict labour caps can force businesses to innovate and raise wages.
While the aspiration is admirable, importing another country's labour policies without replicating its economic foundations risks creating stagflation.
First, these economies began moving away from low-cost labour after building deep domestic capital markets, world-class research ecosystems and large-scale high-value export industries.

Second, consider how these economies actually operate today. Singapore remains heavily reliant on foreign workers in construction, marine and service sectors. Japan and South Korea have also expanded special technical intern and agricultural visa programmes over the past decade because of shortages of domestic workers willing to take up 3D jobs.

Even advanced economies recognise that modern service and technology sectors cannot function without an operational foundation. High-value engineers, chefs and supply chain planners cannot do their jobs if no one is clearing construction sites, preparing kitchens or moving freight.
A smarter path forward

Reducing dependence on foreign workers over the long term is the right direction, and most progressive businesses understand this. They also accept their responsibility to pay statutory wages, provide proper worker accommodation and healthcare and combat the employment of illegal foreign workers.

What we need is proper policy sequencing: reassessing sectors where cutting foreign worker numbers would be counterproductive and creating jobs that match the aspirations of Malaysians, rather than assuming the two are mutually exclusive.

When we treat foreign workers as a problem rather than vital contributors to the economy, and fixate on outward currency transfers while ignoring the far greater tax revenue generated by their economic output, we risk continuing to score own goals against our own economic growth.

Our businesses, especially SMEs, want to become the dynamic, high-wage companies policymakers envision. But restricting foreign workers in lower-skilled jobs is not the way to achieve that. Give businesses the workforce they need at the operational level so they can build the high-wage, automated economy Malaysia wants tomorrow.
William Ng is president of the Small and Medium Enterprises Association of Malaysia.

2d5d412f1f98d7b7: From Samirul Othman
Pasir Mas MP Ahmad Fadhli Shaari asks why MISC should borrow RM2.27 billion to buy into Yinson Holdings Berhad, a company that owes billions. He asks if it amounts to a bailout.

My answer is that MISC can spend years expanding its overseas offshore business, one vessel at a time, or buy a stake in a platform which owns vessels already at work, with paying customers and teams that can compete for the next contract.

Take Yinson’s Agogo vessel in Angola. It is a floating facility that processes oil and gas at sea. It took 29 months from winning the contract to producing its first oil, even though Yinson delivered ahead of schedule. It is now on a firm 15-year contract.
In Brazil, Yinson’s Anna Nery is on a 25-year contract with Petrobras that runs to 2048. MISC would be investing in an established business with vessels already in operation and generating revenue.

The consortium of MISC, Yinson’s founding Lim family and the Employees Provident Fund is offering RM2.50 a share for the remaining 55.2% of Yinson. The RM4.03 billion goes to shareholders who sell their existing shares in Yinson.
MISC plans to put up RM3.03 billion, about three quarters of the sum it borrowed. Borrowing spreads the cost and keeps some of MISC’s cash available for the rest of its fleet.

The Lim family is not only keeping its money in the business but adding about RM1 billion in cash. This clearly doesn’t sound like a bailout. EPF is carrying over its roughly 17.1% stake without putting in fresh cash for the buyout. Again, no public funds are going into the deal.
Weighing acquisition against organic growth
Based on Yinson’s latest quarterly announcement, offshore production contracted revenue backlog amounted to approximately US$19.3 billion.

This represents future receipts from leases and charters that customers have committed to. That money will come in over many years, and the company has bills and lenders to pay. But it gives MISC a starting point for valuing the stake based on contracts already signed.

MISC’s first ultra-deepwater vessel began producing oil at Brazil’s Mero field in 2024. It already knows that market. The Yinson deal adds three vessels in Brazil and brings new relationships in markets such as Ghana and Angola.
In Ghana, Eni recently hired Yinson to expand the gas processing capacity of a vessel it already runs there. An operating fleet gives a supplier a track record that can win the next job.
The offshore industry rewards suppliers that can deliver the same kind of work again and again. In Guyana, ExxonMobil’s local affiliate recently awarded SBM Offshore its sixth vessel contract.

A builder that can build on proven engineering solutions, call on engineers who have worked together before and show that its vessels run reliably can make a stronger bid. That is the advantage I am expecting MISC to seek from Yinson.

MISC could also bid with Yinson on individual projects. Buying a stake not only gives it a share in contracts already earning money but gives both companies a reason to invest in engineering teams they can use across several bids.
For Petronas, that means its marine infrastructure arm can build a bigger business serving oil producers around the world, including on fields that Petronas is invested.

I take it that MISC has put a value on that head start. It can compare the price of buying into an operating platform versus the cost of building vessels, hiring the teams and waiting three to four years for contracts to start paying. It should run the numbers on both routes to see which brings in more cash, and how soon – balancing risks with expected long-term business impact.
The debt has to pay its way

Fadhli is right that Yinson’s lenders and holders of preference shares rank ahead of ordinary shareholders. In October, for example, Yinson announced a bond issue to replace existing debt on the Agogo vessel. That debt is tied to an operating asset with a paying customer. The proposed MISC loan has a different job. It would fund the share purchase, while Yinson continues to service its own debt.

What does the loan cost MISC? Its published illustration puts annual borrowing costs at about RM107 million. Using Yinson’s last audited results up to January 2026, MISC estimates it would have recorded about RM176 million as its share of profit. That offers an early indication of how the purchase could contribute even after interest. MISC still needs to show how much of that profit can reach it as cash.

Also, the full RM2.27 billion of borrowings quoted by Fadhli needs to be considered properly against Yinson’s equity value. Assuming a 16% premium using MISC’s announcement, MISC's borrowings to buy the Yinson shares at the current trading price would have been around RM1.96 billion.

Therefore, the real question is whether MISC’s borrowings for this premium, of around RM310 million, is more than that required to incentivise Yinson shareholders to sell their shares. This is something that MISC’s independent adviser would have to consider in its report.

RM3.03 billion is a lot of money, but this should be considered in the context of large offshore assets which can cost up to US$3 billion to construct. Also, the proposed RM2.50/share offer price doesn’t seem inconsistent with the RM2.26–3.83/share range of target prices that analysts had previously estimated for Yinson before the deal was announced.

Ultimately, MISC’s board should show that the vessels in the Yinson portfolio can generate cashflow to pay both the holders of preference shares and support a sensible return to MISC and its partners.
The writer is a Malaysian economist, international relations analyst and senior consultant.

a908b34b17ee8786: India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens.

The platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants.
DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities.

India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka

India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.”

“An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.”
eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an update that fixes the problem.

While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities.
Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®
