In response, Lavrov said Russia wanted to build a new security framework that would encompass all of Europe and Asia – echoing the Soviet Union’s communist alliances during the Cold War. A new arrangement like this would be “committed to the principles of indivisible security, openness and equality”, Lavrov said, adding European nations were welcome to join. Russia does not “desire nor plan any war whatsoever with Europe”, he stressed. But he added: If Europe, as it threatens, is itself preparing for war and initiates one, we are ready. A security proposal based on “sovereignty” and “equality” may sound appealing to some states across the region. However, there are several reasons to be sceptical. What Europe wants The prevailing view in Europe is that Russia is the continent’s principal security threat. So, the idea of European states joining Russia in a new arrangement of any sort is unlikely to gain broad acceptance. And despite Russian President Vladimir Putin’s claims he is not against “having a dialogue with Europe, Moscow has made clear it does not want European representatives in the Ukraine peace talks. So it stands to reason Europe wouldn’t have a voice in a future security agreement either. That said, the political view towards Russia in Europe is evolving. As economic pressures continue to mount, support for right-wing, populist parties is growing, including one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party opposes financial and military support for Ukraine, arguing the war is not in Germany’s national interests. In fact, its platform in one recent eastern state election where it finished first called for a revival of Russian language teaching, an end to sanctions and closer energy ties with Russia. This highlights the diversity of views in some countries on both the war and Europe’s broader strategic priorities. Some have raised the possibility of a more robust Organization for Security and Co-operation (the only European security group that Russia belongs to), or a revived NATO-Russia Council. However, this seems far-fetched in the absence of trust between the two sides. Many in Europe believe Russia’s true aims for a new security framework are to carve up the continent into Cold War-era spheres of influence and expand its influence beyond its borders. Read more: Russia wanted a new world order. This wasn’t the one it had in mind What China wants Second, it remains unclear how China, the region’s other major power, and its own security ambitions fit within Russia’s vision. Chinese foreign policy has long emphasised a principle of not interfering in the domestic affairs of other states. This has proven attractive to many authoritarian countries. At the same time, China has successfully advanced major global economic initiatives, notably the Belt and Road Initiative. And Beijing often promotes its own vision of the international order. As such, Russia’s proposed security framework would need to accommodate another major power with its own interests and priorities. Despite their growing cooperation in recent years, China and Russia are also competing for influence in a pivotal Eurasian region – Central Asia. While Russia has traditionally been the dominant power in the region, China has quietly advanced to the point where it can now compete with, if not surpass, Russia’s influence. What the rest of Asia wants Lastly, Eurasia is already home to a complex landscape of international organisations, blocs and multilateral security agreements. Beyond the European Union, these include the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the BRICS (the group originally comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), and the Gulf Cooperation Council, among others. Each of these groupings has its own distinct strategic interests and priorities. So, it remains unclear how a new Russia-led security framework would interact with these groups, or potentially compete with them. Indeed, there seems to be a growing preference, especially in Asia, for smaller alliances between countries with similar ideological world views, such as the new security pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey. At the same time, other nations, particularly those in Southeast Asia, have held fast to their non-aligned status, preferring to seek partnerships with an array of countries that suit a variety of interests. Read more: What Australia could learn from its Southeast Asian neighbours about power and the changing global order What comes next? We may be witnessing the gradual erosion of the post-second world war international order. Now, the big question is what comes next. While Russia’s aims seem reminiscent of Soviet influence during the Cold War, this is a new world, and there are too many hurdles for its vision of a new security framework to become a reality. New international orders do not emerge overnight. Rather, they evolve through the cumulative decisions of states pursuing their own interests, forming new alignments, alliances and partnerships along the way. Dilnoza Ubaydullaeva receives funding from the Japan Foundation Program.
c23365c8add12072: Eleven days. That is how long it took for a disgrace to become a homecoming.
On Nov 12, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president and CEO, days after he admitted to an extramarital affair.

Reports linked him to Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly believe was recruited by Beijing to get close to him. China calls this a smear, and nothing has been proven in public. He confessed to it.

On Nov 17, board chair Harvey Jones told investors the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. On Nov 23, the board voted unanimously to bring him back, calling him the “right person to lead Nvidia” and his return is “in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.

Stockholders first. Not one word about integrity, about the code of conduct the company itself said he had breached, or about a wife of four decades whose private pain became global headlines. The stock had fallen more than 16% after his confession. The board did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic won.
Surprise, surprise. Except, none at all.
When the powerful fall into scandal, it is our children left asking the questions.
Today, the Malaysian version is playing out in Jalan Langgak Duta.
Najib Razak was convicted in the SRC International case for misappropriating RM42 million. That conviction was upheld by the Federal Court, and he went to Kajang prison in August 2022.
In September this year he received a conditional royal pardon, allowing him to be placed under house arrest subject to payment of a RM50 million fine.
His party ran a crowdfunding drive in his name, succeeded and paid the entire fine. He has, since Nov 10, been serving what remains of his sentence under house arrest until August 2028.
Within days, the prisons department was explaining a nearly eight-hour outing for Friday prayers, a hospital appointment and other engagements.
And all this while he appeals a separate 1MDB conviction carrying 15 years' jail and an RM11.4 billion fine.

The king’s prerogative of mercy is enshrined in our constitution, and I do not question it. Nvidia's board answers to shareholders by law. An affair is a moral failing, not a crime. Najib's supporters sincerely believe he has suffered enough, and some believe he was persecuted.
All true. And all beside the point.
The question is not whether these outcomes are legal. The question is what they teach.
The lessons our children are learning
Children do not learn values from speeches. They learn from watching what happens to people who break the rules.

And what are they watching? A man who betrayed his marriage and allegedly let a suspected foreign agent into his inner circle is back on the throne within a fortnight, thanked for his “humility”. A former prime minister convicted of abusing public funds is welcomed home with prayers, crowds and political rallies in his name.

The lesson is clear: consequences are for ordinary people. The clerk who pockets RM500 from the till is sacked and never works in that industry again. The schoolboy caught copying in his SPM exam has his results cancelled.
But if you are valuable enough, powerful enough, connected enough, a conviction becomes an inconvenience and a scandal becomes a sabbatical.

Where is dignity in this? Not with the wife who learned of her husband's betrayal along with the rest of the world. Not with the rakyat whose money vanished into luxury and lawyers' fees. Dignity, it seems, has been outsourced to whoever holds the shares or the votes.
Where is respect? We now “respect” results. We have stopped respecting character.
What we must teach instead

So what do I tell my grandchildren? Talent without character is a loaded gun. Brilliance makes you useful. Integrity makes you trustworthy. The world will always try to sell you the first as a substitute for the second. Do not buy it.
Sorry is not the same as accountability. Anyone can issue a statement "with the greatest humility". Real remorse costs something, and it is paid before the comeback, not instead of it.
Do not cheer for the fallen powerful. When you clap for a convicted man, you are telling every corrupt official waiting in line that the crowd will forgive them too.
Judge leaders by how they treat people who can do nothing for them. A spouse. A taxpayer. A junior employee. That is where character lives.
The rules must apply to everyone. The day we accept two sets of rules, one for the rich and one for the rest, is the day our children stop believing rules matter at all.
Boards will chase stock prices. Politicians will chase votes. But families, schools and communities do not have to follow them.
The real test is not what Nvidia's board or Malaysia's political class does next. It is what we say at the dinner table tonight, when a child looks up from the news and asks: “Is that okay?”
Our answer will shape a generation. Let it be a clear, unashamed “No”.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
d7eb7800e9b4155a: Agentic AI has supercharged demand for inference infrastructure. According to Goldman Sachs, token consumption is set to jump 24-fold to 120 quadrillion tokens per month between this year and 2030. Enterprises, wary of frontier model sticker shock, are now building their own GPU estates to cope.

Those enterprises shouldn't blindly follow hyperscalers' lead when taking AI inference kit into production. The indicators of success for such companies are different than those for a frontier model provider, and so are the constraints. DIY AI infrastructure at the enterprise level has to earn ROI quickly, meaning that enterprises must focus on sustained operation. That makes engineering criteria such as uptime, heat and power, service windows, and deployment times doubly important. The performance benchmarks that hyperscalers focus on won't matter nearly as much to the average bank or retailer.

ASUS is presenting the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, built on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, as a worked example of sustained AI inference infrastructure. It announced two models at NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October: the 3U hybrid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BHFS and the 2U fully liquid-cooled XR R1I12B-M1BLFS.
Agents change the compute bill

Agents represent a hockey stick curve for token consumption because an agent isn't a single prompt. It loops until the job's done, often spawning other versions of itself in the process. This is how it breaks a goal into steps and works through them iteratively.

While training is a batch workload, agent inference is a production service that runs around the clock and only gets bigger. NVIDIA is making each generation of systems more powerful than the last to keep up with the demands of both.

Running at scale, day after day, is another matter. A useful way to think about the infrastructure that does it is as a token factory: it takes in power, data and GPU compute and turns out tokens. What counts is throughput, meaning how many tokens, and how many users, the same power and floor space can serve, hour after hour.
Enterprises move from pilots to AI factories

Enterprises are moving ahead quickly with their AI factory projects. According to Deloitte's AI infrastructure survey, published in March, 64 percent of respondents have started limited or at-scale AI factory deployments, while 88 percent expect to do so by 2028. They are spending more on AI infrastructure to do it: 86 percent expect their budgets to increase over the next three years.

Enterprises have different problems from hyperscalers and frontier model companies, though. Model builders often get to design greenfield campuses around their GPUs. Conversely, enterprises are often working with small operations teams in existing datacenters that may not have been built with AI in mind. That means they need to think harder about maintenance windows, existing management tooling and predictable deployment. And they'll often be retrofitting halls whose racks rarely draw more than 30 kW.

In token factory terms, the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System is the core compute engine. Each system puts eight NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPUs on the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 platform, linked by sixth-generation NVLink. ASUS has designed its equipment to support the constraints above. Its customers can choose between the hybrid and fully liquid-cooled models, and they can opt for partial or full rack configurations by buying multiple trays. This enables them to match their facilities' needs.
Peak performance versus sustained performance

The other difference between model providers and enterprises lies in which numbers they care about. Peak performance is different from sustained performance. The first is a specification sheet number, while the second is what the GPU actually delivers hours into a heavy workload.

Production inference tends to run continuously, especially when it uses agents, as opposed to training, which is a sporadic job. So the sustained figure is the one that buyers pay for. Heat becomes a real issue here because when cooling can't keep up, GPUs throttle their clocks to protect themselves. In a token factory, a throttled GPU is a slower production line.

The more advanced the architecture becomes, the higher the stakes get. NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU has raised them to their highest point, delivering up to 400 petaflops of NVFP4 inference per eight-GPU board, according to NVIDIA's sparse specification. This is screamingly fast, but the increased heat per board means less margin before throttling.

ASUS designed both models to put direct-to-chip liquid cooling on every GPU. Only the 3U unit leaves the CPUs on air cooling. ASUS also says it puts every configuration through a 168-hour stress test.
Power and heat set the shape of the rack

As boards increase their compute density, pushing up the power and heat requirements, planning naturally has to move out of the server room and into the facility. That's the case whether you're talking about an entire NVL72 rack or a stack of eight-GPU servers like the ASUS systems.

There are other things to consider beyond heat. Few datacenters run racks drawing more than 30 kilowatts, says the Uptime Institute. Yet a single liquid-cooled tray of the ASUS systems draws up to 23.9 kilowatts, and a full rack of nine has a power budget of about 216 kilowatts.
Floor loading and power distribution matter as much as cooling.

NVIDIA HGX Rubin GPU raises the stakes again. The eight-GPU format enables organizations to buy their computing power in more granular steps. That's where the two ASUS systems come into their own. With few enterprises needing a training cluster at NVL72 scale, the advantage is that an HGX box lets them buy AI compute in digestible pieces.
The ASUS systems also come with a 54V busbar and cable-free board-to-board design. ASUS says this simplifies assembly and improves reliability.
Connectivity, storage and management

So that's space, power and heat. But a GPU board won't produce many tokens if the network, storage or operational tooling can't feed it properly. Agent workloads move context and data all the time, so east-west bandwidth and local storage are key to effective utilization. Any new equipment should ideally slot straight into the enterprise's existing management and monitoring tooling.

ASUS ships the whole rack, including servers, networking, power and storage, as a single blueprint. ASUS pre-validates this AI Factory reference architecture at rack scale so that organizations can plan for future growth. That includes dedicated management nodes and a management switch.

Inside each tray, ASUS has sized the data paths to keep the GPUs fed. Eight OSFP ports on NVIDIA ConnectX-9 give every GPU 800Gb/s of east-west bandwidth to the rest of the cluster, and an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU adds two 400GbE ports. Within the board, the eight GPUs talk to each other over NVLink at 3,600GB/s, ASUS says. The 2U tray takes up to 4TB of DDR5 system memory and has eight E1.S NVMe bays for fast local data access, while the 3U model offers a choice of U.2 or E1.S drives.
Built to be serviced

The other issue for enterprises putting AI inference into production is service and maintenance. In a liquid-cooled box, routine fixes can mean draining a coolant loop, which is downtime, and lost token output, that most enterprises can't afford, especially when dealing with non-batch workloads such as inferencing. So ASUS set out to make components quicker to swap.

On the 2U fully liquid-cooled model, ASUS did it with independent, tool-less CPU and GPU sleds, each with its own direct-to-chip cooling. On the 3U hybrid, ASUS says the air-cooled CPU sled cuts maintenance time by up to 50 percent.
From loading dock to first token

Services aren't just about server maintenance. They're also about decreasing the time to value for AI. Most enterprises won't have in-house rack-scale GPU integration skills, which is why pre-validation and design services are so important.

ASUS says its services run from early facility assessment through to operations. Its professional services cover five offerings: infrastructure design, deployment, performance optimization, AI platform development and lifecycle management. For rapid deployment, ASUS uses its own automation platform, the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center (AIDC).
Production needs a partner, not just a part number

So, with an enterprise token factory judged on how reliably it keeps producing rather than on peak FLOPS, in-house AI deployment teams will be back to focusing on the basics, albeit while dealing with an innovative technology. That means they'll be asking questions about sustained performance, heat and power in existing facilities. They'll be looking at integration at the rack level and with management software, along with service windows and deployment time. ASUS is positioning itself as a partner that can answer those questions with the ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System, which it's making available this quarter.
Find out more about the liquid-cooled ASUS NVIDIA HGX Rubin System
d3ed840d59d336ff: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 — The Malaysian Palm Oil Board (MPOB) has been urged to clarify the rules on mixing palm oil products from different countries in the same vessel tank, especially how such cargo should be declared before export.
Maritime expert Datuk Seri Jeyenderan Ramasamy said clear guidelines were needed so that the country of origin, grade and quantity of palm oil cargo were recorded accurately.
He said the issue went beyond how palm oil was handled during shipping. It also involved export documentation, licensing requirements and Malaysia’s reputation as a major palm oil exporter.
“When palm oil from Malaysia is mixed with products from another country in the same vessel tank, what country of origin should be stated in the export documents?
“Should both countries be identified, or can the entire cargo be declared under one country? These are questions that need clear answers,” he said.

Jeyenderan said it was important to tell commingling apart from blending. Commingling mixes palm oil products of the same type and grade, while blending combines products of different types or grades.
He said MPOB should clarify whether both were allowed when the products came from different countries, and whether specific licences or approvals were needed.
The board should also explain the laws and regulations covering such activities, including how the grade and country of origin of the final cargo must be declared, he added.
Jeyenderan said physically mixing products did not automatically change their legal country of origin, which depended on the applicable rules of origin and trade requirements.
He said buyers relied on export documents to verify the source, quality and quantity of what they bought.
“Any difference between the actual cargo and the information stated in the documents could lead to commercial disputes, difficulties in verifying shipments and possible regulatory issues,” he said.
Jeyenderan also claimed that MPOB officers no longer routinely boarded vessels to check documents and inspect cargo after the Covid-19 pandemic.

“Before Covid-19, MPOB officers would usually come on board ships to check the relevant documents whenever commingling or blending took place. When Malaysian palm oil cargo was mixed with other Malaysian cargo, they would check the documents from both the ship and the shore to make sure the operation followed MPOB’s rules.
“But after the pandemic, we no longer see MPOB officers coming on board to carry out these checks,” he alleged.
He said MPOB should clarify whether its inspection procedures had changed, and what alternative arrangements were in place to verify cargo properly.

Jeyenderan said companies handling cargo from different sources should keep proper records of the quantity, grade and country of origin of each product loaded into a vessel tank, along with details of any later mixing or blending.
These records would let the authorities verify what a cargo contained and make sure export declarations were accurate, he added.
He said unclear requirements could also lead exporters, traders, cargo owners, shipping companies and vessel operators to read the rules differently.
Jeyenderan said a formal clarification from MPOB would give businesses more certainty, especially those in international palm oil trading.
“Seeking clarification is not about restricting legitimate trade. It is about ensuring that businesses understand the rules and that every cargo is properly declared.
“Malaysia must protect its reputation as a reliable palm oil supplier. Accurate documentation and transparency are essential to maintaining the confidence of international buyers,” he said.
822ed28b282a2835: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 27 — The ringgit opened flat against the US dollar on Friday as cautious sentiment in the foreign exchange market continued to support demand for the greenback amid geopolitical and economic uncertainties.
At 8 am, the local currency was unchanged at 4.1135/1200 against the US dollar from Thursday’s close of 4.1135/1175.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the foreign exchange market was expected to remain guarded amid ongoing geopolitical tensions in West Asia and concerns over developments in the global economy.

He said the US financial markets were closed on Thursday in observance of Thanksgiving Day, while other markets remained active, with Brent crude oil prices rising 2.07 per cent to US$96.57 per barrel.
The increase followed a strike on a Saudi Arabian oil refinery in the southern province of Jazan, which temporarily halted some of the facility’s operations.

He said the conflict in West Asia continued to affect fuel supplies, while the market had fully priced in a 25-basis-point increase in the US Federal Funds Rate at the Federal Reserve’s December meeting.
“Besides that, there are concerns over excessive investment in artificial intelligence (AI), as well as a hawkish stance by the US Congress and administration towards China.
“Hence, we foresee the forex market will continue to remain guarded, which would result in higher demand for the US dollar,” he told Bernama.
Mohd Afzanizam expects the ringgit to trade within a narrow range of RM4.10 to RM4.12 against the US dollar today.
At the opening, the ringgit traded mostly lower against a basket of major currencies.

It increased against the euro to 4.5121/5192 from 4.5133/5177 at Thursday’s close, edged up vis-à-vis the British pound to 5.3912/3997 from 5.3924/3976, and was slightly higher against the Japanese yen at 2.5824/5866 from 2.5834/5860.
Against its ASEAN peers, the ringgit traded mostly flat.
It fell against the Thai baht to 12.0825/1095 from 12.0712/0875, but was unchanged against the Singapore dollar at 3.1878/1931 from 3.1878/1911.
The local note was also flat versus the Philippine peso at 6.45/6.46 and the Indonesian rupiah at 224.0/224.4. — Bernama
19a7a89567588f35: From Boo Jia Cher
My blood boiled when I read that the works ministry had received several highway proposals from the private sector, supposedly to "tackle congestion" on the Federal Highway.
It is absolutely absurd that, in 2026, the government's response to the Federal Highway receiving an "F" grade for traffic congestion is to entertain proposals for yet more tolled highways.

Every Klang Valley commuter knows this movie by heart. A highway gets jammed. Private companies step in with glossy proposals for a new elevated expressway. The government approves it, tolls go up, concrete pours over whatever green space or neighbourhood buffer is left, and for a brief honeymoon period, traffic moves.

Then, the law of induced demand kicks in. More lanes simply invite more cars. Within a few years, the new highway is just as gridlocked as the old one, and taxpayers are locked into decades-long concession agreements. And then a new highway gets proposed.
Go to the comments section of almost any post about this news and you'll find Malaysians overwhelmingly questioning the need for yet more highways.
What people want is less road expansion and better public transport. Those at the top clearly aren't listening.
We are trapped in a cyclical, illogical and deeply regressive loop of highway expansion. More highways, more cars, more congestion, and somehow the answer is always another highway.
This needs to stop.
Outdated thinking

Our traffic planners are measuring the wrong thing. Grading the Federal Highway based on "level of service" is an outdated, car-centric metric that treats a road as a pipe for moving metal boxes rather than a corridor for moving human beings.
A single lane choked with single-occupant cars gets an "F", while a dedicated lane carrying thousands of commuters on buses gets ignored.

Our traffic engineers and highway authorities urgently need to update their playbooks, education and policies. Efficiency should be measured by how many people reach their destination on time, not how many cars we can cram onto a road.
Fragmented planning hurts rakyat the most
The left hand of the government clearly does not know what the right hand is doing.

While the transport ministry is pouring billions into rail networks like the LRT3 and MRT3 and the Selangor government is trying to improve first- and last-mile connectivity, the works ministry is still entertaining highway extensions that actively encourage more driving.
Planning transport and infrastructure in rigid silos guarantees failure. You cannot tell people to take the train with one breath while building brand-new highways alongside the tracks with the next.
Say no to 'private sector proposals'

Even worse are the endless unsolicited private-sector proposals. Private highway concessionaires have no business dictating public urban planning. Their goal is not to solve traffic; their goal is to collect tolls and guarantee returns for shareholders.

This broken system of letting private companies pitch "solutions" to public congestion is a symptom of crony capitalism that, since the 1990s, has carved up the Klang Valley into a spaghetti junction of tolled roads and destroyed walkable neighbourhoods.
Public infrastructure must be driven by public need, not corporate profit margins.
A real solution
The Federal Highway connects some of the densest, most economically vital areas in the country: KL Sentral, Bangsar, Petaling Jaya, Subang, Shah Alam and Klang.
Trying to solve congestion along this spine by adding more car lanes is like trying to lose weight by buying larger pants.
If the government wants a real, immediate and cost-effective solution, it should stop studying new highways and build a proper Bus Rapid Transit system right down the Federal Highway corridor.
Dedicated, physical bus lanes – protected from private cars – can move tens of thousands of people an hour at a fraction of the cost and construction time of a new expressway.

Pair that with reliable first- and last-mile feeder buses, safe and comfortable walkways, cycling lanes and seamless integration with the LRT3 and KTM Komuter, and people will willingly ditch their cars.
Let's stop regressing
Putrajaya admits that widening the Federal Highway is too expensive and socially disruptive. Good. Apply that same logic to the private highway proposals. Reject them.

The NPE2 is already underway, carving up yet more parts of Kuala Lumpur like Sri Pantai, Angkasapuri and Mid Valley. Yet we continue entertaining more highways while the Kelana Jaya LRT line keeps breaking down and our bus system – a vital artery of any functioning, major city – remains a joke.

Politicians across the political spectrum keep playing up race and religion to divide us but where is the same urgency in addressing the issues that affect every Malaysian, regardless of race or religion? Our transport, our neighbourhoods, our air quality and the future of our cities.
It is absolutely depressing that the government, supposedly the most progressive to date, is still regurgitating the same tired, discredited policies.
Tear down the silos between ministries. Retire 1990s highway-building dogma. Stop building cities around cars, and start redesigning them around people.
Boo Jia Cher is an FMT reader.

38eeadadb38c9316: In previous seasons, Arsenal v Manchester City was an early pointer in the title race; Sunday’s clash looms like a parting of ways.
Even without the elephant in the room, the gap between the new champions and the usual champions is wide and widening.
The Gunners now have the crown and look likely to hold it for the foreseeable future. City?
Even they don’t seem to know what they are. A vastly expensive work in stuttering progress? Or a collection of condemned men soon to be put out of their misery?
No club since Sheffield Wednesday in 1904 has won its first seven games and then lost its next three.
City have drawn a couple since, but even AI would struggle to make head or tail of those stats.
Indeed, the bravura of their early-season siege mentality, which many thought was their way of dealing with the guilty verdict, has disappeared.
And while the hierarchy remains defiant, it isn’t just the players who are struggling; it’s the fans.
On Tuesday, their ground could once again reclaim the title, ‘The Empty-had’.
After boos had greeted the draw with Fulham, at the next match, the huge upper tiers were eerie vaults of disillusionment.
Napoli, recently Italian champions with old City hero Kevin De Bruyne to salute, were not unattractive opponents.
As a bonus, a couple of former United players were along to jeer. But it was a poor turnout.
It’s as if the fans have eaten all those bananas they were waving and the players have slipped on their skins.
Or is the loss of their incomparable manager, combined with two iconic players, finally catching up with them?
Yes, to lose one icon may be unfortunate, but…
Saying adios to Pep Guardiola, who won six EPL titles in 10 years, including four in a row, was akin to Nvidia losing Jensen Huang.
If the results don’t compare, the loss is similarly incalculable.
And to lose Pep’s lieutenant, Spain’s World Cup-winning captain and former Ballon d’Or winner, Rodri, as well… no team can cope with that.
Not forgetting Bernardo Silva! He was just the guy who might have held the fort for a while – past his prime, but capable of acting as a manager on the field.
Like grief, sometimes it takes a while to sink in.
With wholesale changes, come fresh faces and a ‘new manager bounce’: between them, they may bring a honeymoon period.
But now, the realisation has dawned and, without Rodri protecting them, City’s defenders are no longer so surefooted.
Even the great Gianluigi Donnarumma is no longer looking like one of the world’s best goalkeepers.
England centre-back Mark Guehi is a shadow of the solid, cool ‘Mr Dependable’ of late last season.
And, in a team short of leaders, the armband has gone to Erling Haaland, who is finding captaincy isn’t one of his attributes.
For all his monstrous power and pace, the Norwegian’s reluctance to join the action often sees him setting records for the fewest touches.
He can get away with it as a member of the rank and file, but it’s not the sort of leadership that a crisis-ridden club needs right now.
A midfield that cost circa £300m still isn’t quite clicking, although Elliot Anderson is doing his bit and Ayyoub Bouaddi is finally getting a chance.
It’s Enzo Fernandez that isn’t justifying his £ 100m-plus fee.
In cool contrast, Arsenal motor on. If they win on Sunday, they could be looking at a 15-point lead by Christmas and a stroll to the title.
They are being compared to a smooth-running machine – a north London version of ‘Vorsprung durch Technik’, the label once associated with German cars.
Ironic, then, that their one potential weakness – the lack of a top replacement keeper – could haunt them on Sunday.
The brilliant David Raya missed the Napoli game with an injured shoulder and, all week, Gooners have been sweating over how long the Spaniard would be missing.
Early fears of serious damage were soon allayed and the latest news is that he’ll make it for the big game.
But it is a rude reminder that neither Kepa Arrizabalaga, who stood in against Napoli, nor former Leeds stopper Illan Meslier, fills the faithful with confidence.
If Raya’s shoulder does improve, it can expect a buffeting inside the six-yard box.
Even if he survives in one piece, don’t be surprised to see another keeper arrive in January. Mikel Arteta doesn’t need any more sleepless nights.
But just as Arsenal are what City are not, neutrals would much rather watch City.
In Bouaddi, Ryan Cherki, Jeremy Doku, they have players with a bit of flair, elan and unpredictability, qualities that Arsenal lack.
They don’t need the awful orange kit they introduced against Napoli as yet another blatant marketing gimmick.

Don’t be surprised if the orange goes the way of the bananas – Mancunians, who can be a tight-fisted lot, won’t be taken for fools and this is yet another insult to the sacred colours of a club. When will owners ever learn?
Perhaps they are thinking they might need the money soon. They’ve probably been told there are no potential colour clashes in the second and third tiers.
If we can forget the impending sanction and appeal process for a moment, from a football point of view, it would be good if City were to pull off a surprise.
A City win would close the gap with the leaders to three points while Liverpool, who go to Everton in the early game, could be just four behind at kick-off.
We could have a title race after all, and even if it’s rendered a non-event by the end of the season, it could be fun while it lasts.

c459f414ef1a8740: A long-exposure image of the Orion Nebula with a total exposure time of 208 minutes showing satellite trails in mid-December 2019. A. H. Abolfath/WikimediaThis week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “Starmind” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation. If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places. SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth. But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit? Ups and downs We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature. The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day, while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000. But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites. To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day. This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences. When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors. Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers. It’s getting busy Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky. If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon. Satellites are already common enough, and Starmind would make matters worse. Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change. Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are. The orbital clutter comes with real risks. Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable. Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail. Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger. Regulator or promoter? The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts. However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”. There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”. This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “Dyson sphere” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy. But can it work? One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process. Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do. Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat. And apart from the physics there’s the finance. Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues. And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth. If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth. Michael J. I. 324933b619f6eefc: One of the quiet truths, or quirks if you like, that I have observed in life is that often - though not always - the more consequential moves are the ones we don’t make.

When Barisan Nasional and PAS announced they would sit out Sarawak’s coming state election, that restraint quietly handed Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) room to manoeuvre that it did not have to ask for.
Not to be outdone, Pakatan Harapan components PKR and Amanah followed suit by announcing that they too would not contest the state election.
At first glance, it is tempting to read such abstentions as a retreat, or even an admission of weakness.
Yet step back from the daily noise of Malaysian politics, and it looks far less like surrender and much more like a calculated gift.

Its real value lies not in Kuching today, but in Putrajaya tomorrow: whether the 16th general election ends in another hung parliament, just as GE15 did in 2022, continuing a pattern since 2008 where no coalition has managed to win a majority in Peninsular Malaysia on its own.

If that happens again, what keeps GPS’s price high is simple: freedom of choice. It can pick its federal partners without being tied down to any of them. Of course, if a single Peninsular bloc manages to cross the 112-seat mark by itself, East Malaysia becomes optional and this quiet advantage loses much of its shine.

Peninsular BN’s decision to stay away comes as no surprise. It rests on an old understanding — dating back to the days when Umno crossed into Sabah while leaving Sarawak’s local parties to manage their own house — that took on new form after GPS left BN in 2018.
Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi called it continuity, and he is right: BN stayed out of the 2021 Sarawak polls too, honouring an older convention that kept Peninsular parties off Sarawak’s turf.
What makes one pause longer are the decisions of PAS, PKR and Amanah.

GPS, meanwhile, will contest all 82 state seats on its own and politely declined formal pacts with any Peninsular party - just as it did in 2021, keeping even its federal partners at a polite distance.

To ask who looks weak in this arrangement is really to ask the wrong question. Peninsular BN no longer has the grassroots machinery in Sarawak that once belonged to its former local allies, while PAS faces steep odds and limited resources. Stepping aside spares both parties bruising fights they cannot win, while leaving GPS with a clear field and zero political debts.
PKR and Amanah too – which lost all the seats they contested in the 2021 state elections - have read the signs.

The logic becomes clearer when we look at how GPS has handled Putrajaya since 2018. It has backed three prime ministers in a row - Muhyiddin Yassin, Ismail Sabri Yaakob, and Anwar Ibrahim - without ever locking itself permanently into any camp.
That kind of agility requires peace at home. After all, it is never easy to sit across a cabinet table with people who were campaigning against you in your own backyard just weeks earlier.
Seen this way, these abstentions look very much like a low-cost insurance policy: a quiet premium paid by Peninsular parties to keep the door to Kuching unlocked after GE16.

We see this not so much in what politicians say, but in what they do. In 2021, BN stepped back and left the ground to GPS; this time, PAS followed suit, citing current political developments. For PAS, restraint avoids a campaign that could rally Christian and Dayak voters against perceived Peninsular Islamic overreach, while saving energy and funds for the peninsular battle.
By stepping aside, BN and PAS enjoy the optics of goodwill while keeping their lines to Kuching open. It is the same with PKR and Amanah.

But the DAP does not have the luxury of sitting out the polls because it holds two seats and has a following in urban areas. The party has announced that it will contest 12 seats, a modest number compared with the 26 it contested in 2026.

In the end, how much East Malaysia can ask for after GE16 comes down to a simple equation: how far the largest Peninsular bloc falls short of 112 seats. When the gap is small, GPS can fill it almost single-handedly - the strongest hand any negotiator can hold. When the gap widens, other parties and rival kingmakers enter the picture, diluting GPS’ federal hold.

Even so, what GPS has gained from a divided Peninsula is measured in status, influence, and revenue alike. It has secured senior federal posts — most notably Fadillah Yusof serving as deputy prime minister — alongside steady progress on rights under the Malaysia Agreement 1963.

While the long-standing call for a 20% oil royalty remains unmet and the 1974 Petroleum Development Act remains unamended, Sarawak has secured substantial financial and regulatory gains through other means, from its state sales tax on petroleum products to a stronger role for Petros in local gas distribution.

Before 2018, East Malaysia’s parliamentary weight was channelled through BN, which leaned heavily on Sabah and Sarawak seats to stay in power. That old order crumbled when BN fell in Putrajaya and Sarawak’s ruling parties walked out to form GPS.

Where once a strong federal centre under Dr Mahathir Mohamad intervened freely in East Malaysian affairs, especially Sabah, today’s fractured Peninsular landscape has given Kuching far more room to set its own terms. That advantage stands out even more by contrast with Sabah.

While GPS swept 76 of Sarawak’s 82 seats in 2021, Sabah’s 2025 state election left a much more divided assembly split closely between GRS and Warisan. A divided Sabah finds it harder to bargain with one voice, leaving GPS as East Malaysia’s steadier broker - though if Borneo’s leaders decide to speak with one voice, their combined weight would definitely be harder to ignore.

Yet nothing in politics lasts forever. GPS’s strength rests on delicate ground: unity within a coalition anchored by PBB, restraint from Putrajaya over federal fiscal levers, and a Peninsular electorate that remains split enough to keep kingmakers in demand.

By stepping aside in Sarawak, BN, PAS,PKR and Amanah have placed a quiet wager that they will need Kuching’s goodwill when the next general election arrives. Whether that bet pays off will not be decided in Sarawak’s polling booths, but in the shifting moods and quiet choices of voters across the South China Sea.

3b2b7b1913cdbfc6: Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week.
ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July.

Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more.
The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet.
Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX.
Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July.
Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages.
According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present.

Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once.

As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too.
It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free.
Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses.

"In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain.

"Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor."

Notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers users, chaining attacks at machine speed.

In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it said the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale.
AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions.

Some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®
f97ba7ee0bd5f5eb: The independent Ladybird web browser has reached an important milestone: an alpha test version. What's more, it works well. These may not be the criteria by which some will judge it, though.

Earlier this week, the developer behind the Ladybird web browser announced that Ladybird is now in alpha. We've given it a brief test, and it performed very well. It's more stable and works better than its alpha label would suggest.
There are downloads available, covering macOS on Apple Silicon, as well as for Linux on x86-64; for the latter, there's a Flatpak package, as well as native Ubuntu and Fedora packages.

It's an open source project, so you can download the source code from the GitHub repository and compile it yourself, but in an unusual move, back in June the project announced that the developers would no longer accept public code contributions.

We first mentioned Ladybird as part of our early 2022 look at its original parent project – SerenityOS: Remarkable project with its own JS-capable web browser. Both the name and the date are significant: the former is a nod to the Serenity prayer, recited at the end of Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. The date of the article is because it's well before the launch of ChatGPT at the end of 2022.

About a year and a half later, we reported that Serenity OS turns five and emits first offspring, Ladybird. Both the OS and the browser were still hand-coded, but now the browser could be compiled and run on other OSes. That freed it up to call upon external libraries which didn't exist for SerenityOS.

Earlier this year, we wrote Ladybird flutters toward Rust with a little help from AI. At one point, developer Andreas Kling used Apple's Swift language, but this year, he changed course and adopted Rust instead, using LLM tools to convert some existing code. Some will dismiss Ladybird because of this, but as our first coverage shows, the browser and its original host OS were established projects before the current wave of AI-assisted development.

Kling does use LLMs, but Ladybird is not some sloppy vibe-coded effort. The macOS download is 68.4 MB in size, which in 2026 is remarkably small. The Flatpak is larger – about 111 MB – but it also pulls in some KDE dependencies which increase its size.

We tested it on Pop!_OS. It handles sites such as The Register and Hacker News and everything else we tried perfectly, and took just 6 percent of our Dell XPS13's CPU to play full-screen HD video from YouTube smoothly. In our short testing, we saw no crashes, hesitation, or any other problems at all.
The developers nevertheless warn that the alpha can crash, some websites will not work, and they make no security guarantees at this stage.

The use of LLMs will put some people off. However, this is not the only controversial thing about the project. As we have noted in our previous coverage, Ladybird belongs to the same political wing of the FOSS movement as Omarchy, XLibre, and other right-wing projects. If the LLM use doesn't put you off, the political views may. On the other hand, as we've seen from our earlier coverage of Omarchy and XLibre, the same factors also attract others.

The modern Web is an entire complex compute platform in its own right, and currently, only three tools support it – and two of those are interrelated. The dominant engines are Google's Blink, used by Chrome and other Chromium browsers; Apple's WebKit, used by Safari; and Mozilla's Gecko, used by Firefox. Blink was forked from WebKit.

Some day, when the Servo project matures some more, it may be another. Even so, today, the first preliminary release of Ladybird means that there are now four competitive modern browser engines. That's a significant step. ®

eefc75c7c3c24ae0: Years of technical debt, increasingly complex systems, and underinvestment in IT operations have left organizations vulnerable to major outages, according to Forrester.
The analyst pointed to a seven-day stretch in November when failures disrupted Microsoft 365, US air traffic control, banking, and other critical services.
The coinciding outages provoked "a slew of conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and AI," Forrester said.

"The real culprit is tragically mundane: the culmination of decades of technical debt, the frenetic buildout of massively complex and highly interdependent systems, the concentration of risk, and the underinvestment in advanced operations."

Forrester urged technology suppliers and in-house IT teams to prioritize resilience as their systems grow more complex. Otherwise, "the tech estate will collapse like a house of cards, taking down consumer and business trust with it."

Earlier this month, Microsoft was left struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became "overwhelmed" and its attempts to fix the problem failed. Some of its services did not recover for another 24 hours.

In October, Google Cloud blamed a "power event" for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe. Affected services included BigQuery Data Transfer Service, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, and Google Kubernetes Engine.
In October last year, a major outage impacted Amazon Web Services (AWS), with even Amazon's own web page reported to be offline and dozens of other online services and websites affected.

Aviation and banking were also hit this month. A communications outage triggered a nationwide ground stop in the US on November 13, while incidents involving JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, Workday, Gmail, and other services added to the sense of widespread instability.
"Claims that these were all part of one connected cyberattack or conspiracy are highly unlikely. The real story is much more mundane," the report said.
Forrester argued that organizations have prioritized visible improvements over repairs to the underlying technology.

"Modernization investments have favored visible change over structural renewal," wrote report authors Lauren Nelson and Mark Moccia. "Organizations routinely fund new customer experiences, cloud migrations, platform consolidation, and AI initiatives because leaders can connect them to growth or productivity.

"They are less enthusiastic about updating core systems, simplifying architectures, retiring obsolete components, and eliminating fragile interfaces. The result is a modern front end resting on an aging, brittle, and increasingly interconnected estate."

Forrester's recommendations are to map dependencies, test failures and recovery under realistic conditions, and use incidents and near misses to identify weaknesses before they cause another outage. ®
8030417e575dab36: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.
Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment."

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to."
The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.
The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.
The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model.
The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.
"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.
The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®
1ec52ab2acfcb198: Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) says "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.
The Brisbane-headquartered company said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.
Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated.
Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident.

An initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information.
Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company said.

"FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes."
Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said.
The company said it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their plans.
Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information.
The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels.
More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October.
Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time.
Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft.

Speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or quickly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach.

"Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®
394e9f5b4e5d096c: Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.

In a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz said its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8. Any workloads still running at that point will be terminated, and customers will no longer be able to access their data.

"Following the recent security incident affecting Rackspace Spot, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the service," the company said. "Spot customers are being notified with the wind-down timeline, instructions for retrieving their data and steps to secure their environments."
Customers will have to contend with the fallout from the breach while simultaneously trying to get their applications and data off the platform.

According to a customer notification seen by The Register, the attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot over a period of almost 22 hours on November 17. Rackspace only learned of the intrusion the following day, after a customer raised the alarm.
The intruders impersonated legitimate users, created pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, gained access to stored credentials known as Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and storage volumes.
"With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held," Rackspace told customers.

Rackspace has since revoked the affected tokens and sessions, removed the pods planted by the intruders, and changed the affected platform and storage keys. Customers must also reissue API tokens, download new Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their clusters, including database passwords and third-party API keys.
Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and chief growth officer of Platform9, which co-developed Spot with Rackspace, shed some light on the root cause in a November 20 GitHub post.
"An observability system was breached using a compromised credential," Raghuram wrote. "This was obviously a critical error on our part and we are very sorry we let this happen."
Raghuram said the incident necessitated significant changes to the underlying infrastructure clusters, prolonging the outage.

Spot's selling point was cheap compute. The service operated an auction-based pricing model, allowing customers to bid for cloud infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of conventional on-demand instances. Rackspace advertised savings of up to 90 percent for customers willing to tolerate interruptions to their workloads. A permanent interruption probably wasn't what they had in mind.

ec9fbbb151b965da: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.
So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.
“Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”
The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®

c9d929f7e8b12eb6: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

db125f4552756b9b: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Grand Theft Auto VI is 2026’s breakout entertainment event. By the numbers, it made roughly $3.79 billion in revenue at launch, outpacing the lifetime earnings for megahit films like Avatar, The Odyssey, and Avengers: Infinity War. PlayStation called it their biggest launch of all time with over 39 million players on the platform alone. It’s the center of the current cultural zeitgeist, whether it’s because of the game’s controversy, music, love story, cultural legacy, or its accolades.

Entire households are playing GTA VI with one slight hitch: unlike movies, TV shows, or even books you can read side by side, a single-player, 40+ hour experience is tough to enjoy when you live together.

For some couples, the solution has been using more than one console or even multiple copies of the game. Married couple Meagan Kelley and Kyle Prahl typically switch between playing different games in the same room, or the same platforms in different parts of the house. The two are parents who find time to game after putting their son to bed. “The nice thing about having really young kids is they do go to bed super early,” Kelley told me. “Usually [my son] goes down and is asleep before eight, so then that's kind of like our prime gaming time.” The couple often plays different games in the same room, but for GTA VI “we're playing separately, so that kind of sucks because it's like we don't get a lot of time for each other,” Kelley said.

Although some men online have whined about Grand Theft Auto VI’s central romance, complaining about doing favors for their in-game girlfriend Lucia (“cuck simulator” being one common refrain), Kelley says the benefits to her real-life relationship are only positive. “It's funny that there's so much online discourse about GTA splitting up relationships and stuff when it's like something that can bring Kyle and I closer,” Kelley said. “Especially as we become parents and need to have more perspective on making sure that we're making time for ourselves.”

Dividing up time to play and sharing their experiences, she said, adds a new dimension to their mutual hobby. “When we are together taking care of our kid or having conversations, it's almost like book club,” Kelley said. “We share the different ways that we're experiencing the game with choices and stuff like that.”

Justin Massongill, another GTA VI player, and his wife recently had their second child. “She's taken on a lot,” he said. He bought the game for her, giving her priority to play so she could de-stress.

Massongill watched his wife play the first hour of the game; the next morning, he started his own. “We're kind of trying not to look too much at the other player's screen,” he said. “I don't want to, you know, get spoiled on things. But it's also such a massive game that what are the chances that we're going to see the same thing in the first place?”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> Madeline Blondeau and her fiancée decided to buy their copy of Grand Theft Auto VI together. The $80 price tag wasn’t so bad between the two of them; they downloaded the game, knowing that even with a PlayStation 5 and a PlayStation 5 Pro, they’d have to divvy up time between their single copy.

“We have been alternating our schedules,” Blondeau said. Her fiancée wakes up at 5 a.m. to start her IT job. Blondeau’s shift starts around 10 a.m. “We've sort of worked this out—me playing while she is working, and then her playing while I am finishing up my shift, trying to tiptoe around spoilers.”

Even as a queer couple, there’s an equality and care for each other in the experience Blondeau finds reassuring. “I think there's these very gendered expectations in relationships in terms of who games, who is the gamer of the household,” Blondeau said. You even see it in Grand Theft Auto, she adds, where Jason, the game’s male protagonist, will be the one with a controller in his hand. “Breaking down the gendered expectations of who is the gamer in the relationship really opens up a whole avenue for not getting into fights with your partner over video games,” Blondeau said.
“It feels like two people who figure their shit out, working out equitable time to experience something they've liked their whole lives, and talk about it.”

This past weekend, Blondeau’s fiancé left to grab groceries. She came back with something extra: the Grand Theft Auto trilogy for Nintendo Switch, a consolation prize for whoever wasn’t playing their shared copy of GTA VI. “I was in the mood to play Vice City,” her partner said. “We can trade off."
