3e44a71fc7f63f38: More than eight years after Rodrigo Duterte announced the Philippines would withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the country’s former president is about to begin his trial in The Hague. Duterte faces charges of crimes against humanity over alleged killings carried out during his deadly war on drugs. The trial, which begins on 30 November, comes at a precarious moment for the court, as the United States ramps up its efforts to undermine the institution. “Nothing has really quite approached this level of hostility we’re seeing coming from President Trump, or more particularly Marco Rubio,” explains Carrie McDougall, an associate professor at Melbourne Law School, speaking on The Conversation Weekly podcast. The US has never joined the ICC, citing concerns about politically motivated prosecutions of its nationals. But the court can investigate alleged war crimes committed by Americans on the territory of its member countries. McDougall says the US has “made no bones” about its opposition to the investigation of US nationals and the prosecution of Israeli nationals. In October, the Trump administration extended sanctions against individual ICC judges and prosecutors to the court as a whole. The sanctions threaten the court’s access to banking and IT services, as well as its ability to engage with victims and witnesses, McDougall says. The US has also been pressuring countries to withdraw from the court. McDougall attributes the decisions by Venezuela, Chad and Nauru to withdraw from the ICC to that pressure. Meanwhile, Duterte’s case illustrates both the powers and limitations of the court. “The reality is that the court itself doesn’t have any enforcement powers,” McDougall says. Instead, it relies on the Security Council – which has never used its enforcement powers to assist the court – and countries to cooperate with it. Duterte was arrested by his own country’s authorities. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu are both subject to ICC arrest warrants, but Russia and Israel have refused to cooperate in the arrest of their leaders. Neither country is a member of the ICC. While the ICC doesn’t have its own enforcement powers, arrest warrants still have some power; they can restrict leaders’ ability to travel overseas and potentially deter others from committing crimes. And, McDougall says: There is no statute of limitations, so those ICC arrest warrants can be enforced after individuals have lost power and lost the protection of their states. Duterte’s case also demonstrates that withdrawing from the ICC does not necessarily shield political leaders from prosecution, explains McDougall. Once a state … files a notice of withdrawal, it takes a year to become effective, and the ICC retains jurisdiction over any crimes committed up until that effective withdrawal date. So will the ICC survive? McDougall says the US sanctions “will impede the court’s ability to fulfil its mandate” and that the threat is “very serious.” She also warns that US attacks on international institutions risk emboldening other countries, including China and Russia, that want to reshape that order. “I think we are facing something of a crossroads,” she says. McDougall describes the ICC as the “canary in the coal mine” for the international legal order: It is required to hold to account those responsible for international crimes, particularly when we’re talking about the leaders of states. And so that puts a really big target on its back for would-be spoilers. Ultimately, though, McDougall does not expect a mass exodus from the ICC. I think a lot will actually hinge on how robustly other ICC states’ parties stand up for the court. 38bebe8b01f35c10: TOKYO, Nov 26 — US President Donald Trump’s fresh tariff blitz aims to pressure Asian countries into sealing trade deals with Washington so as to avoid unfavourable duty rates, analysts said on Thursday.
The proposed levies announced on Wednesday affect a range of nations in the region, from long-time US competitor China to allies like South Korea and Japan.
They could result in rates of up to 20 per cent on exports from the targeted countries, but face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

The announcement came after Washington concluded a months-long probe into alleged excess production in the targeted economies, which itself followed the US Supreme Court’s decision ruling that Trump’s previous “Liberation Day” duties were illegal.
But “several of these economies already have prior negotiated tariff rates with the US, which would effectively cap the appliable rate”, said MUFG economist Lloyd Chan in a note.
The US has also indicated that the new tolls will not stack on top of other tariffs already imposed on 60 countries over forced labour concerns. Instead, the higher rate will apply.
“In all, that should help contain the incremental tariff shock, assuming prior negotiated commitment remains in place,” Chan said.
However, it does mean that Washington has established higher tariff ceilings that can be activated “should trade negotiations or existing commitments break down”, he added.
Stephen Brown of Capital Economics also noted that “the US has left open its ability to hike these tariffs if trade agreements fall apart”, particularly with China.
Room for leverage
In Beijing’s case, the new levies stand at 20 per cent, meaning the total rate could jump to 40 per cent if its current trade truce with Washington, set to expire in January, is not extended.
Such a scenario “could take the two largest economies back to the trade wars of 2025”, Josh Lipsky, of the Atlantic Council, wrote in a note.
However, that is not something Trump wants, he added.
Instead, the US president is banking on an extension of the truce, though this is “far from a sure thing”, Lipsky added.
Trump and China’s Xi Jinping are set to meet next in December at the G20 summit in Miami.
“Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone’s interest,” Beijing’s foreign ministry warned on Wednesday.
Other Asian economies, also in Trump’s crosshairs due to significant trade imbalances, are likewise under pressure.
Vietnam faces a maximum additional tariff of 35 per cent on goods, which could be cut to 20 per cent if a trade deal is reached.
Hanoi reiterated on Wednesday that it has made commitments under a framework agreement in October 2025, and that it is working for a final deal “as soon as possible”.
India uncertain, Taiwan bullish
India said on Wednesday that trade concerns should be addressed in ongoing talks with Washington for a bilateral trade deal.
The US has proposed a 17 per cent rate on Indian goods, rising to a possible 25 per cent if no deal is reached.
The countries reached an interim agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.
But the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s levies days later, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

“By deploying a dual-rate structure — threatening steep baseline tariffs against countries that refuse a pact while offering lower rates to those that sign — Washington reclaims the bargaining power to impose duties at will and extract unilateral concessions,” Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, told Bloomberg News.
In contrast with Indian uncertainty, Taiwan, which reached a deal with Washington in early 2026, struck a reassuring tone.

“We are confident that when tariffs are finalised early next year, we will return to a 15 per cent non-stacked tariff under the agreement between Taiwan and the US,” Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun told a news briefing. — AFP

c726a5af6b120d4c: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.
The loss of a limb

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”

Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
New connections

A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
COURTESY OF AVI DAVIDSON
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
Becoming bionic

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”

Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

f067e2f75ccbe3a4: Donate to our Independent Journalism Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Image made via Canva Pro. All images fair use.

Journalism has been a vital part of society for centuries. Writing about what happened and sharing it with others; reading about what happened somewhere else and discussing it with those around you; having a platform for letters, comments, and opinion about everything from the niche to the rich. Journalism has toppled governments and CEOs, revealed complicated scams, brought out the beauty of ethnographically observed daily life, recorded our qualms and foibles for posterity, and whipped up outrage, empathy, and triumph.

But journalism is on a precipice. The shift from print to digital has opened up new possibilities, as well as vulnerabilities. Changes in how we interact, especially at a distance, have changed what (and how) people want to read, listen to, or watch to understand the news.

This decade has seen dramatic changes in the field, from the loss of foundational trust in the institution, to digital, legal, and physical threats to journalists to the near-complete erosion of financial security for people who carry out this work. Increasingly authoritarian governments turn on the media, and the press in countries from Hong Kong to Myanmar to Russia to Nicaragua has been forced into exile.

Even countries such as the UK and the US have seen government targeting of journalists for critical reporting. Israel’s genocide in Gaza has laid bare the hypocrisy of the international press establishment, causing a crisis of confidence, while small local news outlets and independent journalists continue to report despite this.

Through it all, journalists have kept documenting, analyzing, responding, and reporting, even when they are underpaid and overworked, face hostile governments and terrible technology, sometimes from exile, in terrible conditions, even at risk of their lives. As we begin 2027, Global Voices will turn the spotlight onto these voices that continue to speak truth to power and bring to light the news that we all need to know. We will look at civic journalism, find out what is changing, and meet some of these indefatigable defenders of our right to free speech and our right to information.

df3ad65f3021d36a: BEIJING, Nov 26 — China said Thursday it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Washington unveiled new tariffs that could shake the uneasy truce in the two economic giants’ trade war.
Chinese commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong told a regular briefing that citing “overcapacity” as a reason to impose tariffs was a “pretext for protectionism”.

“Such actions not only fail to address their own structural imbalances but also disrupt the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains, hinder industrial cooperation, drive up global inflation, harm the direct interests of businesses and consumers and pose long-term, systemic risks to global economic growth,” He said.
“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” He added.
“China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”
US President Donald Trump has long criticised China’s yawning trade surplus with the United States, which he has blamed for a decline in local manufacturing prowess and jobs.
After starting a second term in office last year, Trump imposed new tariffs on Chinese goods, kicking off a tit-for-tat escalation that at one point saw duties touch 145 per cent.
The trade ceasefire struck by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2025 is due to expire in January, after a two-month extension was agreed in September.
The two men met last week at an APEC summit in Shenzhen in southern China and are due to see each other for the fourth time this year in December at a G20 summit in the United States.
The proposed new US levies target a range of trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan and range up to 20 per cent.
China is among those facing the highest 20-percent rate, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

“China understands that we’re going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding,” he told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that the US was offering China exemptions on around US$30 billion (RM121 billion) of goods. — AFP
f19b0991de69df17: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 26 — Allianz Malaysia Berhad has unveiled “Allianz Eterna,” a specialised wealth management and protection platform tailored for high-net-worth individuals, leveraging its newly established offshore subsidiary in Labuan to court the country’s surging affluent demographic.

The launch marks a strategic push by the insurer to capture a rapidly expanding tier of affluent family offices and business owners whose financial requirements have outgrown conventional domestic insurance structures.
Speaking at the launch today, Allianz Life Insurance Malaysia Berhad chief executive officer Giulio Slavich explained that regional wealth dynamics are undergoing profound structural shifts.
“The wealth landscape is changing, both here in Malaysia and across the region,” Slavich said during the launch.

“The combined wealth of Malaysia's 50 richest individuals reached US$116 billion (RM475.6 billion) this year, an increase of nearly 30 per cent. Meanwhile, the country's ultra-high-net-worth population is expected to grow by more than 20 per cent between 2026 and 2031.”

Slavich observed that private wealth management among local entrepreneurs is becoming increasingly global, pointing to Department of Statistics Malaysia data showing the nation's direct investment abroad reached RM639.7 billion as of the third quarter of 2026.
“Malaysian businesses are looking beyond our borders, and the people behind some of these businesses may have financial needs that go beyond Malaysia too,” he added.

To bridge domestic and international jurisdictions, the proposition operates through a dual-market architecture, combining Allianz Malaysia's onshore retail distribution with the offshore underwriting capabilities of Allianz Labuan Limited, which was incorporated in the Federal Territory of Labuan effective Oct 1, 2026.
This offshore gateway enables the insurer to structure foreign currency-denominated life policies for affluent domestic families and international investors operating within the financial hub.
Allianz Malaysia chief executive officer Sean Wang said the new platform responds directly to clients seeking financial structures that are “as borderless as their ambitions.”

“With the launch of Allianz Labuan and Allianz Eterna, we are bringing together Allianz Malaysia’s established expertise with genuine offshore and international capabilities under one roof,” said Wang.
“It is our promise that wealth does not only grow, but it connects, endures and transcends,” he added.

The flagship product launched under the platform is “Horizon Infinite,” a foreign currency legacy indexed universal life (IUL) contract designed for long-term capital preservation and intergenerational succession planning.

Structured as a limited-pay policy, the instrument accommodates policyholders entering up to age 80 and incorporates a zero per cent floor rate on its Index Account, protecting policyholders from market losses while enabling them to participate in market gains.

Complementing the financial instruments, the platform integrates a suite of lifestyle concierge privileges branded as "Exclusives," encompassing dedicated relationship ambassadors, VIP medical screening concierges, comprehensive international travel insurance, and bespoke private events.
Allianz Eterna solutions will be distributed through a combination of the insurer's institutional bancassurance partners, international brokerage houses, and independent financial advisers.

He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. So, just before I started secondary school, my mum asked one of my friends’ parents if she could name them as our next of kin. They said yes, but not wanting to rely on others, she continued to work hard to ensure we, as well as her family in Iraq, would have as much financial security as possible. Continue reading...
0cd88d2cf652a020: Mikhail Svetlov/Getty ImagesAs early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports. If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation, albeit without giving any potential launch window. These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow. Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems. Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial, it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”. What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite? A lesson on cooperation The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia. During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”. A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to: place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner. Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere. Read more: Too many satellites? Earth’s orbit is on track for a catastrophe – but we can stop it A nuclear ‘aurora’ No country is known to have ever placed a nuclear weapon in orbit. But there are examples from history of states detonating nuclear weapons off-Earth. One summer’s night in 1962, people in Hawai'i gazed upward and saw what was, in effect, a nuclear “aurora”. One eyewitness, then a teenager, who was watching with her sibling from a spot overlooking Pearl Harbor, recalled the “exploding sky” and how it later turned “a deep blood red that lingered”. The US had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometres above the Pacific Ocean in a classified test code-named Starfish Prime. The US and the Soviet Union were testing nuclear weapons in space almost in lockstep, each demonstrating its advancing technological capabilities. Starfish Prime was more than a visual spectacle. Of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time or launched in the following weeks, at least a third suffered damage. The Starfish Prime ‘aurora’ seen from Honolulu. Capnez/Wikimedia What happens in space is a threat on Earth Today, the European Space Agency estimates there are about 15,800 functioning satellites in Earth’s orbit. These satellites support the critical infrastructure we rely on every day, from navigation for transport to timing for banking and telecommunications. Whether we realise it or not, we are all “space citizens”. Some satellites also support nuclear command, control and communications functions. Others give early warning of missile attacks. Researchers at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute examine this “space–nuclear nexus”. During a conflict, leaders might interpret an attack on an early-warning satellite as “a precursor to a nuclear-first strike”. How they respond to that ambiguity could have escalatory risks and significance. Mitigating the threat through verification So, what can the global community do to mitigate possible and actual threats of nuclear weapons in space? As a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, Russia could veto a resolution responding to the current allegation. Indeed, in 2024, it vetoed a US–Japan draft resolution reaffirming the Article IV prohibition. The Outer Space Treaty sets out no specific procedure for verifying whether a satellite carries a nuclear weapon, nor does any other international instrument. Three think tanks working on global and space security have led expert dialogues on how to do so. In their latest joint report, they conclude that verification is “feasible”, albeit challenging, and should be pursued even if “progress may be incremental”. The report canvasses multiple options. These include nations working together to test ways of detecting a nuclear weapon in orbit, agreeing on how to handle disputed evidence, and inviting pre-launch inspections. In my research, I have been exploring how nuclear safeguards could advance non-proliferation by verifying nuclear material on board a space object before launch. As global nuclear arsenals continue to expand and modernise, we must not lose hope of a world one day free of nuclear weapons, an aspiration reflected in the disarmament pillar of the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968. The onus must also rest heavily on states actually capable of launching nuclear-armed satellites, whether or not they face allegations. The US, China and Russia could discuss verification options in the trilateral dialogue they recently agreed to hold on nuclear risk. In a strained geopolitical context, a nation’s verbal reassurances alone are unlikely to give the global community the confidence it needs. Nations agreed nearly 60 years ago to keep nuclear weapons out of space. Verifying whether they keep that commitment will take cooperation, too. Art Cotterell's postdoctoral fellowship is co-funded by the UNSW Nuclear Innovation Centre and UNSW Law & Justice. He is affiliated with the Australasian Centre for Space Governance.
a3894a1164fefbce: The Conversation, CC BY-SATo get the most out of Black Friday sales, a bit of research is always useful. Ideally, this involves working out what you might want to buy – and checking prices – before sales begin. Once the sales are under way, comparing prices, delivery costs and delivery times at different stores can feel onerous and time-consuming, especially if you’re worried you might miss out on a deal. To streamline their search for a bargain, some shoppers are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) tools to do the research for them. Can AI really help you snag a deal? The answer is yes, maybe. But there are reasons to proceed carefully. Sending bots on a bargain hunt AI is being used to take the legwork out of all sorts of tasks. It makes sense consumers across the world are increasingly putting it to work as a shopping companion. Say you’re looking for a new coffee machine or laptop this Black Friday. Rather than trawl through dozens of different sites yourself, you might ask a tool such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to search the web for you and prepare a spreadsheet with a list of options. A recent survey by the Australian Retail Council and market research firm Roy Morgan found this Black Friday, one in four respondents were planning to use an AI chatbot for research. Among this group, 72% said it would be their first time doing so. If you fall into this category, there are a few things to be aware of as you check any recommendations. Bogus bargains, ‘ghost stores’ and ads Hallucination is a well-known feature of generative AI tools. In the context of shopping with AI, this means some products, prices and stores may be entirely made up or misinterpreted. A related concern is whether AI tools can reliably distinguish between genuine online stores and the fake or “ghost stores” that spring up online during sales periods. Then, of course, there’s advertising. Many AI tools, including the free and low-cost versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google Search’s AI Overview and AI Mode, have already started rolling out advertising. Both OpenAI and Google say advertisements shown to users are clearly labelled. But depending on your settings, the ads you see may be informed by your previous conversations with these tools. Other generative AI tools don’t have ads. Anthropic, for example, has pledged to keep Claude ad-free. And Google’s Gemini app remains free of advertising, at least for now. The other side of the checkout Even if you decide not to use AI this Black Friday, it could still shape the deals you see. Some retailers are reportedly already using AI to guide their discounting strategies. AI is already changing the way companies decide what discounts to offer to everyone. Ashkan Forouzani/Unsplash This includes using sophisticated models and past sales data to work out the smallest discount they need to offer to sell a product. Another potential headwind for shoppers is the use of AI by retailers to personalise prices to the amount a consumer is likely to be prepared to pay, sometimes called “surveillance pricing”. Currently, this is not explicitly against the law unless the surveillance pricing involves discrimination based on protected characteristics such as race, sex or disability. Read more: AI is using your data to set personalised prices online. It could seriously backfire Handing over your wallet By Black Friday next year, new tools which go beyond simple research may be more commonplace: AI shopping agents. These tools can find stores selling what you’re looking for, compare prices and then complete the purchase on your behalf. For example, Meta’s Muse agent, which launched in Australia last week, integrates with existing social media accounts and can complete tasks on your behalf. Other tech companies are also venturing into the space. OpenAI recently launched its Dots agent, and Google’s offerings include Agentic Checkout and Gemini Tasks. Amazon offers its own shopping agent but blocks other third-party agents from accessing its site. Can we make agents safe? Developers such as Meta say they are building in protections to prevent consumer AI agents “going rogue” and overstepping their authority or spending instructions. But even with safeguards in place, other risks could be amplified. AI agents rely on “context” to execute the purchases their consumers are likely to prefer. Essentially, this means information about your previous interactions is used to predict what you might want in the future. More broadly, there is the risk AI tools may not be working in shoppers’ best interests. An OECD paper this month warned commercial partnerships could shape which products and prices AI tools recommend, in ways that may not be understood by shoppers. The federal government has flagged new laws may be needed to respond to the rise of AI shopping agents, including to guard against manipulation or exploitative personalised pricing. Some old-fashioned common sense So, what’s the advice? By all means, use AI to find a Black Friday bargain, if you choose. But be sceptical. Treat its recommendations as just one piece of information. It is worth checking the policies of your preferred AI tool to see if you can turn off its memory of earlier chats. You may also be able to limit advertising and prevent your prompts from being used for training. Ultimately, getting the best deal still means weighing up your options, sticking to a budget and thinking about whether you really need what’s on sale. Jeannie Marie Paterson receives funding from the Austrlian Research Council and the Medical Research Future Fund.
4d7510a105797812: Terlebih dahulu, saya perlu memberitahu bahawa 'Tan Sri' dan 'Dato Seri' pada tajuk penulisan ini ialah anugerah kebesaran yang dipakai Presiden PAS Hadi Awang. Artikel ini sekadar menjelaskan apa yang dinyatakan beliau tempoh hari adalah salah.
Saya petik laporan FMT kelmarin. Kata Hadi partinya semakin mendapat sokongan golongan bukan Islam, namun golongan yang beliau maksudkan ialah mereka yang dia sifatkan sebagai 'tidak ekstrem'.
Jadi adakah Hadi menyifatkan semua orang bukan Islam yang tidak menyokong PAS golongan 'ekstrem'?

Apakah takrif 'ekstrem' menurut pandangan presiden PAS itu? Siapakah golongan 'tidak ekstrem' yang presiden PAS itu maksudkan? Saya kira MCA, MIC dan juga Gerakan, kerana Hadi pernah kata PAS boleh dan sudah bekerjasama dengan tiga parti itu.

Namun, penerimaan Hadi akan MCA dan MIC ialah berdasarkan dua parti itu komponen Barisan Nasional, dan PAS mempunyai persefahaman dengan BN sejak PRN Negeri Sembilan. Gerakan pula sememangnya komponen Perikatan Nasional. Maka, tidak bolehlah kita menyamakan sokongan tiga parti itu dengan sokongan masyarakat bukan Islam, kerana tiga parti itu tidak lagi mewakili komuniti itu secara menyeluruh.

Apa pun, menurut Hadi, PAS yakin mampu menewaskan PH pada PRU16 kelak berdasarkan 'keputusan memberangsangkan' dalam beberapa PRN baru-baru ini. Jelas beliau merujuk kepada PRN Johor, Negeri Sembilan dan Melaka.
Tetapi keputusan memberangsangkan di tiga PRN itu tercapai hasil kerjasama dengan Umno. Hakikatnya, gandingan PAS-Umno disokong pengundi Melayu, bukannya pengundi bukan Melayu bukan Islam.

Diakui Hadi banyak menyumbang kepada pencapaian bergaya itu apabila menyeru penyokong PAS mengundi BN. Kenyataan beliau bahawa wajib orang Islam sokong calon Islam diakui sebilangan besar pengundi Melayu. Bagaimanapun that same statement telah menyaksikan golongan bukan Islam bukan Melayu menjauhi PAS. Bukanlah rahsia mereka tidak senang dengan kenyataan Hadi, sedangkan ramai pemimpin bukan Melayu yang baik dan bersih. Bahkan, perasaan orang bukan Islam terguris apabila Hadi mendakwa orang bukan Islam sebagai punca gejala rasuah.
Jadi apabila Hadi kata PAS semakin dapat sokongan bukan Islam adalah sesuatu yang tidak betul.

Untuk double confirm pendapat saya itu, saya bertanya beberapa penyelidik yang membuat kaji selidik di lapangan semasa tiga PRN tempoh hari. Seorang daripada mereka memberitahu saya bahawa apa yang dikatakan Hadi itu tidak betul, menurut dapatan para penyelidik. Seorang lagi kata "finding saya: tak betul".
Ringkasnya, Hadi salah dalam rumusannya.

Kenyataan Hadi sememangnya pelik. Saya yang tidak berbekalkan hasil penyelidikan pun boleh rasa majoriti orang bukan lslam tidak sokong PAS, tidak kira 'ekstrem' atau 'tak ekstrem' (sekadar meminjam istilah Hadi).

Daripada mana Hadi dapat maklumat sehingga beliau boleh merumuskan sokongan bukan Islam kepada PAS semakin meningkat? Mustahil para penyelidik PAS tak tahu keadaan sebenar -- tak mungkin mereka tidak beri laporan tepat dan benar kepada presiden.
Adakah Hadi punya intel sendiri? Maklumlah presiden memang wajar ada banyak saluran maklumat tetapi apa yang beliau umumkan itu tidak betul.

Mungkinkah apa yang Hadi katakan itu bertujuan menyuntik semangat pemimpin dan ahli parti supaya mereka mempunyai keyakinan bagi menghadapi PRU kelak? Tetapi, bak dikata tadi, tentu mereka juga ada maklumat sendiri mengenai keadaan sebenar.
Atau mungkin Hadi sekadar main psywar untuk menakutkan pihak lawan, atau Hadi mahu menenangkan perasaan Umno yang mungkin gusar kenyataan Hadi akan membuatkan orang bukan Islam menjauhi PAS-Umno?
Mungkinkah juga untuk tenangkan perasaan ahli PAS sendiri yang memendam rasa tetapi risau kata-kata Hadi akan menyusahkan parti memikat hati pengundi bukan Islam?

Imbau kembali PRN Melaka. Tidak sampai 48 jam sebelum orang Melaka keluar mengundi, Hadi berucap di pentas grand finale BN-PN untuk memberi peringatan tentang pentingnya umat Islam keluar mengundi. OK, no problem with that.

Kata beliau, dalam Islam perkiraan politik dibuat berlandaskan faktor dosa dan pahala berbanding orang bukan Islam yang dituduhnya 'zalim'. Katanya lagi, kesan daripada orang Islam tidak keluar mengundi ialah 'orang lain' yang akan jadi pemerintah, dan menurut Hadi mereka akan bertindak mengikut perkiraan sendiri dan mengabaikan amanah yang diwajibkan Allah.
Siapakah 'orang lain' yang beliau maksudkan? Saya kira umum tahu.
Apapun beliau kata sebab itu orang Islam mesti tunaikan kewajipan mengundi untuk memimpin seluruh manusia. Do you think orang bukan Islam senang dengan kata-kata itu?
Apa lagi ini: "sejahat-jahat orang Islam seburuk-buruk orang Islam memerintah negeri, mereka tidak sezalim orang bukan Islam." Tuduhan ini memang menyakiti hati orang bukan Islam.

Menurut Malaysiakini, setiausaha politik kepada Hadi iaitu Syahir Sulaiman memberitahu portal berita itu bahawa kenyataan Hadi kononnya merujuk kepada apa yang berlaku dalam sejarah pemerintahan Islam.
Bagi saya, penjelasan itu sukar diterima kerana maksud dan sasaran Hadi memang jelas. Ia mencetuskan kemarahan orang bukan Islam termasuk parti yang mengaku sekutu PAS.

Menyusuli kenyataan Pejabat Presiden PAS yang mendakwa kata-kata Hadi dipetik di luar konteks, ini pada hemat saya tidak lebih daripada usaha damage control. Hakikatnya apa yang Hadi kata tidak boleh atau susah dipertahankan. Apatah lagi ada video ucapan.
Realitinya Hadi did say what he said. Soal luar konteks tidak timbul. Pejabat Presiden PAS pun tidak menafikan, cuma mendakwa kenyataan Hadi was taken out of context.

Mungkin Hadi mahu buktikan kepada semua pihak termasuk ahli parti bahawa kenyataannya tidak mendatangkan mudarat -- sebaliknya PAS semakin dapat sokongan orang bukan Islam meskipun facts and figures showed otherwise.
Kesimpulan terbaik dibuat seorang penganalisis politik, apabila berkata: "Kalau Hadi yang kata, yang pelik-pelik ni tak menghairankan."
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
0c6bc9d95e3a2ca7: Entah berapa banyak agaknya jumlah wang syiling 50 sen yang saya genggam, turut terisi mengembung saku di kedua-dua belah seluar. Semata untuk menghubungi Pak Samad Said dari telefon awam berwarna kuning yang sobek berkarat di bucu.

Setiap kali dering berlaga di gegendang menalun, jantung saya tidak berhenti berdetak bergetar dengan keras. Setiap kali juga, suara Kak Rashidah menyambut di hujung. Lantas mendepani baton FRU, belantan ganas polis, semburan gas pemedih mata dan berdiri tegak di hadapan pelbagai demonstrasi (Bapak menamakannya tunjuk kasih, dan bukan tunjuk perasaan).

Sehingga hari ini, Bapak satu-satunya sasterawan yang meletakkan seni itu sebagai sebahagian daripada kehidupan jelata. Hanya seorang sasterawan berani turun ke jalan raya. Namanya A Samad Said, hatta saya tidak akan berdaya melakukannya.

Ketika tahun-tahun pengajian saya di UKM, Bapak akan sering bertanya dan mendoakan agar saya mendirikan rumah tangga. Pada Oktober 2009, Bapak ke Melaka sekali lagi, kali ini ditemani Kak Rashidah. Mereka menaiki bas menghadiri kenduri perkahwinan saya di Dewan Hang Tuah. Terdapat sehampar sketsa, dianugerahkan buat saya. Ia lakaran sebatang pohon yang katanya, 'akar terbenam ke bumi'.

Di antara tahun-tahun 2012-2017 saya mengalami depresi. Berat badan saya bertambah, tekanan membahana. Nama saya diburukkan oleh Zahid Hamidi, mufti Perlis dan pentadbiran Najib Razak. Karya saya dilarang, Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka tiba-tiba memutuskan hubungan. Sebagai pengarang sepenuh masa, saya kehilangan mata pencarian.

Bapak sudah mahir menggunakan emel, dan Bapak menjawab begini dalam balasannya bertarikh 6 Jun 2012; "Bapak berdoa ia akan berakhir dengan baik. Betapa pun, jika buruk keadaannya, janganlah pula tergesa melawan. Teliti dan timbang dulu kesannya, termasuk kesannya terhadap kedudukanmu di varsiti. Walaupun, sebenarnya, sangat wajar dilawan."

Saya memfailkan permohonan semakan kehakiman di Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur pada 29 Jun 2015 untuk buku-buku saya yang diharamkan. Keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi pada Ogos 2016 ialah Hakim Hanipah Farikullah menolak permohonan tersebut dan memutuskan bahawa tindakan Kementerian Dalam Negeri adalah munasabah. Tiada seorang pengarang Malaysia pun bersama-sama dengan saya. Serasa seisi bumi mentertawa. Mereka malah menghindari saya.
Kecuali Pak Samad Said dan Kak Rashidah datang menaiki bas dan teksi untuk memberi sokongan.

Segala ombak kenangan itu menghempas pantai benak saya berulangan kali. Semakin stereng kereta saya bergegar tatkala memasuki petak parkir hospital. Di wad Mawar, Az dengan lesung pipit menyambut, dan aduh senyum serta kelembutan Kak Rashidah terpapar lagi, "Faisal masuklah, Faisal sapa Bapak... kalau Bapak buka mata dan bangun."

Saya membelai rambut Bapak, saya ingin mengucup tangan Bapak seperti selalunya akan tetapi saya khuatir ada jarum terlekat, serta topeng oksigen Bapak akan terlorot. Saya meronta-ronta ingin meneriak nama Bapak. Saya ingin memberitahunya bahawa seluruh dunia saya sebetulnya pernah terbangun oleh sosok kecil ini.

Seisi alam remaja saya begitu bergantung kepadanya. Saya terngiang-ngiang kembali tawa Bapak, dan cungap kami menyusuri laluan dari Masjid Negara, merentasi Daya Bumi ke Pasar Seni. Saya tahu detik masanya seakan tiba. Saya tidak memahami mengapa Kak Rashidah semacam tenang dan aman-aman sahaja. Saya merintih di celah bacaan Yasin, saya terngiang kembali kasih Bapak. Betapa banyak dikau memberi. Betapa banyak.

Di kuburan, tatkala mereka mengambus tanah di pusaramu, saya berasa ingin menerkam dan menjeritkan, jangan ayohai tolong jangan dulu. Nusa bangsa ini masih memerlukan keberanianmu. Kita barangkali akan turun lagi ke jalanan. Saya masih ingin melaungkan, ternyata banyak belum kita laksanakan kerana kuasawan dan korupsi masih bermaharajalela.

Tetapi saya menyaksikan semua yang hadir membiarkan kepal tanah keras itu menelangkup. Talkin dibaca. Mereka kemudian menyirami air di atas kuburan itu. Perlahan-lahan saya melihat pusara Bapak sempurna. Bapak bersemadi, dan saya tidak percaya.
Serasa sunyi dan sendiri. Ada sekawanan merpati tiba-tiba melayah rendah, hingar-bingar teman dan saudara. Beberapa pembesar dan orang terkenal bertingkah seperti biasa.

Pun ombak kenangan menerpa, dan Ya Allah, kaca mata saya memburam dan saya mendengar suara Bapak, sayup-sayup di hujung gagang telefon. Lirih tetapi padat, tergagap tetapi teguh; ketawa Bapak. Langit saya lihat makin keruh, membawa gerimis.
Kembali di gegendang telinga saya, denting syiling 50 sen yang segenggam itu jatuh ke dalam tampungan telefon awam, sekeping demi sekeping.
Sehingga ke syiling terakhir.
Suara Bapak terputus tiba-tiba.

23f83af51db231e9: Karim Ibrahim wants the police and Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) to investigate RM10 million he claims has gone missing from Malaysia Athletics (MA), along with more than RM500,000 allegedly missing from state associations.
These are grave allegations. But before the former MA president points investigators towards others, he must answer some uncomfortable questions about his own stewardship.
Karim says he secured RM10 million in sponsorship for athletics and now wants to know where the money went. Yet he was not an outsider watching from the sidelines.
He was at the helm of the national governing body when, by his own account, the sponsorship was secured.

If he brought in that money, he should be able to identify the sponsor, explain the terms of the agreement, state how much MA actually received and account for what the funds were supposed to support.
There is also a fundamental difference between securing a sponsorship package worth RM10 million and having that entire sum deposited into MA’s accounts.

Was the figure a contractual commitment, the total value of a sponsorship deal or money actually paid to the association? Were payments made in one lump sum or released in stages against agreed programmes?
The questions become even more pressing because nobody appears to know who this supposedly generous sponsor was.

A sports body landing RM10 million would normally shout it from the rooftops. Its leaders would hold a press conference, parade the corporate partner and trumpet the deal as a vote of confidence in the sport.
They would tell athletes, coaches and the public what the money would deliver. Such a windfall would be a major achievement, not something to keep under wraps.
Yet there appears to have been no public fanfare, no named corporate partner and no clear account of the initiative the money was meant to support.
Who put up the sponsorship? Was the agreement ever announced? What programmes did it fund, and what did MA promise in return?

A sponsor committing such a sum would also expect answers. It would want to know whether the money had reached its intended programmes, whether agreed targets were being met and how the association had used the funds.

Did MA provide progress reports or financial accounts? Did the sponsor ask for updates? If payments came in instalments, what evidence of progress did MA have to provide before receiving the next tranche?
These are not peripheral details. They go to the heart of whether the RM10 million deal existed in the form Karim now describes, how much money changed hands and what happened to it.
The sponsorship agreement, payment records, bank statements and audited accounts should provide the answers.
Karim should put the details on the table rather than leave the public to chase a figure without a name attached to it.
Serious allegations need hard evidence

Karim’s claim that some money went into personal accounts is even more explosive. It suggests possible misappropriation, yet the interview reported by Scoop offers no transaction details, names, dates or documents to substantiate it.
Which accounts received the money? How much was transferred? Who authorised the payments? What evidence led him to conclude that the transactions were improper?
The same scrutiny must apply to his claim that more than RM500,000 has disappeared from state associations.
He cites RM18,000 involving Selangor athletics, more than RM100,000 linked to fixed deposits and almost RM200,000 involving the national association.
But he does not explain how these figures were established or whether they refer to missing funds, unexplained withdrawals, disputed transactions or accounting discrepancies.

These are different things. A fixed deposit that cannot immediately be traced does not, by itself, prove that money has been stolen. Nor does an unexplained entry in an account establish that someone pocketed the funds.

Karim says he knows about the alleged irregularities because he examined state association accounts as MA president. If so, he should identify the associations, the periods involved and the transactions that triggered his suspicions.
He should also say whether he raised these concerns with MA’s executive council. Checks with council members indicate that they are unaware of the allegations and shocked by the claims.
If Karim had formally alerted them, there should be a record of when he did so and what action followed.

The executive council will have an opportunity to address the allegations when it meets on Nov 29. Its members should use the meeting to seek a full account of the sponsorship Karim claims to have secured, examine the financial records and establish whether anyone raised concerns about the transactions while he was president.
The association cannot afford to let such serious claims drift without a formal response.
There is another question he cannot duck. As MA president and a signatory to its cheques, Karim had the authority to seek financial records, question payments and demand explanations.
Did he exercise that responsibility? Did he ask for an audit, challenge suspicious transactions or alert the relevant authorities while he was still in office?
If he did, he should produce the correspondence and explain what happened. If he did not, he must explain why he waited until after his disqualification to raise such serious allegations.

Karim says he wants the police and MACC to investigate. If he has evidence of wrongdoing, he should put it before them. Has he lodged a report with either agency, the sports commissioner or MA? Has he handed over the documents on which his claims rest?
Calling for an investigation is easy. Giving investigators something concrete to pursue is another matter.

The timing deserves scrutiny, too. Karim has made these claims after his disqualification from the MA presidency. That does not make them false, and MA cannot brush them aside simply because of who is making them.
But if he knew of suspected financial wrongdoing while leading the association, why did he not expose it then?
MA has been asked to respond to the allegations. Its account is essential, and it must answer for any financial irregularities that the evidence establishes.
Any credible evidence of wrongdoing deserves an independent investigation, regardless of who is implicated.

But accountability cannot be a one-way demand. Karim is entitled to ask where the money went. He must also account for what he knew, what he did and what records he left behind when he led the association.
He cannot demand that others explain the money while leaving his own stewardship beyond scrutiny.
If there are culprits, name them and produce the evidence. But Karim must start by answering for his own time at the helm.

099ddd8378bba93f: At 5pm on June 28, 1982, a research reactor in Bangi called TRIGA PUSPATI reached its criticality for the first time, ushering Malaysia into the nuclear age. Forty-four years on it is still running, yet we have never produced a single unit of nuclear electricity.

That's not for want of trying. Under then prime minister Najib Razak, Malaysia planned two nuclear plants by 2021 and set up the Malaysia Nuclear Power Corporation in January 2011, two months before a tsunami crippled Japan's Fukushima Daiichi plant.
Then in 2018, Dr Mahathir Mohamad's new government scrapped the plan, citing a lack of expertise and worries over radioactive waste.

Now nuclear is back. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's 13th Malaysia Plan names it a viable clean power source, with implementation targeted from 2031, and Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Chang Lih Kang told Parliament last month that no decision on technology or construction will come until four key studies are completed within 12 months.
I can't help but feel we are about to study our way into another lost decade. We need nuclear more than ever, and here's why.
We are living on a diet of coal

While we dithered, coal took over. According to energy think tank Ember, coal's share of Malaysia's power generation rose from 6% in 2000 to 43% in 2024, and Reuters' analysis of grid data shows it supplied 58.6% of Peninsular Malaysia's electricity last year.
Most of it isn't even ours, with a record 36.3 million tonnes of thermal coal imported in 2025, about three-quarters of it from Indonesia.

We pay for it with our lungs and our climate. Oxford's Our World in Data project estimates coal kills nearly 25 people for every terawatt-hour of electricity it produces, and deputy prime minister Fadillah Yusof has said coal power accounts for nearly half of our national emissions.

We have rightly promised to retire coal by 2044, but here's the kicker: economy minister Akmal Nasrullah Nasir said in September that we expect to add about 9GW of gas-fired capacity, swapping one fossil fuel for another.

There's a cleaner swap, and it doesn't get any cleaner than nuclear. A 2021 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe study found nuclear had the lowest lifecycle emissions of any power source it studied, at 5.1 to 6.4 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour, against 751 to 1,095 grams for coal.
Sure, solar should still do the heavy lifting by day. But to replace coal we need something that runs at 3am every night of the year, whatever the weather, and nuclear does exactly that.
The fears don't survive the data
Many Malaysians hear "nuclear" and think of Chernobyl. Yet per unit of electricity, Our World in Data finds nuclear causes 99.8% fewer deaths than coal.

Even after Fukushima, the UN's scientific committee on radiation found that "no adverse health effects among Fukushima residents have been documented that could be directly attributed to radiation exposure".

The waste is smaller than most imagine too, with the US Department of Energy saying all the spent fuel America's commercial reactors have produced since the 1950s could fit on a single American football field, stacked less than 10 metres deep.
On expertise, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Mariano Grossi said in June that "there are many people in Malaysia who know nuclear technology and know what a nuclear reactor is".
So how do we get it right this time? Three things.
1. Set a decision date that outlives elections
Putrajaya should commit now to naming its reactor technology and first site within three months of the four studies landing, making the reports a starting gun rather than a resting place.
It should also give the programme its own act of Parliament, because a programme that takes more than a decade to deliver cannot be at the mercy of every new Cabinet.
2. Buy proven, and buy in a series

The United Arab Emirates shows what a first-timer can do. It began building its Barakah plant in July 2012, and today four identical Korean-designed reactors supply 25% of its electricity, with cost, time and labour falling by 40% between the first unit and the fourth.
We should do the same, ordering several identical units of a design already operating elsewhere rather than becoming any vendor's guinea pig.
3. Build the workforce now

Machang MP Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal says many nuclear engineering graduates from Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia now work in unrelated jobs, while Fadillah says quite a number of Malaysians work at French reactors.

MyPower, the agency coordinating the programme, should track these engineers down, and every cooperation deal we sign with France or the US should guarantee training places for Malaysians. Turkey, Wan Fayhsal notes, will switch on its first plant next year, 17 years after proposing it, so he is spot on: "Start today."

The little reactor in Bangi has been running since 1982, proof that Malaysians can be trusted with the atom. Every year we wait is another year of burning imported coal, so when the studies land, what Putrajaya needs is not another study but a date, a design and the courage to stick to both.

fd249d673f599e08: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.

Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.

But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.
54a49e0b84455d63: Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi's blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

I was genuinely surprised at how poorly the media covered the October 30 and Nov 6 sell-offs. Lazy, superficial discussions of that Thursday crash begged to be corrected last week — and so I did:

Rumors circulated that ~108 separate pods closed and unwound on Thursday in what is best described as “forced liquidations.” That might help explain the fastest $2.5 trillion wipeout on record. (Note we saw a somewhat less ugly selloff on the last trading day of October).

For those unfamiliar with the term “pod shops,” these are multi-manager, multi-strategy hedge funds that have hundreds of small, semi-autonomous trading teams – aka “pods” – on the same platform. Many of the best-known multi-strat funds run large amounts of capital: Millennium ($98B), Citadel ($77B), Point72 ($55.5B), Balyasny ($37B), Schonfeld Strategic Advisors ($23.5B), Hudson Bay Capital ($20B), etc. Add to that Viking and many other Tiger shops, and it all adds up to a rather sizeable amount of capital — close to half a trillion dollars.
It felt to me like the sell-off was driven by forced liquidations:

Last Thursday felt (at least to me) like many of these pods got caught in a crowded, systematic, long-leveraged growth equity trade. Think mega-cap growth, momentum, and tech names, especially AI/Semis.
The multi-strat shops are disciplined, mechanical, and formulaic. Any pod that hits a specific drawdown limit (~5% or 7.5%)4, it triggers a hard stop automatically.
When I refer to forced liquidation, this is precisely what I mean.

Start-up founders and entrepreneurs should pour all their time, effort, and money into their venture. You likely won’t have spare cash for a Treasury portfolio, much less retirement accounts. 4c492292819f51db: John Mead/Mirrorpix/Mirrorpix via Getty ImagesOn November 26 1976, a London-based punk band released a record that created shock waves around the world. While not the first punk single to be released (The Damned’s New Rose, Radio Birdman’s Burn my Eye EP, and I’m Stranded by the Saints were released a few weeks earlier), Anarchy in the UK, by the Sex Pistols set the tone and a high bar for what was to follow. With its snarling lyrics (“I am an antichrist”) and raw sound, the song blew a gaping hole in 1970s complacency. The Sex Pistols are often thought to be obnoxious anarchists who promoted chaos. But in many ways they were the opposite. Here are five ways they created a template for a more inclusive, more tolerant, and better balanced society that remains relevant in today’s uncertain world. 1. Social and political convention Like many parts of the developed world, Britain in the mid-1970s faced economic decline, industrial unrest and growing disillusionment with established institutions. Anarchy in the UK, followed by the band’s next single, God Save the Queen, released during Queen Elizabeth II’s Silver Jubilee in 1977, voiced the anger and alienation of many people while raising questions about national authority and identity. The Pistols opened a door for many young people, inviting them to challenge established regimes, and to say no. Their assertion that there was “no future” is also relevant today. 2. Style and fashion Alongside their strong influence on music, the Pistols heavily influenced style and fashion. It is sometimes claimed the Pistols were conceived as a vehicle for Vivienne Westwood’s iconic clothing, which included bondage wear. As well as wearing her clothes, the band also took their name from her shop SEX on Chelsea’s Kings Road in London. Westwood’s punk stylings encouraged others to create distinctive clothes and outfits from everyday and discarded items, including bin-bags and safety pins. Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren and Viviane Westwood outside Bow Street Magistrate Court, after being remanded on bail for fighting in 1977. Daily Mirror/Bill Kennedy/Mirrorpix/Mirrorpix via Getty Images Based on her work with the Sex Pistols, and their manager Malcolm McLaren, Westwood’s career as a fashion iconoclast continued until her death in 2022. Elsewhere, graphic designer Jamie Reid’s combination of “ransom note” typography and situationist style détournement has had a lasting effect on graphic art and design, while the filmic work of Julien Temple (who made the Sex Pistols 1980 film The Great Rock ‘n’ Roll Swindle) has heavily influenced the development of the rock biopic. 3. DIY One of the Pistols main influences was in the emergence of a DIY approach to music. This is perhaps epitomised in the Pistols infamous gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4 1976, which inspired attendees to form their own bands (famously: Joy Division, Buzzcocks and The Smiths). The Sex Pistols perform at the Lesser Free Trade Hall, Manchester, June 4 1976. Paul Welsh/Redferns via Getty Images. In this, the myth that the Pistols “couldn’t play” simply inspired the realisation that anyone could pick up a guitar and make a record. This DIY approach also involved the dissemination and promotion of music and the artists, through home-made fanzines, the precursor to the blogs and zines that proliferate today. 4. Gender and inclusivity The Pistols encouraged women to become musicians. Siouxsie Sioux was a member of the Pistols entourage, the Bromley Contingent, contributing to the chaos of the Sex Pistols’ infamous TV confrontation with Bill Grundy before founding the Banshees. Palmolive and Viv Albertine of the Slits were previously members of the (unrecorded) Flowers of Romance along with John Ritchie (aka Sid Vicious). Chrissie Hynde, who had worked at SEX, went on to form The Pretenders. Poly Styrene was inspired to form X-Ray Spex having seen an early Pistols gig in Hastings in 1975. The Pistols were central to a London punk scene that embraced and promoted diversity and difference at a time of racial tensions and intolerance. 5. Global influence The Pistols soon found fans across the world, including in many countries in the Soviet orbit, where their anti-establishment pronouncements found a resonance among disaffected youth. In Indonesia, the circulation of semi-legal cassette tapes, and the few music publications tolerated by President Suharto’s “New Order” ultimately inspired an anarcho punk scene typified by Bandung band Runtah. Thriving punk scenes have developed across the globe from Brazil to Japan, from Australia to the Arctic. 2a494ad604ec9734: In what sounds like an avian riff on The Wire, scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders in order to listen in on their interactions with fishing vessels across the world’s oceans, according to a study published on Wednesday in Science Advances.

The approach exposed a large number of so-called “unseen” vessels that did not have their location trackers switched on. Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship’s location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons—such as evading pirates—or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities.

The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming “bycatch” when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.

Unseen vessel activity “is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal,” said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a “powerful tool for improving risk assessment” by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map.

Scientists have previously attached audio recorders to birds, such as penguins, to better understand their vocalizations and behavior, and teams have also probed seabird-vessel interactions with bird-borne radar.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> Rutter and his colleagues were inspired to combine these approaches by attaching audio recorders to three seabird species—the northern gannet, Balearic shearwater, and Westland petrel—which all frequently interact with fishing vessels. The team tracked the movements of the birds with GPS, and then analyzed whether the audio overlapped with AIS data at the same time and location during recorded interactions.

The recordings showed that about 32 percent of the audio captured by seven gannets in the North Atlantic were from ships with their trackers off, while 12 percent of the audio captured by four shearwaters in the Mediterranean Sea were from unseen vessels. The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off.

Rutter noted that the shearwaters were likely often interacting with smaller Mediterranean fishing boats that are not legally required to keep trackers on. However, the gannets encountered larger commercial vessels that are obligated to keep trackers active. While the researchers made a very conservative estimate that these birds visited unseen vessels for about one-third of the total duration of their daily encounters (or, about 22 minutes out of 68 minutes), it may well exceed half of that time.

“The fact that we found at least one third, and probably more than one half, of the audio detections being unseen was pretty surprising,” Rutter said. “This is not the same thing as saying that half of vessels are unseen; it's half of the time that gannets go to vessels, those vessels are unseen.”

“There are multiple reasons this could be,” he continued. “It could be illegal disabling, but at the same time, it could be poor satellite reception. There are lots of reasons that AIS can be off, and we want to emphasize that illegal fishing is a possibility, but that is not actually what we're showing. It's showing that there's a lot we're not seeing.”

Seabirds are attracted to fishing vessels to feed on discarded catch, but many perish during these encounters after becoming tangled in lines or caught on baited hooks. Rutter and his colleagues hope that their study could help to prevent these deadly incidents, while also providing a new tool for monitoring unseen vessel activity.

While this approach could enable real-time vessel detection, the team urged “caution in the use of animals as a fisheries surveillance tool, lest fishers come to mistrust scientists and/or marine animals themselves,” according to the study.

Though environmental and commercial interests are often at odds, there is plenty of collaboration between fisheries and conservation scientists with the goal of sustainable and healthy long-term fish stock. Fisheries that adhere to regulations also have an interest in working with researchers to combat illegal activity by competitors.

In addition, these audio recordings offer a new way to eavesdrop on wild seabird behavior. For example, the petrel’s recordings captured distinct landing and takeoff sequences previously observed in albatrosses, opening a new avenue of research into the flight patterns of this species. The recordings also highlight how human activity has upended food webs, as seabirds have become dependent on fishing vessel waste as a major source of food.

“One of the advantages of this is that we can understand in a more unbiased way how much [seabirds] actually interact with vessels—every day, multiple times a day for all the species we looked at actually, which is crazy if you think about it,” Rutter said.
“They're going out every day and just visiting boats all the time, and that shows the impact that we have on them as humans is really changing their feeding ecology,” he concluded.

For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it. The international dimension Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both prior to and after Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need. Providing aid to Ukraine has continued for the past four years, despite disruptions caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process. The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased domestic arms production, outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, air defence. Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies have and continue to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war has hit the Ukrainian economy, economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens. Countries in Central Asia and the Middle East have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials. Targeting support In a conflict that is increasingly defined by attrition, it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of industrialized warfare and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own. Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has reached an equilibrium. In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting. For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict. The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent. Ukraine has focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws. The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that the West has flouted international norms for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South. Russia has put forward several narratives to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine. Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains in Africa and earning support among far-right European parties. Narrative campaigns, however, typically unfold over a long time frame. As both Ukraine and Russia seek immediate ways to boost morale and undermine their adversary, direct military operations abroad have become all the more significant.
