f82e2058d3bb9c30: Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.  Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way. Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages. “Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says Evelina Fedorenko, who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper. The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing. Parsing the linguistic mind Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere. “Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center. While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way. For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker? It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence. Where AI meets the brain Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing lens into the human mind. Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope. “Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach. Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input. Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages. A mental bridge between languages The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages. “We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.” Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication. What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko. In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language. But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out. In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko. De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.
da45b84cc5fd1d8d: President Donald Trump is among those who pushed to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Kevin Dietsch/Getty ImagesThe story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump, who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. Chip Somodevilla/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks. Another issue is moral hazard: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” Nvidia’s board has come under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted, then reinstated, its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct. In the runup to Huang’s return to Nvidia, the public debate had largely been centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight. The decision to reinstate him suggests that political pressure can interfere with companies’ hiring and firing for misconduct, and that powerful CEOs are above the normal corporate considerations that would lead to dismissal. The Nvidia case might set a precedent, as other CEOs and boards now know the playbook for getting away with misconduct. It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.” This article was updated on Nov. 23, 2026, to reflect Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. The reinstatement, announced Monday morning, is "effective immediately" and was based in part on "input from senior levels of the United States government" that assured the board members that "Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk."

362b561c4f5d2c55: The farmer-poet Wendell Berry once described a dystopian world where society is singularly directed toward “the objective” – a relentless drive for industrial extraction that leads to the destruction of nature and communities. The idea captured Berry’s concerns about the industrialization of agriculture and the expansion of natural resource extraction that became prominent across rural America in the latter decades of the 20th century. Over nine decades, Berry watched how agribusinesses’ and farm owners’ pursuit of productive efficiency and maximum profits led to machines and synthetic chemicals replacing human farm labor, and the replacement of diversified farms with monocropping and concentrated animal-feeding operations. Across the U.S., he saw small farms disappear, often consolidated into vast corporate businesses with absent owners. What gets lost in this pursuit of production and profit, he noted, are community, human dignity and flourishing, natural beauty and ecological well-being. People are the heart of rural towns, like Waubeka, Wis. Farm consolidation has shrunk many of America’s rural towns since the mid 1900s. AP Photo/Teresa Crawford As agriculture researchers and rural sociologists, we, like Berry, have seen how the industrialization of agriculture has changed the face of rural America and hollowed out its communities. Once-thriving main streets in rural towns have slowly lost their businesses, with fewer farm-related jobs to keep local residents in the area. Machine dealers and suppliers of farm input such as seeds, fertilizer and pesticides have disappeared. Local grocery stores have been replaced by gas station convenience stores. Schools have shrunk or consolidated with the population decline. Hospitals have closed. This “unsettling of America,” in Berry’s words, shows that the farm economy and the rural economy no longer rise and fall together. Rural communities continue to decline despite farm booms and busts. Losing farming’s rural economy multiplier effect Since the late 1940s, the number of farmers in the U.S. has plummeted by nearly 90%, falling from 5.9 million in 1948 to only 715,000 by 2025. During the same period, the agricultural workforce has shifted from mostly farm owners – about 78% – with a few hired hands in 1948 to one today where most of the work is done by farm laborers, about 68% of the workforce. This means profits from farming mainly flow to a small number of farm owners, while the people doing the farm work are paid much less. The loss of small, owner-operated farms, where a farm family could make a living, is one reason many rural communities have lost population over the past century. In prior eras, farming energized rural communities as money circulated in the rural economy, supporting rural businesses and populations – what is termed a “multiplier effect.” Today, local suppliers and services are harder to find, and farm profits instead flow to owners outside the community. Agriculture today resembles capital-intensive natural resource extraction, like mining, where a small number of very profitable businesses operate most acres in the county. Such farms employ few people at low wages, and profits accrue to distant landlords and investment firms. This shift further reinforces rural decline. The farm economy of the 21st century does little to create additional jobs in rural America. An analysis of 11 counties in Iowa found that every US$1 million of agricultural sales creates 2.4 total farm jobs and 1.6 spin-off jobs in other nonfarm businesses, for a total of four new jobs. By contrast, healthcare creates 10 new jobs and construction creates seven new jobs in all for every $1 million in sales. Both pay good wages, which keeps rural people from leaving and helps rural economies thrive. Both also create more spin-off jobs. In short, agriculture produces profits for the company, whereas healthcare and construction produce good-paying jobs for rural residents. More small farms can help communities thrive In the mid-1940s, the U.S. Senate commissioned two studies on the social impacts of economic concentration and corporate monopolies. In one, Walter Goldschmidt, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, described two agricultural communities in California, one with a few large farms and the other with numerous smaller farms. He evaluated the social qualities of each and found that the community with more small farms had a higher standard of living and quality of life than the community with a few large farms. The other study, overseen by Columbia sociology professor C. Wright Mills, compared urban manufacturing areas in the Midwest. It found that locations with many small companies had a more robust economic life, with higher socioeconomic well-being, than areas dominated by a few large firms. Many rural sociologists have tested these findings since then. One, a Cornell study led by rural sociologist Thomas Lyson, found a way to counter the effects of farm consolidation. Using U.S. Census of Agriculture and other county-level data, it found that communities with large-scale industrial-style farms that also had politically active populations and a high percentage of people running small, independent businesses tended to have higher levels of social well-being than those without. The effect of economic concentration Looking at the agriculture sector in 2026, it’s clear that policymakers have not listened to the concerns raised by Berry or the rural sociologists. According to the latest Census of Agriculture, America had fewer than 2 million farms in 2022. Fewer than 6% of those farms accounted for over three-quarters of all agricultural production. Farms are getting larger and more specialized. Economist Jim MacDonald documented that half of all cropland in 2017 was on farms with 1,445 acres, more than double the 650 acres in 1987. Half of all dairy farms had more than 1,300 cows in 2017, up from 80 in 1987. Half of all pig farms in 1987 marketed 1,200 pigs or more – the midpoint is currently over 50,000 pigs per year. The number of American farms fell while the size of those farms grew as consolidation became common across the country in the second half of the 20th century. USDA The supply chain is also shrinking, leaving farmers with fewer choices. Today, fewer companies control more of the markets where farmers buy their fertilizers and pesticides or sell their products, which means that farmers have less control over what they can raise or sell. For instance, just two companies accounted for 71.6% of the U.S. corn seed market in 2018-2022, and those same two companies accounted for 65.9% of the soybean seed market, according to USDA researchers. Twenty years earlier, the top two companies in those markets accounted for 47.2% of the corn seed market and 41.8% of the soybean seed market. When four or fewer firms control 40% or more of a market, farmers tend to pay more for seeds, fertilizer and pest control and receive less for their commodities, while consumers continue to face higher prices. Consolidation of land and commodity markets at the farm level often goes unnoticed and sometimes undocumented. University of Iowa economist Silvia Secchi describes how changes in the U.S. Census of Agriculture in 2002 and in 2017 “obfuscates the degree of consolidation” in the farm sector by allowing farms to report up to three or four farm operators. These changes have led to the official count of over 3 million farm operators, even though there are fewer than 2 million farms. By looking at the volume of sales, Secchi found that fewer than half of these 2 million farms produce commodities worth more than $1,000 annually. She contends that this way of counting farmers does a double disservice to small farm operators. First, it lumps disadvantaged farmers into a group that includes retired farmers and farmland owners who might be using their land as a tax write-off. Second, when the overall farm incomes are averaged, the inclusion of these small farmers make the large, high-value farmers appear to need more federal support. How to improve conditions in farm country Restoring the vibrant rural farm economy of the past may be unrealistic, but some policies could at least improve conditions. Devising new – and enforcing existing – antitrust laws to break up oligopolies and monopolies in the materials farms need, such as seeds and fertilizer, as well as in processing and trade could give farmers more choices about what to raise and where to sell it, while protecting consumers from high prices. Irrigated fields stretch for miles in many rural farming regions across the middle of America, including on Colorado’s eastern plains. Jim Wark /Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) Right-to-repair laws could help farmers gain more control over their expensive machinery. Farm subsidies could be directed to smaller farmers who produce food – many of whom were inspired by Berry to become farmers – rather than toward the largest farmers who produce a few commodities at a massive scale. And finally, policymakers can develop rural policies that actually invest in the rural environment and communities, rather than simply subsidizing commodities in ways that primarily benefit the corporate owners of vast areas of farmland. 41496c8a0956b93d: Tech stocks are on a bumpy ride, weighed down by the slump in Nvidia's shares. Liu Yanan/Xinhua via Getty ImagesAfter stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south. While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks. Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year. As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing. Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it. Here are some basic facts to guide your planning. Many Americans are saving on autopilot Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund, which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s important to first explain how these funds work. About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you. Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund. About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion. Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices: U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds. For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund, who expect to retire imminently. The idea of target-date funds is that you can put your retirement savings on autopilot, with the mix of stocks and bonds getting more conservative the older you get. Brano on Unsplash Tech volatility is forcing new questions That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia. In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers, Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4%. Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned. By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month. That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar. More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement plan on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility. Target-date funds have significant tech exposure Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit. But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold. And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies. By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500, according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings. In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly. Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund, with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a big impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix. And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips. Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average. What to check now if you own a target-date fund In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing. But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund. For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone. The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest. When markets are jumpy, savers should review the funds they hold and consider rebalancing toward lower risk if they’re close to retiring. Towfiqu Barbhuiya on Unsplash, CC BY But a saver still needs to check three things. First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year. Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk. Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests. What to do if you hold other funds About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly. For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do. Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund, and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times. Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target. Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each. None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. But the pattern can flip quickly: International stocks gained about 29% in 2025, far ahead of the S&P 500’s 16%. Align your savings to your timeline How much this month’s news matters depends on when you’ll need the money. If you’re decades from retirement, a downturn can work in your favor, because every paycheck contribution buys shares at lower prices. Keep contributing and capture your full employer match. My own research with a colleague has found that accounts on systematic investment plans akin to 401(k)s earned better market-adjusted returns than accounts funded with lump sums. If you’re within 5-10 years of retirement, the bigger danger is what planners call sequence-of-returns risk: A large loss right before or just after you start withdrawing can permanently shrink what your savings can support. A good defense is to hold several years of expected withdrawals in lower-risk assets, such as bonds or money market funds, so you’re never forced to sell stocks after a drop. For retirees, Morningstar’s Christine Benz suggests one to two years of withdrawals in cash and five to eight more in bonds. What not to do The costliest mistake is usually the most tempting: selling everything and waiting for the dust to settle. During the 2008-09 financial crisis, about 117,000 Fidelity 401(k) participants moved entirely out of stocks. Those who stayed out saw their balances grow just 2% by mid-2011, while those who kept some stock exposure saw balances rise 50% on average. Other moves to avoid include stopping your own 401(k) contributions, chasing whatever theme looks safe this month, and pulling money out early, which can mean taxes, penalties and a locked-in loss. Last, don’t hand the decision to a chatbot. It will likely give you sound general guidance, such as diversifying and not panic-selling, and that consensus advice is where AI is reliable. But it is weakest on high-stakes questions that turn on your own situation. cb733f0aea6c2643: Women in Niger face barriers accessing their rights in disputes over land, inheritance, and child custody
Originally published on Global Voices
Nigerien women gathered at an awareness-raising session on the fight against jihadism. Screenshot via France 24's YouTube channel. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In 2024, Niger had a population of over 27 million. However, according to the Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey (eJNS) conducted by the Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) and the Ministry of Justice, more than half experienced justice problems that year.

Overall, 61 percent of the population has experienced at least one issue accessing justice. And while men are more likely to report these problems (70 percent) than women (52 percent), this does not in any way mean women suffer fewer injustices. Instead, it underscores the fact that many women either do not recognize their challenges as justice problems or do not advocate for themselves. The survey results therefore indicate that while women need justice just as much as men, they face greater obstacles in obtaining it.

Long before reaching any courtroom, women face barriers not only within their families and communities, but also in the resolution of disputes, often over land, inheritance, and child custody. This survey also shows how the outcome of a dispute can ultimately shape a woman’s income, economic security, and ability to invest in her future.
Invisible problems

Within Niger, the gap between men and women’s rights is obvious. As 41 percent of women say they are unaware of their legal rights, women (38 percent) are more likely than men (34 percent) to drop an ongoing court case. What’s more, almost two-thirds (64 percent) of women also have no formal education, compared to 47 percent of men.

Domestic violence (DV) is the most pressing issue faced by women in Niger, far surpassing crime, neighbor conflicts, and land disputes, with 29 percent saying they have experienced some kind of intimate partner violence. Between 2022 and 2024, domestic violence jumped from the eighth most serious problem for the general population to the third. According to HiiL, this may signal a shift in attitude toward reporting such incidents.

Across different datasets, land disputes over field boundaries, inheritance, contested sales, and crop damage rank second (17 percent) behind crime (23 percent) among the most serious justice problems. In its October 2026 report, HiiL also found that land problems accounted for 23 percent of all recorded justice problems, with a severity score of 7.1.

For women in rural areas, where more than 80 percent of Nigeriens currently live, land provides food, income, and economic autonomy. However, traditional practices, family pressures, and systems where people farm land they do not own keep their access uncertain. HiiL thereby conducted a qualitative study in the Dosso and Tillabéri regions, ultimately producing a best-practice manual for justice practitioners.
Inheritance: A silent injustice

Nigerien statutory law grants women the right to own, use, and inherit land. However, in practice, customary and family rules often deny them what is rightfully theirs. In some areas, once married, women are thought to belong to their husbands’ families, precluding them from inheriting land from their birth families.

In its 2025 Annual Report, HiiL shares real-life stories, such as Saouda’s, exemplifying this reality. Widow and mother of five, Saouda lost access to her late husband’s land when his relatives claimed ownership, but successfully regained it after learning about her rights through an awareness-raising campaign.

This exclusion has a direct economic impact on those women. They not only lose inherited land, but also a source of income, food security, and the ability to invest in livestock, trade, or farm improvements.
Child custody

After a separation, divorce, or the death of a partner, family-made agreements often determine where the children live, who provides for them, and whether their mother can maintain a meaningful relationship with them. These decisions are often made out of court, where customary norms hold considerable sway.

In its report, HiiL highlighted this issue through Amina’s story. Detained following a custody battle over her children, Amina thought her only hope was her family. After being told she could not legally win custody after a divorce under Islam, she had no idea she had such rights.
In this region, customary rulings tend to favor male authority in family matters, with customary chiefs typically awarding custody to fathers on religious grounds.

In 2020, the General Report of the National Consultation on Justice found that women were underrepresented in the judiciary, accounting for just 39 of the 399 magistrates in late 2017. Although customary court hearings may be more welcoming for women, no women sit among the customary assessors, prompting the report to recommend their inclusion.
The social norm burden

For almost a third of women, preserving family relations is the main reason they do not turn to courts or customary authorities. Any woman who claims her share of inheritance or custody of her children could be seen as “causing problems” or dividing her family. Consequently, testimonies gathered across the country tell stories of women fearing they will damage their families’ honor and relatives advising them to stay silent, at the expense of their rights.

Economic constraints only add to their difficulties. Due to insufficient funds, about four percent of women say they did not take action even when they knew their rights were being violated. Financial dependence on their partner or family also limits their ability to pursue legal proceedings. Quoting an NGO official, HiiL shared:
Les femmes viennent souvent nous voir après avoir épuisé leurs maigres ressources. Elles sont alors coincées, incapables de poursuivre leurs quêtes de recherche de solution à leurs problèmes.
Caught in a bind and unable to pursue their search for solutions, women often come to us after exhausting their already limited resources.

About a quarter of women with justice problems choose not to act, believing that legal action will not lead to a fair outcome. Zara, a 25-year-old Nigerien woman unable to afford legal fees and forced to drop a domestic violence case, stated:

Même si je préfère aller devant le juge je ne pourrai pas car je n’ai pas les moyens. Je ne suis qu’une vendeuse d’eau fraîche et de Bissap, même si je sais que je peux aller devant le juge si mon mari ne me nourrit pas, je n’ai pas de quoi supporter les aller-retours et autres frais qu’on demande à la justice.

Even though I would prefer to take my case to court, I can’t afford it. I only sell chilled water and bissap [herbal drink]. While I may be entitled to go to court if my husband didn’t support me, I couldn’t afford the round trips and other legal fees.

Even when women know about their rights, they still tend to choose customary justice over formal justice. Although it is often biased and patriarchal, it is also faster, closer to home, and delivered in their native language. As such, 40 percent of women identify family as a source of support, compared to just 28 percent of men. Meanwhile, only four percent of women and six percent of men turn to formal courts.

According to data published in the daily newspaper Le Sahel in 2024, men (75 percent) take legal action more often than women (71 percent). While this gap may be modest, it nonetheless compounds other obstacles.
Solutions exist

Typically, Nigeriens will seek out informal pathways to settle disputes. In the 2024 Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey, direct negotiation (40 percent), family (33 percent), and customary or traditional authorities (24 percent) were the most commonly cited sources of help, far surpassing formal courts (five percent). HiiL subsequently recommended including these actors in the justice process by conferring full legal status on customary decisions or strengthening mediation and conciliation pathways.

Established under Law No. 2011-42, the National Agency for Legal and Judicial Assistance (ANAJJ) provides free consultations, information on rights, guidance, and legal aid for those in financial need. According to the 2025 statistics, 33,394 beneficiaries received legal assistance, including 8,489 women. Meanwhile, its regional offices awarded 3,747 legal aid grants, including 550 to women.

In December 2025, during the first National Week of Legal and Judicial Assistance for women and children, Minister of Justice Alio Daouda presented different figures. Such discrepancies — at odds with independent NGO and journalistic findings — mean that official administrative reports must be read with caution.

The ANAJJ covers all of the country’s eight regions, but leaves many rural areas underserved. That said, additional initiatives do exist, including those led by the Association of Women Lawyers of Niger, an organization that has offered women and children legal assistance for 35 years.

However, resolution remains a stumbling block. According to the 2024 Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey, 56 percent of justice problems remain unresolved, with 20 percent on hold and 36 percent dropped. Conversely, 72 percent of solutions achieved are considered fair. While taking action significantly improves the chance of resolution, the main challenge is no longer just access itself, but seeing cases through to their conclusion.
Justice for women

The issue is not just the existence of courts, but ensuring women know they have rights, understand how to enforce them, and can do so without fear of rejection from their family or community. Awareness of their rights should go hand in hand with the ability to exercise them and the support of religious and traditional leaders alike.

In rural areas, practical steps are being taken to make this a reality. Traditional, female, and religious leaders have all received training in women’s land rights. After a female leader called for access to a plot of land for her group, the village chief publicly committed to finding one. Radio and theater, in local languages, have also enabled some women to claim their rights. According to HiiL, the objective is not only to recognize their rights in legislation, but to create practical conditions for exercising them.

Achieving justice that truly meets Nigerien women’s needs requires several steps: legal information in local languages, legal clinics in rural areas, training for traditional and religious authorities, protection for women’s inheritance, support in land and family disputes, and the inclusion of women among customary assessors.

As long as land, inheritance, and child custody decisions are made behind closed doors, with no guarantee of fairness, a considerable number of Nigerien women will continue to lose not only their assets but also a significant proportion of their economic independence.

315fb775dc30231e: A new technique developed by MIT researchers could help engineers use artificial intelligence to streamline the design and innovation of analog integrated circuits, semiconductor chips that perform vital functions like communication and power management in electronic devices. In the future, this method could allow engineers to prototype faster, explore a wider range of chip designs, and discover new design schemes that might improve the performance and energy efficiency of robots, medical monitors, or industrial sensors. Designing analog integrated circuits that meet specific requirements is usually a cumbersome manual process due to the enormous number of possibilities. Frontier generative AI models have shown success in automating the process, but using these resource-intensive, cloud-hosted models could expose proprietary circuit design and semiconductor foundry data to malicious users. The MIT method, called Small LM Iterating on Circuits, or SLIC (pronounced “slick”), enables engineers to train a small language model to perform analog circuit design as well as or better than a frontier large language model (LLM).  This small model is inexpensive and efficient enough to run on a laptop. Because it’s trained and deployed locally, it can use a company’s circuit design data without raising privacy risks.  When compared to complementary baselines and open-weight frontier LLMs, a small model trained by SLIC more effectively generated designs that achieved the circuit objectives.  “We’ve provided an alternative option to automate analog circuit design. With our technique, engineers can train a small, locally deployable model, using their own confidential data, and then deploy it in their own environment to ensure their assets remain protected,” says Yan Xu, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student and lead author of a paper on this technique. She is joined on the paper by senior author Ruonan Han, a professor of EECS and a member of the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics; Zhengqi Gao PhD ’26; Wenjie Lu PhD ’18, a former MIT postdoc who is now a principal research scientist at Analog Devices, Inc.; Xin Zhang, a research manager at IBM Research; Duane S. Boning, the Clarence J. LeBel Professor in EECS and MIT vice provost for international activities; and others at IBM Research and Analog Devices. The research will be presented at the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  “Through some specialized training and area-specific research, we can use much smaller models that consume far fewer resources to achieve almost the same results as flagship models in analog circuit design,” says Han. “This opens many more possibilities in the design of complex chips, especially if we care about costs, data privacy, and customization.” Mimicking human learning Analog integrated circuits enable a device to interact with the physical world. For instance, these circuits boost incoming wireless signals in smartphones and process outputs from sensors that track a car’s engine temperature.  Real-world signals tend to be unpredictable, so engineers must balance a wide and complex array of targets and tradeoffs to maximize analog circuit performance. This has made the design problem especially challenging for AI models. “To design a circuit, engineers find a good starting point based on their intuition and then, drawing on their knowledge of circuit design, tune a few knobs toward the performance they want,” says Xu. “There is no universal way to solve every circuit design problem.” Even if a powerful, cloud-based model could design a circuit as well as a human, most companies would be reluctant to send their foundry-specific data to external AI service providers. With SLIC, the MIT researchers created a training method that teaches a smaller, less expensive, faster language model to design analog integrated circuits that meet user specifications.  The SLIC model uses a few billion parameters, making it several thousand times smaller than frontier models that use trillions of parameters and require enormous amounts of computational resources.  “We tried to mimic the behavior of how a human learns to design a circuit,” Xu says. They used a technique called multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where a model works through a multi-step task while adapting to environmental feedback.  When given an analog circuit optimization task, SLIC uses a large LLM to generate several demonstrations of the open source design process. Then SLIC then uses these demonstrations to guide the small model in mimicking this design process.  After the small model gains some initial knowledge about circuit design, SLIC lets it practice by tackling a new design problem on its own. The model makes an initial guess of the design parameters, performs simulations, evaluates the results, and iteratively refines the design using knowledge it gained about analog circuits. Once a design achieves the user’s goals, SLIC prioritizes additional marginal gains. This means the model keeps learning to make improvements that boost performance even when several designs meet the user-defined targets.  An interpretable process Importantly, because SLIC employs models that describe their reasoning using natural language, the user can understand the decisions it makes along the way. “Although the whole process is automated, the user can see what is going on inside the model. This could help the user gain some new ideas about circuit design, and it also adds a lot of confidence about the decision-making process,” Han says. An engineer could utilize SLIC by adapting the researchers’ trained model to their data using a fine-tuning process. Or they could employ the SLIC training process to build their own model with company data, allowing for more customization. “We are seeing an increasing demand for analog chips, but the speed of design has not kept up. This research is trying to bring new capabilities to AI to solve a problem that industry has been stuck on for decades,” Lu says. When the researchers tested SLIC’s ability to design a circuit that met desired performance metrics, their small model came close to matching the performance of the latest GPT model (GPT-6-Astra). It did this while using a fraction of the computational resources.  The researchers also found that the SLIC model maintained its performance when tackling previously unseen circuit structures and adapting to more advanced technology nodes (design and manufacturing rules) and real commercial processes. Because SLIC teaches a model the general chip design process, the system is not tied to any company. This makes it a more scalable approach that could be used by many organizations for a range of circuit applications. “The knowledge the model has gained about circuit design is universal in nature. That is the powerful aspect of this tool,” Han says. In the future, the researchers want to explore self-improving models that can independently learn to handle more diverse topologies and design targets. They also want to use SLIC to build a multi-agent framework, in which many small language models work on different parts of a complex circuit design task. “Yan’s work shows that a locally deployable model can learn transferable design behavior and iterate with a circuit simulator to improve a design, which could reduce repetitive manual tuning for engineers. This is the kind of work the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab makes possible. We see it as opening the door to more sophisticated custom design, including RF and microwave circuits, in the settings where industry actually works,” says Zhang. This research is funded, in part, by Analog Device, Inc., IBM, and the John L. Ocampo Endowment Fund of MACOM Technology Solutions.
18408ba5f27f7998: From Azrul Khalib

A medicine may be manufactured in Malaysia, packaged locally and supplied by a Malaysian company, yet still depend on a single factory overseas for a critical ingredient. If that factory shuts down or exports are disrupted, the local manufacturing line can also grind to a halt.

That is a vulnerability Malaysia cannot afford to overlook. We have invested billions of ringgit in hospitals, clinics, medical equipment and healthcare professionals. But the ability to deliver treatment ultimately depends on a less visible system: the supply chains that provide essential medicines.

Malaysia has a sizeable pharmaceutical industry, producing generic medicines, sterile preparations and other products while developing domestic human vaccine manufacturing capacity. But production is only one part of the chain. Manufacturers may still depend on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), chemical intermediates, excipients and specialised materials.

According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida), pharmaceutical imports totalled RM11.30 billion in 2023, compared with RM2.92 billion in exports. An earlier Mida assessment found that approximately 39% of medicines on the National Essential Medicines List were imported. These figures underline Malaysia's reliance on international pharmaceutical trade, although they do not in themselves reveal how concentrated the country's upstream suppliers are.

That is the question policymakers need to ask. A manufacturer might have two suppliers in different countries, only to discover that both buy a key ingredient from the same upstream producer. What looks diversified on a procurement spreadsheet may be a single point of failure in practice.

Medicines are also harder to substitute than many other imported goods. Finding an alternative producer of an API is not the same as being able to use it immediately. Supplier audits, product validation, changes to regulatory documentation and approvals can take months. In a prolonged disruption, those delays matter.

Malaysia's ageing population and growing burden of non-communicable diseases make the continuity of treatment especially important. People living with diabetes, hypertension or cardiovascular disease need regular medicines. Hospitals depend on antibiotics, anaesthetics and critical-care products. Unlike a consumer purchase, treatment cannot always be postponed until prices fall or shipments resume.

More recent geopolitical tensions, tariffs and volatility in energy and shipping costs underscore why the next disruption may come from outside the pharmaceutical sector altogether. Inexpensive generic medicines, often produced and distributed on narrow margins, can be particularly exposed when costs rise or deliveries become uncertain.

China and India supply around 80% of bulk synthetic APIs, starting materials and complex generic powders to this country. India is Malaysia's primary foreign source for generic drugs, supplying roughly 30% of Malaysia's generic medicine and supplier base. The Covid-19 crisis and the geopolitical crises in 2026 have repeatedly raised vulnerabilities and risks to Malaysia should these countries decide impose export restrictions to protect their local supply of critical medicines.
The answer is not to manufacture everything domestically.

Instead, the government should start with the National Essential Medicines List and identify products whose interruption would cause the greatest harm. For those medicines, it should map not only where finished products are imported from, but where their APIs and other critical inputs actually originate. The exercise should distinguish genuine alternative manufacturers from distributors that ultimately rely on the same source.

That assessment should guide selective action. Some products may justify targeted incentives for domestic production, technology transfer or public-private manufacturing partnerships. Others may be better protected by qualifying alternative suppliers, arranging longer-term purchasing commitments or developing complementary manufacturing capacity with Asean partners.

Malaysia's New Industrial Master Plan 2030 already identifies pharmaceuticals, biologics and APIs as industrial development priorities. The next step is to connect those ambitions with actual healthcare vulnerabilities, rather than treating additional factory capacity as an end in itself.

Procurement policies also need to recognise that the lowest price is not necessarily the lowest cost. For strategically important medicines, buyers should consider the reliability of suppliers, geographic concentration, backup production capacity and whether alternative API sources have already been qualified.

Savings on a contract mean little if a subsequent shortage interrupts treatment. For vulnerable medicines, purchasing authorities should also consider advance ordering, contingency arrangements and whether contracts leave room for qualified backup suppliers. Such measures may carry a cost, but that cost should be assessed against the consequences of disrupted care.

Regional cooperation could strengthen this approach. Asean countries need not duplicate every expensive facility. Coordinated regulatory work, complementary production networks and emergency stock-sharing could create more options when an international supply chain fails.
Stockpiles remain important, but warehouses are not a substitute for supply-chain visibility.

Malaysia needs a more integrated monitoring system linking healthcare facilities, manufacturers, wholesalers and logistics providers so that emerging shortages can be detected early. The National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency's medicine-shortage and discontinuation reporting requirements are a useful foundation, but information is most valuable when it enables timely action.

Pharmaceutical supply resilience should be embedded in Malaysia's national health security planning, including its National Action Plan for Health Security 2025–2030. Success should be measured in fewer shortages, faster recovery, more qualified alternative sources and uninterrupted treatment, not simply in the number of pharmaceutical factories built.

Malaysia does not need to eliminate every foreign dependency. It needs to know which dependencies are critical, which are dangerously concentrated and how to reduce the risks before a disruption makes them visible to patients.
Azrul Khalib is the CEO of Galen Centre for Health and Social Policy, a health think tank.

d7f1aa6d6e23a0d1: From Hisham Othman

Sadiq Asyraf argues that Pakatan Harapan is blaming the sea for its sinking ship. After Melaka, he says, its leaders pointed to machinery, candidates, turnout, and identity politics while avoiding the deeper problem facing PH.

He is right that PH has a problem. In particular, PKR which contested 10 seats and won none. A party that holds the premiership needs to do better in the Malay and mixed constituencies it is meant to reach.

But PH leaders have also named the larger force shaping those contests. Identity politics has long influenced how Malaysians vote. Many Malay voters remain wary of PH because of DAP’s place in the coalition. When Umno and PAS offer them a common candidate, PH has to compete against both parties’ existing support at once.

PH must examine its machinery and candidates because those are things it can improve. It should also be honest about how much ground it needs to gain. Even an excellent campaign in Melaka would have had to overcome a gap that existed before nominations.
Landslide came from votes BN and PN already had
In 2021, Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional contested against each other in Melaka. BN won 21 seats and PN two. PH won five.
This time, BN and PN backed one candidate in each constituency. Together, they won 24 of the 28 seats. PH retained four and lost one.
The combined BN and PN share of valid votes was 62.7% in 2021 and 63.2% this year. Their share was broadly stable. The change was that the two coalitions now stood on the same side.
Bukit Katil - the seat PH lost - makes the point. Adly Zahari won it in 2021 with 6,805 votes while his BN and PN opponents split 9,463 between them.

This year, Adly received 8,698 votes, but his share fell from 41.6% to 34.5%. With BN’s support, PAS candidate Ridzuan Sarif won 15,305 votes. The electorate had grown, and the combined opposition to Adly was now behind one candidate.
The BN-PN partnership deserves credit for bringing those voters together. Its strength in Melaka also came from support the two sides already had.

That does not mean PH can be complacent. Its statewide share fell from nearly 36% in 2021 to about 29% this year. The changing electorate, a different set of contests and PH’s decision to leave four seats to Bersatu make comparisons imperfect. The decline still deserves scrutiny.
Negeri Sembilan showed a related problem. PH won the largest share of the vote at 40.2%, yet fell from 17 seats to 11 after BN and PN agreed to divide the constituencies between them.

In both states, the way support is distributed matters. PH can win substantial numbers of votes and still struggle to turn them into seats when a larger opposing vote is concentrated behind one candidate.
The bargain moves north
The first hope for PH is that BN and PAS find a national agreement harder to reach than their arrangements in the south.

In Johor, PAS urged supporters to back BN where it had no candidate. In Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, the two sides divided the seats. PAS can now reasonably expect BN to return the favour in the north and on the east coast.

The old PN won 39 of the 40 parliamentary seats across Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu at GE15. Under an incumbency principle, BN would have to stand aside in most of them. That would be difficult for an Umno leadership seeking to reclaim Putrajaya.

Terengganu menteri besar Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar has indicated how PAS sees the negotiations at state level. He has said five seats held by Bersatu representatives could be discussed with BN. PAS holds the other 27 and would expect to defend them.

In Kelantan, BN could press its case for Gua Musang, where it won the Nenggiri state by-election. In Kedah and Perlis, constituencies won by Bersatu under the old PN banner may be contested in negotiations by Umno and Hamzah Zainudin’s Wawasan. Parliamentary and state seats will each have their own local demands.
Then there is the premiership. BN will want enough seats to claim it. PAS has its own ambitions, and Samsuri has rejected the idea that either side should act as a senior partner.

They could agree on seats before the election and decide who leads after the results. They could also fail to reach an agreement and contest separately. The outcome matters greatly to PH, but it will be decided by BN and PN.
A three-way fight is only an opening

At GE15, PH and its allies won 82 parliamentary seats, PN won 74 and BN won 30. Malay voters were divided between the latter two coalitions. After a hung parliament, PH formed a government with BN and parties from Sabah and Sarawak.

A three-way contest at GE16 could again help PH win seats where BN and PN divide the vote. But the conditions facing PH have changed. PKR is under pressure, while DAP has also lost ground in some places. DAP held all four of PH’s seats in Melaka, but its tally in Johor fell from 10 to six, and it failed to win any of the eight seats it contested in Sabah.
The 82 seats won in 2022 are, therefore, a target to defend. They are also 30 short of the 112 needed for a majority.

If PH falls substantially below that figure, even a split between BN and PN may not be enough to keep it in government. The two could contest against each other and still join forces afterwards. If PN emerges as the larger bloc, Samsuri or Hamzah could be among those considered for the premiership. If BN wins more seats, it could seek PN’s support for its own candidate. Parties in Sabah and Sarawak would again have an important say in assembling a majority.
PH’s most immediate task is, therefore, to recover its lost ground, defend as much of its 2022 tally as possible, and seek to remain the largest bloc.
The task facing PKR and DAP
PH has two ways to expand beyond its present support. One is to persuade more Malaysians to vote across established racial and party loyalties.

That happened to an extent in 2018. Anger over the cost of living, GST and 1MDB helped move voters away from BN. Dr Mahathir Mohamad also gave some Malay voters confidence that their interests would carry weight in a government that included DAP. Both helped make PH a viable choice.

A change on that scale by GE16 is possible, but PH cannot count on it. Young voters may bring new priorities, including wages, housing, and the cost of starting a family. Yet GE15 also showed that many young Malay voters were attracted to PN. Research has found that family and community can shape their political choices.

The second route is to add a strong Malay partner. Bersatu played that role in 2018, although it won only 13 parliamentary seats. By GE15, Bersatu and PAS were together in PN, which became the largest bloc drawing primarily on Malay support. PN still ended up outside the federal government.

Khairy Jamaluddin has suggested reviving a partnership along the lines of Barisan Alternatif, which once brought PKR, PAS and DAP together. PAS would bring a substantial Malay base to such an arrangement. But Abdul Hadi Awang has said he would only respond to the prospect of joining Anwar Ibrahim’s government once DAP was out. For now, that makes a reunion a distant prospect.
That leaves PH with work it can begin itself. DAP needs to retain the confidence of its supporters by showing progress on good governance, reforms, and the everyday concerns that brought them to PH.

PKR needs to rebuild its reach in Malay and mixed seats. That requires stronger local machinery, credible candidates chosen early and a clearer account of what the government has delivered. The “sakau” campaign may remind voters of the past, but they also need to hear what PKR intends to do next.

A practical Bumiputera agenda should speak to jobs, skills, business opportunities, and economic security. PKR must show that it can protect Malay interests, lead a multiracial coalition, and hold its ground when it disagrees with DAP. It also needs younger leaders with real responsibilities and a message that speaks to their generation.

There is still time before GE16 for PH to make that case. Whether BN and PAS can agree on northern seats will shape the contest. Whether PH is strong enough to take advantage of a split will depend on what PKR and DAP do with that time.
Hisham Othman is a FMT reader.
